    ρ^\hat{\rho}: Spearman corr. 0.95±0.010.95\pm 0.01

  • •

    A^F\hat{A}_{F}: Spearman corr. 0.79±0.060.79\pm 0.06 (lower due to ratio normalization)

Rankings for S^a​e\hat{S}_{ae}, χ^\hat{\chi}, and ρ^\hat{\rho} remain >0.90>0.90 at m=2048m=2048, while A^F\hat{A}_{F} is 0.76. Cross-dataset pairs (disjoint label spaces under the shared-output embedding) have Fisher ≈0\approx 0 by construction and are excluded from correlation analysis. Figure 1 shows how correlation improves with sketch dimension.

Wall-clock timing.

To demonstrate the practical speedup from linear-time estimation, we benchmark exact O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) computation against sketched O⁡(n)O(n) computation. Setup: 5 synthetic tasks, d=256d=256 (activation dimension), K=100K=100 (error dimension), m=4096m=4096 (sketch dimension), averaged over 3 seeds. Table 6 shows runtime scaling: The sketched estimator achieves 89×\times speedup at n=2000n=2000 samples/task with m=4096m=4096, with runtime scaling linearly in nn (vs. quadratically for exact computation). Smaller sketch dimensions yield larger speedups (e.g., 437×\times at m=1024m=1024) with slightly reduced accuracy. This makes head Fisher alignment practical at scale. Full-network sketching via structured projections is also linear in hidden sizes and sequence length (independent of parameter count; Appendix B.7); our LLM experiments instead use parameter-subsampled gradients across all layers for computational tractability, while head-level validation uses the kernel identity.

B.7 Full-Network FisherSketch via Structured Rademacher Projections

The head-layer sketching above extends naturally to full-network Fisher alignment by exploiting the per-layer Kronecker structure of gradients.

The computational challenge.

For a full network with LL layers and total parameters p=∑ℓ=1Ldℓ−1​dℓp=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}d_{\ell-1}d_{\ell}, naively computing r⊤​gr^{\top}g for a random Rademacher vector r∈{±1}pr\in\{\pm 1\}^{p} requires O⁡(p)O(p) operations per sample—intractable for modern LLMs with billions of parameters.

Structured projection.

Because the full gradient g=[a0⊗δ1;…;aL−1⊗δL]g=[a_{0}\otimes\delta_{1};\ldots;a_{L-1}\otimes\delta_{L}] is a concatenation of Kronecker products, we can factor the projection. For each layer ℓ\ell, generate independent Rademacher vectors:

rℓ(a)∈{±1}dℓ−1,rℓ(δ)∈{±1}dℓ.r_{\ell}^{(a)}\in\{\pm 1\}^{d_{\ell-1}},\quad r_{\ell}^{(\delta)}\in\{\pm 1\}^{d_{\ell}}.

The block of rr corresponding to layer ℓ\ell is implicitly rℓ=rℓ(a)⊗rℓ(δ)r_{\ell}=r_{\ell}^{(a)}\otimes r_{\ell}^{(\delta)}, and the projection becomes:

r⊤​g​(x)=∑ℓ=1L(rℓ(a)⊤​aℓ−1​(x))⋅(rℓ(δ)⊤​δℓ​(x)).r^{\top}g(x)=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}(r_{\ell}^{(a)\top}a_{\ell-1}(x))\cdot(r_{\ell}^{(\delta)\top}\delta_{\ell}(x)). (11)

This requires only O⁡(∑ℓ(dℓ−1+dℓ))O(\sum_{\ell}(d_{\ell-1}+d_{\ell})) operations—linear in hidden sizes, not in parameter count (with a linear factor in positions for shared-parameter layers). For a shared-parameter affine layer used at positions t∈{1,…,Sℓ}t\in\{1,\dots,S_{\ell}\}, the per-layer term becomes

(rℓ(a)⊗rℓ(δ))⊤​gℓ​(x)=∑t=1Sℓ(rℓ(a)⊤​aℓ−1,t​(x))​(rℓ(δ)⊤​δℓ,t​(x)),(r_{\ell}^{(a)}\otimes r_{\ell}^{(\delta)})^{\top}g_{\ell}(x)=\sum_{t=1}^{S_{\ell}}(r_{\ell}^{(a)\top}a_{\ell-1,t}(x))\,(r_{\ell}^{(\delta)\top}\delta_{\ell,t}(x)),

so the structured projection remains computable in time linear in hidden sizes and the number of positions.

Algorithm: Full FisherSketch.

For task kk with samples {xt}t=1nk\{x_{t}\}_{t=1}^{n_{k}}:

  1. 1.

    Sample mm pairs of structured Rademacher vectors (r(j),s(j))(r^{(j)},s^{(j)}) with per-layer factorization.

  2. 2.

    For each sample xtx_{t}: run forward pass to get {aℓ−1​(xt)}ℓ=1L\{a_{\ell-1}(x_{t})\}_{\ell=1}^{L}; run backward pass to get {δℓ​(xt)}ℓ=1L\{\delta_{\ell}(x_{t})\}_{\ell=1}^{L}.

  3. 3.

    Compute sketch features ψ(j)​(xt)=(r(j)⊤​g​(xt))​(s(j)⊤​g​(xt))\psi^{(j)}(x_{t})=(r^{(j)\top}g(x_{t}))(s^{(j)\top}g(x_{t})) using (11).

  4. 4.

    Average to get mean embedding μk=1nk​∑tψ⁡(xt)∈ℝm\mu_{k}=\frac{1}{n_{k}}\sum_{t}\psi(x_{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{m}.

Full-network Fisher alignment is then AFfull​(i,j)≈cos⁡(μi,μj)A_{F}^{\mathrm{full}}(i,j)\approx\cos(\mu_{i},\mu_{j}).

Complexity.

Per sample: O⁡(L⋅dmax⋅m)O(L\cdot d_{\max}\cdot m) for mm sketch dimensions. Per task: O⁡(nk⋅L⋅dmax⋅m)O(n_{k}\cdot L\cdot d_{\max}\cdot m). Cross-task alignment: O⁡(T2⋅m)O(T^{2}\cdot m). This is independent of parameter count pp (linear in hidden sizes and positions), enabling full-network Fisher at 70B scale.

Implementation note.

We present this structured-projection estimator for completeness; its per-sample cost is linear in layer widths. Our experiments use parameter-subsampled gradients across all layers for computational tractability; the structured-projection estimator provides a full-network sketching option.

Relation to exact theorem.

Full FisherSketch approximates the exact full-network Fisher alignment (Theorem O.18), just as head FisherSketch approximates head Fisher. The structured Rademacher projection preserves the polynomial kernel structure: 𝔼⁡[ψ⁡(x)​ψ​(x′)]=(g​(x)⊤​g​(x′))2=(u⊤​v)2\mathbb{E}[\psi(x)\psi(x^{\prime})]=(g(x)^{\top}g(x^{\prime}))^{2}=(u^{\top}v)^{2}, where u,vu,v are the depth-profile vectors from Definition O.15.

B.8 Fast FisherSketch via SRHT (Implementation Note)

For vocab-scale applications (K>105K>10^{5}), even the factored Random Maclaurin projection can become compute-limited: computing mm dot products of the form r⊤​er^{\top}e with r∈{±1}Kr\in\{\pm 1\}^{K} requires O⁡(m​K)O(mK) operations per sample. The Subsampled Randomized Hadamard Transform (SRHT) reduces this KK-side cost to O⁡(K​log⁡K+m)O(K\log K+m); if activations use dense projections, the total per-sample cost is O⁡(m​d+K​log⁡K+m)O(md+K\log K+m).

Key construction.

Walsh–Hadamard transforms are defined for lengths N=2pN=2^{p}. Let N:=2⌈log2⁡K⌉N:=2^{\lceil\log_{2}K\rceil} and HN∈{±1}N×NH_{N}\in\{\pm 1\}^{N\times N} be the (unnormalized) Walsh–Hadamard matrix. For e∈ℝKe\in\mathbb{R}^{K}, pad with zeros to e~∈ℝN\tilde{e}\in\mathbb{R}^{N}. Let D=diag⁡(s)D=\mathrm{diag}(s) with s∈{±1}Ns\in\{\pm 1\}^{N} i.i.d. Rademacher. For a fixed row index t∈[N]t\in[N], define r:=Ht,:⋅Dr:=H_{t,:}\cdot D. Then rr has i.i.d. Rademacher entries (each coordinate is a fixed ±1\pm 1 from HNH_{N} times an independent Rademacher sign from DD); in particular, the first KK coordinates are i.i.d. Rademacher and r⊤​e~=∑k=1Krk​ekr^{\top}\tilde{e}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}r_{k}e_{k}.

Fast projection.

Given indices t1,…,tm∈[N]t_{1},\ldots,t_{m}\in[N], all mm projections can be computed as:

  1. 1.

    Pad and sign flip: e~′←D⊙e~\tilde{e}^{\prime}\leftarrow D\odot\tilde{e} O⁡(N)O(N)

  2. 2.

    Compute Hadamard transform: u←HN​e~′u\leftarrow H_{N}\tilde{e}^{\prime} O⁡(N​log⁡N)O(N\log N)

  3. 3.

    Gather entries: {utj}j=1m\{u_{t_{j}}\}_{j=1}^{m} O⁡(m)O(m)

Total: O⁡(N​log⁡N+m)=O⁡(K​log⁡K+m)O(N\log N+m)=O(K\log K+m) (since N<2​KN<2K), instead of O⁡(m​K)O(mK) on the error side.

Memory reduction.

Dense Rademacher matrices require O⁡(m​K)O(mK) entries (about ∼\sim2 GB if stored as float32, or ∼\sim0.5 GB if stored as int8 signs). SRHT requires only O⁡(N)O(N) float32 signs for diagonal matrices (D,D′)(D,D^{\prime}) plus O⁡(m)O(m) integers for row indices; since N<2​KN<2K this is still O⁡(K)O(K). At K=128,256K=128{,}256 (so N=131,072N=131{,}072) and m=4096m=4096, this reduces memory to ∼\sim1 MB.

Unbiasedness.

The SRHT construction preserves the polynomial kernel property. For independent (D,t)(D,t) and (D′,t′)(D^{\prime},t^{\prime}), and zero-padded x~,y~∈ℝN\tilde{x},\tilde{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{N}:

𝔼D,D′,t,t′​[(r⊤​x~)​(r⊤​y~)​(r′⁣⊤​x~)​(r′⁣⊤​y~)]=(x⊤​y)2,\mathbb{E}_{D,D^{\prime},t,t^{\prime}}\big[(r^{\top}\tilde{x})(r^{\top}\tilde{y})(r^{\prime\top}\tilde{x})(r^{\prime\top}\tilde{y})\big]=(x^{\top}y)^{2},

exactly as with dense Rademacher. Thus the SRHT backend targets the same unnormalized product-kernel inner product in expectation; the reported Fisher alignment cosine is the corresponding normalized plug-in estimate.

Dependence across coordinates.

SRHT uses a shared (HN,D)(H_{N},D) and row subsampling, so the mm coordinates are not independent. Unbiasedness still holds, but variance constants can differ from the i.i.d. Rademacher case; we use the 1/m1/m scaling as a practical guide.

When to use SRHT.

SRHT is beneficial when m​KmK is large. For typical LLM settings (K≈128,000K\approx 128{,}000, m≈4096m\approx 4096), the theoretical complexity reduction is O(mK)/O(KlogK)≈255×O(mK)/O(K\log K)\approx 255\times, though empirical speedups depend on hardware (memory bandwidth, cache effects). For smaller vocabularies or moderate mm, dense Rademacher may be faster due to simpler cache patterns and better batching. Our implementation automatically selects based on dimension.

B.9 Fast SRHT Error Projections in PyTorch

For vocabulary-scale errors e∈ℝKe\in\mathbb{R}^{K}, FisherSketch uses an SRHT to avoid storing dense m×Km{\times}K Rademacher matrices. Let K~\tilde{K} be the next power of two ≥K\geq K and let HK~H_{\tilde{K}} denote the K~×K~\tilde{K}{\times}\tilde{K} Hadamard matrix. We sample sign vectors D,D′∈{±1}K~D,D^{\prime}\in\{\pm 1\}^{\tilde{K}} and index sets I,I′⊆[K~]I,I^{\prime}\subseteq[\tilde{K}] with |I|=|I′|=m|I|=|I^{\prime}|=m. Given a batch E∈ℝB×KE\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times K}, we pad to K~\tilde{K} and compute

U=HK~​((Epad)⊙D),U′=HK~​((Epad)⊙D′),U=H_{\tilde{K}}\bigl((E_{\mathrm{pad}})\odot D\bigr),\qquad U^{\prime}=H_{\tilde{K}}\bigl((E_{\mathrm{pad}})\odot D^{\prime}\bigr),

then return U[:,I]U_{[:,I]} and U′[:,I′]U^{\prime}_{[:,I^{\prime}]}. This gives O⁡(K~​log⁡K~+m)O(\tilde{K}\log\tilde{K}+m) cost per batch for the error-side projections.

Batched FWHT (vectorized butterfly).

PyTorch does not provide a native FWHT; we implement the Hadamard transform via an iterative butterfly that uses only reshape/slice/concatenate operations. This avoids Python recursion and runs efficiently on GPU:

B.10 Low-Precision Sign Storage for Fixed Projection Memory

Dense Rademacher projections for activations (and errors, when dense) are stored as int8 signs on GPU and cast on-the-fly to the compute dtype during matmul. This reduces persistent projection storage by 4×4\times compared to float32 while leaving the estimator unchanged.

B.11 Vocabulary-Scale Validation

We validate FisherSketch at vocabulary scale (K=128,256K=128{,}256) using Llama-3.1-8B on 100 domains constructed from eight HF datasets (Table 7). At this scale, storing the error second moment Γe\Gamma_{e} per task requires K2×4K^{2}\times 4 bytes ≈61\approx 61 GiB, so 100 tasks would require ∼\sim6.0 TiB. FisherSketch stores activation projections as dense int8 sign matrices: 2​d​m2dm entries (32 MiB for d=m=4096d{=}m{=}4096). In our PyTorch implementation these signs are cast to the compute dtype (bf16/fp16/fp32) on-the-fly for GEMM; this is an exact re-encoding of the same Rademacher {±1}\{\pm 1\} projections and yields indistinguishable transfer metrics versus storing the same signs in float32. For error projections we use SRHT, which stores only two sign vectors (D,D′)(D,D^{\prime}) and row indices (approximately 1 MB at K=128,256K{=}128{,}256, m=4096m{=}4096). During streaming, we maintain six float64 accumulators per task for split-sample estimation (192 KB per task), but the stored signature is just the float32 μ^a​e\hat{\mu}_{ae} vector (16 KB per task; 48 KB if μ^a,μ^e\hat{\mu}_{a},\hat{\mu}_{e} are also stored). Fixed projection memory is about 33 MiB; for retrieval, the FAISS index stores another copy of μ^a​e\hat{\mu}_{ae}. SRHT on activations can reduce fixed memory further. This is a ∼4.0×𝟏𝟎𝟔\mathbf{\sim 4.0\times 10^{6}} reduction in per-task storage (61 GiB →\rightarrow 16 KB); the working-memory reduction is ∼3.3×105\sim 3.3\times 10^{5} if counting the streaming state (192 KB per task). Accounting for the fixed projections, the total reduction for 100 tasks is ∼1.8×105\sim 1.8\times 10^{5}; with dense error projections, storing the two m×Km{\times}K sign matrices would require ≈1.0\approx 1.0 GiB fixed if stored as int8 (or ≈3.9\approx 3.9 GiB if stored as float32), and the total reduction would be ∼6×103\sim 6\times 10^{3} (or ∼1.6×103\sim 1.6\times 10^{3} for float32).

Datasets and domain construction.

We draw from eight HF datasets, using the train split and the specific text fields shown in Table 7. Each domain is a deterministic subsample; domain names follow the pattern family and family_i (12–13 slices per family), with a fixed seed per domain. We record dataset provenance and sample indices in domain_metadata.json; no fallback or synthetic data were used in the reported runs. We do not redistribute raw text, and dataset licenses follow the respective HF dataset cards.

Sampling and splits.

FisherSketch uses 500 samples per domain (m=4096m{=}4096), keeping texts with ≥100\geq 100 characters and truncating to max_seq_length×\times4. LoRA validation draws 300 texts per domain (200 train, 100 eval) using a separate data seed (default: seed+1); eval samples are disjoint from train by construction. Early stopping uses the source-domain eval split.

Disjointness and auditability.

Validation explicitly excludes the FisherSketch sample indices for each domain (recorded in domain_metadata.json), preventing overlap between sketching and LoRA train/eval data.

Candidate sampling and pair counts.

For each target, we sample 24 candidate sources uniformly from the other 99 domains (uniform protocol), giving 100×24=2400100\times 24=2400 off-diagonal pairs. We also sample a stratified set (3 sources per family across 8 families, filled to 24 if needed); we evaluate the union of uniform and stratified pairs. For the reported run this yields 4,188 unique off-diagonal pairs, plus 100 diagonal pairs for self-PPL. Top-1 and regret are computed within the uniform 24-candidate sets; correlation analyses use the union of evaluated pairs. Candidate sets and metadata are saved in candidate_sources_*.json and pair_sampling_metadata.json.

Transfer validation.

To verify that FisherSketch at K>105K{>}10^{5} produces meaningful alignment, we validate against actual LoRA transfer performance: for each source-target pair, we fine-tune a LoRA adapter on the source domain and evaluate perplexity on the target. The normalized transfer score measures what fraction of possible improvement (relative to self-training) the source provides in loss space (log PPL). On 4,188 off-diagonal pairs (100 domains), FisherSketch with SRHT error projections achieves 45.7% ±\pm 5.0 top-1 source selection (≈\approx10.9×\times random) with max regret 0.119 ±\pm 0.013 (mean ±\pm std over seeds 43–45), confirming that FisherSketch predicts cross-domain transfer at vocabulary scale where baseline methods cannot run.

Loss-space regret.

For completeness, Table 9 reports per-target regret in log-PPL units for the uniform 24-candidate protocol. These values are unnormalized and not comparable across targets; normalized-transfer regret in Table 1 remains the primary metric.

Appendix C Shared-Parameter Affine Layers: Convolutions and Token-Wise Transformer Projections

Many modern architectures reuse the same affine parameters across multiple positions within an example: convolution kernels are shared across spatial locations, and transformer projection matrices (e.g., WQ,WK,WV,WOW_{Q},W_{K},W_{V},W_{O}) and MLP matrices are shared across tokens. In this regime, the per-example gradient is a sum of outer products over positions rather than a single outer product. This section provides (i) an exact kernel identity for the shared-parameter gradient and (ii) an efficient factored sketch that generalizes FisherSketch. Table 10 gives additional exact-Fisher validation for shared-parameter layers. These results validate the shared-layer FisherSketch estimator itself; they do not assume the separable activation/error proxy that is specific to no-sharing heads. As an implementation check, the shared-layer kernel identity matched materialized per-example gradients to machine precision in the Q1 validation (mean absolute discrepancies at most 2×10−162\times 10^{-16} and maxima at most 6×10−166\times 10^{-16}).

Setup.

Fix a task distribution 𝒟k\mathcal{D}_{k} over examples (x,y)(x,y) and fix model parameters θ\theta. Consider a shared affine parameter matrix W∈ℝdout×dinW\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out}}\times d_{\mathrm{in}}} used at SS positions (possibly varying by example). For an example (x,y)(x,y), let at​(x)∈ℝdina_{t}(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{in}}} denote the input vector at position t∈{1,…,S}t\in\{1,\dots,S\}. Define

zt​(x)=W​at​(x)∈ℝdout.z_{t}(x)=W\,a_{t}(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out}}}.

Let δt​(x):=∇ztℓθ​(x,y)∈ℝdout\delta_{t}(x):=\nabla_{z_{t}}\ell_{\theta}(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out}}} be the backpropagated gradient with respect to the pre-activation ztz_{t}. Stack these as column matrices

A⁡(x):=[a1​(x),…,aS​(x)]∈ℝdin×S,Δ⁡(x):=[δ1​(x),…,δS​(x)]∈ℝdout×S.A(x):=[a_{1}(x),\dots,a_{S}(x)]\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{in}}\times S},\qquad\Delta(x):=[\delta_{1}(x),\dots,\delta_{S}(x)]\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out}}\times S}.

We focus on the per-example gradient with respect to WW and its induced Fisher block. If the shared affine map includes a bias term bb, we can augment each ata_{t} with a constant 11 and treat bb as an extra column of WW. All identities below then apply unchanged.

Lemma C.1 (Per-example gradient for a shared affine parameter).

The per-example gradient of ℓθ​(x,y)\ell_{\theta}(x,y) with respect to WW is

∇Wℓθ​(x,y)=∑t=1Sδt​(x)​at​(x)⊤=Δ⁡(x)​A​(x)⊤.\nabla_{W}\ell_{\theta}(x,y)=\sum_{t=1}^{S}\delta_{t}(x)\,a_{t}(x)^{\top}=\Delta(x)\,A(x)^{\top}. (12)

In vectorized form (where vec\mathrm{vec} stacks columns),

gW​(x,y):=vec⁡(∇Wℓθ​(x,y))=∑t=1Sat​(x)⊗δt​(x).g_{W}(x,y):=\mathrm{vec}(\nabla_{W}\ell_{\theta}(x,y))=\sum_{t=1}^{S}a_{t}(x)\otimes\delta_{t}(x). (13)
Proof.

For each position tt, zt=W​atz_{t}=Wa_{t} depends linearly on WW. For any entry (i,j)(i,j) of WW, ∂zt,i/∂Wi​j=at,j\partial z_{t,i}/\partial W_{ij}=a_{t,j}, whereas ∂zt,i′/∂Wi​j=0\partial z_{t,i^{\prime}}/\partial W_{ij}=0 for i′≠ii^{\prime}\neq i. Thus, by the chain rule, only the i′=ii^{\prime}=i term contributes, and

∂ℓ∂Wi​j=∑t=1S∑i′=1dout∂ℓ∂zt,i′​∂zt,i′∂Wi​j=∑t=1S∂ℓ∂zt,i​at,j=∑t=1Sδt,i​at,j.\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial W_{ij}}=\sum_{t=1}^{S}\sum_{i^{\prime}=1}^{d_{\mathrm{out}}}\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial z_{t,i^{\prime}}}\frac{\partial z_{t,i^{\prime}}}{\partial W_{ij}}=\sum_{t=1}^{S}\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial z_{t,i}}\,a_{t,j}=\sum_{t=1}^{S}\delta_{t,i}\,a_{t,j}.

This is exactly the (i,j)(i,j) entry of ∑tδt​at⊤=Δ​A⊤\sum_{t}\delta_{t}a_{t}^{\top}=\Delta A^{\top}. Vectorization uses the identity vec⁡(u​v⊤)=v⊗u\mathrm{vec}(uv^{\top})=v\otimes u, so vec⁡(δt​at⊤)=at⊗δt\mathrm{vec}(\delta_{t}a_{t}^{\top})=a_{t}\otimes\delta_{t}. Linearity then yields the sum. ∎

Lemma C.2 (Token/position Gram identity for gradient inner products).

Let gWg_{W} and gW′g_{W}^{\prime} be the vectorized shared-parameter gradients for two examples, corresponding to (A,Δ)(A,\Delta) and (A′,Δ′)(A^{\prime},\Delta^{\prime}) (possibly with different numbers of positions SS and S′S^{\prime}). Then

gW⊤​gW′\displaystyle g_{W}^{\top}g_{W}^{\prime} =∑t=1S∑s=1S′(at⊤​as′)​(δt⊤​δs′)\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{S}\sum_{s=1}^{S^{\prime}}\bigl(a_{t}^{\top}a_{s}^{\prime}\bigr)\,\bigl(\delta_{t}^{\top}\delta_{s}^{\prime}\bigr) (14)
=⟨A⊤​A′,Δ⊤​Δ′⟩F,\displaystyle=\langle A^{\top}A^{\prime},\;\Delta^{\top}\Delta^{\prime}\rangle_{F}, (15)

where ⟨X,Y⟩F:=tr⁡(X⊤​Y)\langle X,Y\rangle_{F}:=\mathrm{tr}(X^{\top}Y) is the Frobenius inner product.

Proof.

By Lemma C.1, gW=∑tat⊗δtg_{W}=\sum_{t}a_{t}\otimes\delta_{t} and gW′=∑sas′⊗δs′g_{W}^{\prime}=\sum_{s}a_{s}^{\prime}\otimes\delta_{s}^{\prime}. Using bilinearity and (u⊗v)⊤​(u′⊗v′)=(u⊤​u′)​(v⊤​v′)(u\otimes v)^{\top}(u^{\prime}\otimes v^{\prime})=(u^{\top}u^{\prime})(v^{\top}v^{\prime}), we obtain

gW⊤​gW′=∑t,s(at⊤​as′)​(δt⊤​δs′),g_{W}^{\top}g_{W}^{\prime}=\sum_{t,s}(a_{t}^{\top}a_{s}^{\prime})(\delta_{t}^{\top}\delta_{s}^{\prime}),

which is (14). Now note (A⊤​A′)t,s=at⊤​as′(A^{\top}A^{\prime})_{t,s}=a_{t}^{\top}a_{s}^{\prime} and (Δ⊤​Δ′)t,s=δt⊤​δs′(\Delta^{\top}\Delta^{\prime})_{t,s}=\delta_{t}^{\top}\delta_{s}^{\prime}. Therefore,

⟨A⊤​A′,Δ⊤​Δ′⟩F=∑t,s(A⊤​A′)t,s​(Δ⊤​Δ′)t,s=∑t,s(at⊤​as′)​(δt⊤​δs′),\langle A^{\top}A^{\prime},\Delta^{\top}\Delta^{\prime}\rangle_{F}=\sum_{t,s}(A^{\top}A^{\prime})_{t,s}(\Delta^{\top}\Delta^{\prime})_{t,s}=\sum_{t,s}(a_{t}^{\top}a_{s}^{\prime})(\delta_{t}^{\top}\delta_{s}^{\prime}),

which is (15). ∎

A shared-layer Fisher kernel.

Define the degree-2 polynomial kernel induced by the shared-parameter gradient:

kshare​((A,Δ),(A′,Δ′)):=(gW⊤​gW′)2=⟨A⊤​A′,Δ⊤​Δ′⟩F2.k_{\mathrm{share}}\bigl((A,\Delta),(A^{\prime},\Delta^{\prime})\bigr):=\bigl(g_{W}^{\top}g_{W}^{\prime}\bigr)^{2}=\langle A^{\top}A^{\prime},\Delta^{\top}\Delta^{\prime}\rangle_{F}^{2}. (16)

This kernel is positive semidefinite because it is the homogeneous polynomial kernel of degree 2 applied to the feature vector gWg_{W}.

Theorem C.3 (RKHS mean embedding view (shared parameters)).

Let Fk,W:=𝔼(x,y)∼𝒟k​[gW​(x,y)​gW​(x,y)⊤]F_{k,W}:=\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}_{k}}[g_{W}(x,y)g_{W}(x,y)^{\top}] be the empirical Fisher block associated with the shared parameter WW under task kk. Then for any tasks i,ji,j,

⟨Fi,W,Fj,W⟩F=𝔼(A,Δ)∼𝒟i,(A′,Δ′)∼𝒟j​[kshare​((A,Δ),(A′,Δ′))].\langle F_{i,W},F_{j,W}\rangle_{F}=\mathbb{E}_{(A,\Delta)\sim\mathcal{D}_{i},\ (A^{\prime},\Delta^{\prime})\sim\mathcal{D}_{j}}\Bigl[k_{\mathrm{share}}\bigl((A,\Delta),(A^{\prime},\Delta^{\prime})\bigr)\Bigr]. (17)

Equivalently, letting ℋshare\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{share}} denote the RKHS of ksharek_{\mathrm{share}} and μk,W∈ℋshare\mu_{k,W}\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{share}} its mean embedding,

⟨Fi,W,Fj,W⟩F=⟨μi,W,μj,W⟩ℋshare,AF,W​(i,j)=⟨μi,W,μj,W⟩‖μi,W‖​‖μj,W‖.\langle F_{i,W},F_{j,W}\rangle_{F}=\langle\mu_{i,W},\mu_{j,W}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{share}}},\qquad A_{F,W}(i,j)=\frac{\langle\mu_{i,W},\mu_{j,W}\rangle}{\|\mu_{i,W}\|\ \|\mu_{j,W}\|}. (18)
Proof.

By definition, Fk,W=𝔼⁡[gW​gW⊤]F_{k,W}=\mathbb{E}[g_{W}g_{W}^{\top}]. Using bilinearity and trace-cyclicity, and taking independent draws from tasks ii and jj,

⟨Fi,W,Fj,W⟩F=tr⁡(𝔼⁡[gW​gW⊤]​𝔼​[gW′​gW′⁣⊤])=𝔼⁡[tr⁡(gW​gW⊤​gW′​gW′⁣⊤)]=𝔼⁡[(gW⊤​gW′)2],\langle F_{i,W},F_{j,W}\rangle_{F}=\mathrm{tr}\Bigl(\mathbb{E}[g_{W}g_{W}^{\top}]\ \mathbb{E}[g_{W}^{\prime}g_{W}^{\prime\top}]\Bigr)=\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\mathrm{tr}(g_{W}g_{W}^{\top}g_{W}^{\prime}g_{W}^{\prime\top})\Bigr]=\mathbb{E}\bigl[(g_{W}^{\top}g_{W}^{\prime})^{2}\bigr],

where gWg_{W} and gW′g_{W}^{\prime} are independent draws from tasks ii and jj respectively. By Lemma C.2, (gW⊤​gW′)2=kshare​((A,Δ),(A′,Δ′))(g_{W}^{\top}g_{W}^{\prime})^{2}=k_{\mathrm{share}}\bigl((A,\Delta)\allowbreak,(A^{\prime},\Delta^{\prime})\bigr), proving the first identity. The RKHS statement follows from standard kernel mean embedding theory. ∎

SharedFisherSketch: an efficient factored sketch.

Although gWg_{W} (as a vector in ℝdin​dout\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{in}}d_{\mathrm{out}}}) can be very large, it admits a structured projection via Lemma C.1.

Proposition C.4 (Factored Random Maclaurin sketch for shared-parameter gradients).

Let ra,ra′∈{±1}dinr_{a},r_{a}^{\prime}\in\{\pm 1\}^{d_{\mathrm{in}}} and rδ,rδ′∈{±1}doutr_{\delta},r_{\delta}^{\prime}\in\{\pm 1\}^{d_{\mathrm{out}}} be independent Rademacher vectors. Define the scalar projection

s⁡(A,Δ,ra,rδ):=∑t=1S(ra⊤​at)​(rδ⊤​δt)=(ra⊗rδ)⊤​gW.s(A,\Delta;\,r_{a},r_{\delta}):=\sum_{t=1}^{S}(r_{a}^{\top}a_{t})(r_{\delta}^{\top}\delta_{t})=(r_{a}\otimes r_{\delta})^{\top}g_{W}. (19)

Define one sketch coordinate

ψ⁡(A,Δ):=s⁡(A,Δ,ra,rδ)⋅s⁡(A,Δ,ra′,rδ′).\psi(A,\Delta):=s(A,\Delta;\,r_{a},r_{\delta})\ \cdot\ s(A,\Delta;\,r_{a}^{\prime},r_{\delta}^{\prime}). (20)

Then for independent examples (A,Δ)(A,\Delta) and (A′,Δ′)(A^{\prime},\Delta^{\prime}),

𝔼⁡[ψ⁡(A,Δ)​ψ​(A′,Δ′)]=kshare​((A,Δ),(A′,Δ′))=(gW⊤​gW′)2.\mathbb{E}\bigl[\psi(A,\Delta)\psi(A^{\prime},\Delta^{\prime})\bigr]=k_{\mathrm{share}}\bigl((A,\Delta),(A^{\prime},\Delta^{\prime})\bigr)=(g_{W}^{\top}g_{W}^{\prime})^{2}. (21)

With mm i.i.d. coordinates ψ1,…,ψm\psi_{1},\dots,\psi_{m}, define

Ψm:=1m​[ψ1,…,ψm]∈ℝm.\Psi_{m}:=\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}[\psi_{1},\dots,\psi_{m}]\in\mathbb{R}^{m}.

Then the kernel estimator k^m=⟨Ψm​(A,Δ),Ψm​(A′,Δ′)⟩\hat{k}_{m}=\langle\Psi_{m}(A,\Delta),\Psi_{m}(A^{\prime},\Delta^{\prime})\rangle is unbiased for ksharek_{\mathrm{share}}.

Proof.

Fix (A,Δ)(A,\Delta) and (A′,Δ′)(A^{\prime},\Delta^{\prime}) and abbreviate g=gWg=g_{W}, g′=gW′g^{\prime}=g_{W}^{\prime}. Let r:=ra⊗rδr:=r_{a}\otimes r_{\delta} and r′:=ra′⊗rδ′r^{\prime}:=r_{a}^{\prime}\otimes r_{\delta}^{\prime}. By (19), ψ=(r⊤​g)​(r′⁣⊤​g)\psi=(r^{\top}g)(r^{\prime\top}g) and similarly ψ′=(r⊤​g′)​(r′⁣⊤​g′)\psi^{\prime}=(r^{\top}g^{\prime})(r^{\prime\top}g^{\prime}). Since (r,r′)(r,r^{\prime}) are independent and each has 𝔼⁡[r​r⊤]=I\mathbb{E}[rr^{\top}]=I,

𝔼⁡[ψ​ψ′]=𝔼r​[(r⊤​g)​(r⊤​g′)]​𝔼r′​[(r′⁣⊤​g)​(r′⁣⊤​g′)]=(g⊤​g′)​(g⊤​g′)=(g⊤​g′)2.\mathbb{E}[\psi\psi^{\prime}]=\mathbb{E}_{r}[(r^{\top}g)(r^{\top}g^{\prime})]\ \mathbb{E}_{r^{\prime}}[(r^{\prime\top}g)(r^{\prime\top}g^{\prime})]=(g^{\top}g^{\prime})\ (g^{\top}g^{\prime})=(g^{\top}g^{\prime})^{2}.

For r=ra⊗rδr=r_{a}\otimes r_{\delta} with independent Rademachers, 𝔼[ri​jri′​j′]=𝔼[ra,ira,i′]𝔼[rδ,jrδ,j′]=𝟏{i=i′}𝟏{j=j′}\mathbb{E}[r_{ij}r_{i^{\prime}j^{\prime}}]=\mathbb{E}[r_{a,i}r_{a,i^{\prime}}]\mathbb{E}[r_{\delta,j}r_{\delta,j^{\prime}}]=\mathbf{1}\{i=i^{\prime}\}\mathbf{1}\{j=j^{\prime}\}. Hence 𝔼⁡[r​r⊤]=I\mathbb{E}[rr^{\top}]=I. Finally, k^m\hat{k}_{m} is the average of mm i.i.d. unbiased coordinates, hence unbiased. ∎

Sketch variance and estimator caveats.

Unbiasedness uses only second moments, while the variance depends on higher moments and can be large for polynomial-kernel sketches. See standard analyses of Random Maclaurin features and TensorSketch for variance/accuracy tradeoffs (Kar and Karnick, 2012; Pham and Pagh, 2013); the shared-parameter sketch inherits the same behavior.

Computation and relation to the head.

Computing s⁡(A,Δ,ra,rδ)s(A,\Delta;r_{a},r_{\delta}) can be done without forming gWg_{W}: we first compute α:=ra⊤​A∈ℝS\alpha:=r_{a}^{\top}A\in\mathbb{R}^{S} and β:=rδ⊤​Δ∈ℝS\beta:=r_{\delta}^{\top}\Delta\in\mathbb{R}^{S}, then s=α⊤​βs=\alpha^{\top}\beta. This costs O⁡(S⁡(din+dout))O(S(d_{\mathrm{in}}+d_{\mathrm{out}})) per coordinate and is independent of the parameter count din​doutd_{\mathrm{in}}d_{\mathrm{out}}. When S=1S=1, so A=aA=a and Δ=δ\Delta=\delta, Proposition C.4 reduces exactly to the head-layer factored sketch (Proposition 5.1).

Appendix D Preliminaries (Detailed)

This appendix provides full definitions and derivations for Fisher information and linear CKA, expanding the condensed treatment in Section 2.

D.1 Fisher Information and Fisher Alignment

The Fisher information matrix is central to optimization and natural-gradient methods and is widely used in continual learning (Amari, 1998; Martens, 2020; Pascanu and Bengio, 2014; Kirkpatrick et al., 2017). For a given task kk, define the per-example gradient at θ\theta as

gθ(k)​(x,y):=∇θℓθ(k)​(x,y)∈ℝp.g_{\theta}^{(k)}(x,y):=\nabla_{\theta}\ell_{\theta}^{(k)}(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{p}.

We work with the data Fisher—also called the empirical Fisher in population form—defined as the uncentered second moment of per-example gradients under 𝒟k\mathcal{D}_{k}:

ℱk​(θ):=𝔼(x,y)∼𝒟k​[gθ(k)​(x,y)​gθ(k)​(x,y)⊤]∈ℝp×p.\mathcal{F}_{k}(\theta):=\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}_{k}}\big[g_{\theta}^{(k)}(x,y)\,g_{\theta}^{(k)}(x,y)^{\top}\big]\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times p}. (22)

This is the gradient outer product Fisher, standard in continual learning (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017); see Remark D.1 for Fisher variants. We assume ℱk​(θ)\mathcal{F}_{k}(\theta) exists and is positive semidefinite, and we additionally assume positive definiteness where convenient.

In practice, we approximate ℱk​(θ)\mathcal{F}_{k}(\theta) from nkn_{k} i.i.d. samples (xi(k),yi(k))∼𝒟k(x^{(k)}_{i},y^{(k)}_{i})\sim\mathcal{D}_{k} using the sample average:

ℱ^k:=1nk​∑i=1nkgθ(k)​(xi(k),yi(k))​gθ(k)​(xi(k),yi(k))⊤.\hat{\mathcal{F}}_{k}:=\frac{1}{n_{k}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{k}}g_{\theta}^{(k)}(x^{(k)}_{i},y^{(k)}_{i})\,g_{\theta}^{(k)}(x^{(k)}_{i},y^{(k)}_{i})^{\top}. (23)
Remark D.1 (Fisher variants).

Several Fisher definitions appear in the literature:

  • (i)

    True Fisher: ℱktrue(θ)=𝔼x∼𝒟k,x𝔼y∼pθ(⋅|x)[∇θlogpθ(y|x)∇θlogpθ(y|x)⊤]\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{true}}_{k}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}_{k,x}}\mathbb{E}_{y\sim p_{\theta}(\cdot|x)}[\nabla_{\theta}\log p_{\theta}(y|x)\nabla_{\theta}\log p_{\theta}(y|x)^{\top}], where 𝒟k,x\mathcal{D}_{k,x} is the input marginal of 𝒟k\mathcal{D}_{k};

  • (ii)

    Empirical Fisher (sample): ℱ^=1n∑i∇ℓi∇ℓi⊤\hat{\mathcal{F}}=\tfrac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\nabla\ell_{i}\nabla\ell_{i}^{\top}, averaging over data labels (Eq. (23));

  • (iii)

    Head Fisher: restricting to final-layer parameters only.

The empirical Fisher can be a poor approximation to the true Fisher in some settings (Kunstner et al., 2019). Our analysis uses the empirical Fisher on head parameters, which is standard in practice (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017). For an affine head (bias absorbed by augmenting aa with a constant), the gradient has Kronecker form ghead=a⊗eg^{\mathrm{head}}=a\otimes e. With column-major vectorization, vec⁡(e​a⊤)=a⊗e\mathrm{vec}(ea^{\top})=a\otimes e, where aa is the penultimate activation and e=p^−ye=\hat{p}-y with p^:=softmax⁡(W​a)\hat{p}:=\mathrm{softmax}(Wa) and yy a one-hot label.

To compare the Fisher geometry of two tasks, we use the cosine similarity defined in the main text (Eq. (1)). High Fisher alignment indicates that tasks ii and jj emphasize similar directions in parameter space. Low Fisher alignment indicates that the tasks are decoupled in the Fisher metric.

In practice, we estimate alignment A^F​(i,j)\hat{A}_{\mathrm{F}}(i,j) by replacing ℱi,ℱj\mathcal{F}_{i},\mathcal{F}_{j} in (1) with ℱ^i,ℱ^j\hat{\mathcal{F}}_{i},\hat{\mathcal{F}}_{j}.

Lemma D.2 (Expected squared gradient agreement).

Let (xi,yi)∼𝒟i(x_{i},y_{i})\sim\mathcal{D}_{i} and (xj,yj)∼𝒟j(x_{j},y_{j})\sim\mathcal{D}_{j} be independent draws. Define gi:=gθ(i)​(xi,yi)g_{i}:=g_{\theta}^{(i)}(x_{i},y_{i}) and gj:=gθ(j)​(xj,yj)g_{j}:=g_{\theta}^{(j)}(x_{j},y_{j}). Assume ‖ℱi‖F,‖ℱj‖F>0\|\mathcal{F}_{i}\|_{F},\|\mathcal{F}_{j}\|_{F}>0; otherwise set AF​(i,j):=0A_{\mathrm{F}}(i,j):=0. Define the transfer proxy

U⁡(i,j):=𝔼⁡[(gi⊤​gj)2].U(i,j):=\mathbb{E}\big[(g_{i}^{\top}g_{j})^{2}\big].

Then

U⁡(i,j)=⟨ℱi,ℱj⟩F.U(i,j)=\langle\mathcal{F}_{i},\mathcal{F}_{j}\rangle_{F}.

Normalizing yields

U⁡(i,j)‖ℱi‖F​‖ℱj‖F=AF​(i,j).\frac{U(i,j)}{\|\mathcal{F}_{i}\|_{F}\,\|\mathcal{F}_{j}\|_{F}}=A_{\mathrm{F}}(i,j).
Proof.

Using independence and tr⁡(A​B)=⟨A,B⟩F\mathrm{tr}(AB)=\langle A,B\rangle_{F},

𝔼⁡[(gi⊤​gj)2]=𝔼⁡[tr⁡(gi​gi⊤​gj​gj⊤)]=tr⁡(𝔼⁡[gi​gi⊤]​𝔼​[gj​gj⊤])=⟨ℱi,ℱj⟩F.\mathbb{E}\big[(g_{i}^{\top}g_{j})^{2}\big]=\mathbb{E}\big[\mathrm{tr}(g_{i}g_{i}^{\top}g_{j}g_{j}^{\top})\big]=\mathrm{tr}\!\left(\mathbb{E}[g_{i}g_{i}^{\top}]\,\mathbb{E}[g_{j}g_{j}^{\top}]\right)=\langle\mathcal{F}_{i},\mathcal{F}_{j}\rangle_{F}.

Dividing by ‖ℱi‖F​‖ℱj‖F\|\mathcal{F}_{i}\|_{F}\,\|\mathcal{F}_{j}\|_{F} gives the normalized alignment identity. ∎

Gradient-space kernel alignment.

It is useful to view Fisher matrices as Gram matrices of gradient features. Assuming nk>0n_{k}>0, define the gradient feature matrix for task kk as

Φk:=[gθ(k)​(x1(k),y1(k))⊤gθ(k)​(xnk(k),ynk(k))⊤]∈ℝnk×p.\Phi_{k}:=\begin{bmatrix}g_{\theta}^{(k)}(x^{(k)}_{1},y^{(k)}_{1})^{\top}\\ \vdots\\ g_{\theta}^{(k)}(x^{(k)}_{n_{k}},y^{(k)}_{n_{k}})^{\top}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{k}\times p}.

Then ℱ^k=1nk​Φk⊤​Φk\hat{\mathcal{F}}_{k}=\tfrac{1}{n_{k}}\Phi_{k}^{\top}\Phi_{k}. Since the cosine normalization cancels constant factors, Fisher alignment equals a kernel alignment between gradient Gram matrices:

A^F​(i,j)=⟨Φi⊤​Φi,Φj⊤​Φj⟩F‖Φi⊤​Φi‖F​‖Φj⊤​Φj‖F.\hat{A}_{\mathrm{F}}(i,j)=\frac{\langle\Phi_{i}^{\top}\Phi_{i},\Phi_{j}^{\top}\Phi_{j}\rangle_{F}}{\|\Phi_{i}^{\top}\Phi_{i}\|_{F}\,\|\Phi_{j}^{\top}\Phi_{j}\|_{F}}.

This is formally analogous to CKA, which we now detail for representation features.

D.2 Linear CKA for Representations

Linear CKA (Kornblith et al., 2019) extends kernel alignment (Cristianini et al., 2001; Cortes et al., 2012) to compare neural network representations. Let Zi∈ℝn×diZ_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{i}} and Zj∈ℝn×djZ_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{j}} be representation matrices with nn samples (rows) and di,djd_{i},d_{j} features (columns). We assume each column is sample-centered (zero empirical mean). Write Ki:=Zi​Zi⊤K_{i}:=Z_{i}Z_{i}^{\top} and Kj:=Zj​Zj⊤K_{j}:=Z_{j}Z_{j}^{\top} for the corresponding Gram matrices.

The linear CKA between ZiZ_{i} and ZjZ_{j} is defined as:

CKA​(Zi,Zj):=‖Zi⊤​Zj‖F2‖Zi⊤​Zi‖F​‖Zj⊤​Zj‖F\text{CKA}(Z_{i},Z_{j}):=\frac{\|Z_{i}^{\top}Z_{j}\|_{F}^{2}}{\|Z_{i}^{\top}Z_{i}\|_{F}\|Z_{j}^{\top}Z_{j}\|_{F}} (24)

We assume ‖Zi⊤​Zi‖F,‖Zj⊤​Zj‖F>0\|Z_{i}^{\top}Z_{i}\|_{F},\|Z_{j}^{\top}Z_{j}\|_{F}>0 so CKA is well-defined.

Linear CKA is invariant to orthogonal transformations and isotropic rescaling of the feature space. It is typically computed on paired data: the rows of ZiZ_{i} and ZjZ_{j} correspond to the same inputs x1,…,xnx_{1},\dots,x_{n} fed through two different networks, layers, or heads. SVCCA (Raghu et al., 2017b) (with PCA truncation) is invariant to orthogonal rotations and isotropic rescaling, but is not invariant to arbitrary invertible linear transforms in general because the PCA truncation can change the retained subspace. Plain CCA is invariant to invertible linear transforms on the full space. However, practical CCA/SVCCA pipelines (Morcos et al., 2018) can be sensitive to preprocessing choices. CKA is invariant to orthogonal rotations and isotropic rescaling without relying on a truncation step, making it popular for comparing representations across random initializations or architectures.

The key distinction we explore in the main text is between auto-covariance alignment (which governs Fisher geometry) and cross-covariance alignment (which CKA measures). This distinction is made precise in Section 3.

Appendix E Experimental Protocol Details

This appendix provides complete experimental details for the supplementary CIFAR-100 regime experiments and the synthetic overlap/similarity sweeps. The main paper FisherSketch experiments use ViT-B/16 for sketch accuracy and Llama-3.1-8B for vocab-scale transfer; full-network validation additionally includes Llama-3.1-70B (Appendix O.9).

E.1 Architectures and Training (Supplementary)

Supplementary CIFAR-100 regime experiments use torchvision ResNet-18 (He et al., 2016) (ImageNet-style stem: 7×77\times 7 conv, stride 2, maxpool; no CIFAR-specific stem) on CIFAR-100; synthetic overlap/similarity sweeps use small shared-backbone MLPs with randomly generated labels. Training uses SGD (momentum 0.9, weight decay 5×10−45\times 10^{-4} applied to all parameters, including biases and BatchNorm parameters) with PyTorch cosine annealing (CosineAnnealingLR with Tmax=epochsT_{\max}=\text{epochs}, ηmin=0\eta_{\min}=0, stepped once per epoch; no warmup or restarts); source models are trained for 100 epochs with learning rate 0.2 and batch size 1024, and transfer runs use 50 epochs with the same optimizer settings. Data augmentation uses random crop (32, padding 4) and random horizontal flip; test-time uses only normalization (mean (0.5071,0.4867,0.4408)(0.5071,0.4867,0.4408), std (0.2675,0.2565,0.2761)(0.2675,0.2565,0.2761)). For class-subset tasks, we filter CIFAR-100 to the specified 50 classes and remap labels to {0,…,49}\{0,\dots,49\} (25,000 train / 5,000 test; ≈\approx25 steps/epoch at batch size 1024). Linear-probe heads on frozen backbones are trained with SGD (learning rate 0.1, weight decay 1×10−41\times 10^{-4}, cosine annealing) for 100 epochs. For the supplementary CIFAR-100 regime experiments and synthetic overlap/similarity sweeps in this appendix, we use a single fixed seed (42) and do not average over seeds unless explicitly noted; multi-seed validations are called out in Table 11.

Random seeds and averaging.

Table 11 summarizes which experiments use multiple seeds and whether results are averaged.

E.2 Task Pairs, Overlap, and Similarity Sweeps

CIFAR-100 overlap tasks.

We define a fixed source task using classes 0–49 (50 classes). Target tasks are contiguous class ranges with controlled overlap: 0–49 (100% overlap, 50/50 shared), 13–62 (37/50 shared; 0.74 overlap), 25–74 (25/50 shared; 0.50 overlap), 38–87 (12/50 shared; 0.24 overlap), and 50–99 (0% overlap, disjoint). Overlap fraction is |𝒞src∩𝒞tgt|/50|\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{src}}\cap\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{tgt}}|/50. Class identities are preserved (no label permutation).

Synthetic similarity sweeps.

For class-count/overlap sweeps in the synthetic experiments, label overlap is defined by class-set overlap: overlap =1=1 uses identical labels, overlap =0=0 uses disjoint class halves, and intermediate overlap samples labels from the overlapping class ranges. Network similarity is controlled by linearly interpolating two random networks across all layers: Wl(2)←α​Wl(1)+(1−α)​Wl(2,rand)W^{(2)}_{l}\leftarrow\alpha W^{(1)}_{l}+(1-\alpha)W^{(2,\mathrm{rand})}_{l} with α∈{0,1/(N−1),…,1}\alpha\in\{0,1/(N{-}1),\dots,1\} (default N=100N{=}100). We do not renormalize weights after interpolation. Because we do not renormalize, interpolation scales weight norms by α2+(1−α)2\sqrt{\alpha^{2}+(1-\alpha)^{2}}, so α\alpha jointly controls similarity and scale.

E.3 Metric Computation

  • •

    CKA: Computed on centered penultimate-layer activations using the full CIFAR-100 test set (10,000 images) shared across models; optional deterministic subsampling is used only for fast runs.

  • •

    Scov​(Γe)S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Gamma_{e}): Error second-moment matrices Γe=1n​∑ei​ei⊤\Gamma_{e}=\frac{1}{n}\sum e_{i}e_{i}^{\top} computed on each task’s test split, where e=softmax​(W​a)−ye=\text{softmax}(Wa)-y (predictions minus one-hot labels, with masked softmax: logits set to −∞-\infty outside the task’s label block; Assumption F.1). Errors are embedded into the shared 100-class space via that shared-output embedding, so coordinates outside the block are zero; linear-probe runs use the trained probe head.

  • •

    Fisher alignment: Exact head Fisher via the kernel identity (Appendix A) is used only for head-level validation. The CIFAR-100 regime experiments report FA-CKA =CKA⋅Scov​(Γe)=\mathrm{CKA}\cdot S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Gamma_{e}) and the separable proxy Scov​(Σz)⋅Scov​(Γe)S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Sigma_{z})\cdot S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Gamma_{e}) instead, where Σz\Sigma_{z} is the centered covariance of penultimate activations (computed on the same test set as CKA).

E.4 Reported Correlations

For CIFAR-100 regime experiments, correlations (Pearson corr.) are computed across the five target tasks within each regime (five overlap levels). For synthetic similarity sweeps, correlations are computed across the sweep points (NN trials). Because NN is small in the CIFAR-100 regime, correlations are reported for completeness and interpreted qualitatively.

Appendix F Shared Output Space: Details

Assumption F.1 (Shared output space embedding).

Tasks ii and jj predict over a common KK-dimensional output space (e.g., CIFAR-100’s 100 classes), where each task uses only a subset of coordinates (classes). Let 𝒞k⊆{1,…,K}\mathcal{C}_{k}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,K\} be task kk’s label subset. Let Pk∈{0,1}K×|𝒞k|P_{k}\in\{0,1\}^{K\times|\mathcal{C}_{k}|} be the coordinate injection (it embeds subset coordinates into the shared KK-space). Let y~k∈ℝ|𝒞k|\tilde{y}_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{C}_{k}|} be the one-hot vector in the subset space (equivalently, y~k=Pk⊤​y\tilde{y}_{k}=P_{k}^{\top}y for a KK-way one-hot label yy). Given subset logits z~k∈ℝ|𝒞k|\tilde{z}_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{C}_{k}|}, let p~k=softmax⁡(z~k)\tilde{p}_{k}=\mathrm{softmax}(\tilde{z}_{k}) and e~k=p~k−y~k\tilde{e}_{k}=\tilde{p}_{k}-\tilde{y}_{k}. We embed the error as ek:=Pk​e~k∈ℝKe_{k}:=P_{k}\tilde{e}_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{K}. Equivalently, this corresponds to a shared KK-way head with logits set to −∞-\infty outside 𝒞k\mathcal{C}_{k}.

F.1 Setup

To compare error covariances Γe,i\Gamma_{e,i} and Γe,j\Gamma_{e,j} across tasks with different label vocabularies, we use a common coordinate system.

We assume each task kk predicts over its label subset 𝒞k⊆{1,…,K}\mathcal{C}_{k}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,K\}, either via a subset head or a shared KK-way head with masked softmax (logits set to −∞-\infty outside 𝒞k\mathcal{C}_{k}). If tasks use subset heads, we identify their head parameters with a shared KK-way matrix by zero-padding rows outside 𝒞k\mathcal{C}_{k}. Predictions still use the masked softmax, so gradients and errors live in the common coordinate system. We assume label identities are aligned across tasks in this shared coordinate system. To compare error covariances across tasks, we embed these predictions into a common KK-dimensional space via the injection PkP_{k} in Assumption F.1. The embedded error vector ek∈ℝKe_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{K} is zero in coordinates outside 𝒞k\mathcal{C}_{k}. This setup is standard when tasks are subsets of a larger taxonomy (e.g., CIFAR-100 has K=100K{=}100 classes and each task uses a subset). The disjoint-support implications below rely on masked softmax (logits set to −∞-\infty outside 𝒞k\mathcal{C}_{k}); with an unmasked KK-way softmax, probability mass can appear on non-task classes, so the errors need not be sparse.

F.2 Implications

Under this embedding:

⟨Γe,i,Γe,j⟩F=⟨Γe,i​[𝒞i​j],Γe,j​[𝒞i​j]⟩F,Scov​(Γe,i,Γe,j)=⟨Γe,i​[𝒞i​j],Γe,j​[𝒞i​j]⟩F‖Γe,i‖F​‖Γe,j‖F,\langle\Gamma_{e,i},\Gamma_{e,j}\rangle_{F}=\langle\Gamma_{e,i}[\mathcal{C}_{ij}],\Gamma_{e,j}[\mathcal{C}_{ij}]\rangle_{F},\qquad S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Gamma_{e,i},\Gamma_{e,j})=\frac{\langle\Gamma_{e,i}[\mathcal{C}_{ij}],\Gamma_{e,j}[\mathcal{C}_{ij}]\rangle_{F}}{\|\Gamma_{e,i}\|_{F}\|\Gamma_{e,j}\|_{F}}, (25)

where 𝒞i​j:=𝒞i∩𝒞j\mathcal{C}_{ij}:=\mathcal{C}_{i}\cap\mathcal{C}_{j} and Γe,k​[𝒞i​j]\Gamma_{e,k}[\mathcal{C}_{ij}] denotes the submatrix restricted to rows/columns in 𝒞i​j\mathcal{C}_{ij}. If ‖Γe,i‖F\|\Gamma_{e,i}\|_{F} or ‖Γe,j‖F\|\Gamma_{e,j}\|_{F} is zero, then ScovS_{\mathrm{cov}} is undefined (we ε\varepsilon-regularize in practice).

  • •

    Disjoint tasks (no shared classes, 𝒞i∩𝒞j=∅\mathcal{C}_{i}\cap\mathcal{C}_{j}=\emptyset): Error covariances have disjoint support, so ⟨Γe,i,Γe,j⟩F=0\langle\Gamma_{e,i},\Gamma_{e,j}\rangle_{F}=0 and Scov​(Γe,i,Γe,j)=0S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Gamma_{e,i},\Gamma_{e,j})=0 when the norms are nonzero.

  • •

    Partially overlapping tasks: The overlap-restricted inner product above governs Scov​(Γe,i,Γe,j)S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Gamma_{e,i},\Gamma_{e,j}). In a stylized toy model that ignores the simplex constraint 𝟏⊤​e=0\mathbf{1}^{\top}e=0, assume Γe,k=σk2​I𝒞k\Gamma_{e,k}=\sigma_{k}^{2}I_{\mathcal{C}_{k}},33 3 For softmax errors, 𝟏⊤​e=0\mathbf{1}^{\top}e=0 implies Γe,k​𝟏=0\Gamma_{e,k}\mathbf{1}=0 (rank at most |𝒞k|−1|\mathcal{C}_{k}|-1), so a realizable isotropic model on the task support is Γe,k∝I𝒞k−1|𝒞k|​𝟏𝟏⊤\Gamma_{e,k}\propto I_{\mathcal{C}_{k}}-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}_{k}|}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top}.

    Scov​(Γe,i,Γe,j)=|𝒞i​j||𝒞i|​|𝒞j|.S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Gamma_{e,i},\Gamma_{e,j})=\frac{|\mathcal{C}_{ij}|}{\sqrt{|\mathcal{C}_{i}|\,|\mathcal{C}_{j}|}}.
  • •

    Identical tasks: If Γe,i=c​Γe,j\Gamma_{e,i}=c\,\Gamma_{e,j} with c>0c>0, then Scov​(Γe,i,Γe,j)=1S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Gamma_{e,i},\Gamma_{e,j})=1.

Implementation sanity checks.

It is helpful to verify that (i) eke_{k} is zero outside 𝒞k\mathcal{C}_{k} under masked softmax (logits set to −∞-\infty outside 𝒞k\mathcal{C}_{k}), (ii) Eq. (25) holds numerically within floating-point tolerance, and (iii) Γe,k​𝟏≈0\Gamma_{e,k}\mathbf{1}\approx 0 for softmax errors.

This framework applies when tasks are subsets of a larger taxonomy with a fixed label alignment (e.g., selecting animal vs. vehicle classes from CIFAR-100). The resulting Scov​(Γe,i,Γe,j)S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Gamma_{e,i},\Gamma_{e,j}) depends on the chosen embedding. For different label vocabularies, any cross-task embedding is a modeling choice. For tasks with fundamentally different output spaces (e.g., classification vs. regression), error-covariance comparison requires an explicit embedding, while representation-only metrics remain agnostic to gradient compatibility.

Appendix G CKA–Fisher Gap Decomposition (Head Layer)

This appendix provides a self-contained deviation bound that relates empirical linear CKA (on a paired probe set) to population head Fisher alignment. The bound is primarily diagnostic: it separates (i) finite-sample CKA estimation error, (ii) CKA’s inherent cross-vs.-auto covariance mismatch, (iii) centering (mean) effects, (iv) error-geometry misalignment, and (v) activation–error dependence (i.e., Kronecker-factorization violation).

Theorem G.1 (CKA–Fisher deviation decomposition, head layer).

Fix a probe input distribution 𝒟0\mathcal{D}_{0} and two tasks indexed by ii and jj. Let a(i)​(x),a(j)​(x)∈ℝda^{(i)}(x),a^{(j)}(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{d} denote the head-input (penultimate) activations of the two models for an input xx. Let Zi,Zj∈ℝn×dZ_{i},Z_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} be the corresponding centered probe matrices evaluated on paired probe inputs xt∼𝒟0x_{t}\sim\mathcal{D}_{0}; row tt of ZiZ_{i} equals a(i)​(xt)−μ^ia^{(i)}(x_{t})-\hat{\mu}_{i} and row tt of ZjZ_{j} equals a(j)​(xt)−μ^ja^{(j)}(x_{t})-\hat{\mu}_{j}.

CKA terms.

Let CKA⁡(Zi,Zj)\mathrm{CKA}(Z_{i},Z_{j}) denote empirical linear CKA on this paired probe set. Define the population quantity and deviation

Scross​(Σi​j,Σi,Σj):=‖Σi​j‖F2‖Σi‖F​‖Σj‖F,γn:=|CKA⁡(Zi,Zj)−Scross​(Σi​j,Σi,Σj)|,S_{\mathrm{cross}}(\Sigma_{ij};\Sigma_{i},\Sigma_{j}):=\frac{\|\Sigma_{ij}\|_{F}^{2}}{\|\Sigma_{i}\|_{F}\,\|\Sigma_{j}\|_{F}},\qquad\gamma_{n}:=\bigl|\mathrm{CKA}(Z_{i},Z_{j})-S_{\mathrm{cross}}(\Sigma_{ij};\Sigma_{i},\Sigma_{j})\bigr|,

where Σi:=Covx∼𝒟0​[a(i)​(x)]\Sigma_{i}:=\mathrm{Cov}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}_{0}}[a^{(i)}(x)], Σj:=Covx∼𝒟0​[a(j)​(x)]\Sigma_{j}:=\mathrm{Cov}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}_{0}}[a^{(j)}(x)], and Σi​j:=Covx∼𝒟0​[a(i)​(x),a(j)​(x)]\Sigma_{ij}:=\mathrm{Cov}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}_{0}}[a^{(i)}(x),a^{(j)}(x)] (all covariances are centered).

Define the cross-vs-auto mismatch

κi​j:=|Scross​(Σi​j,Σi,Σj)−Scov​(Σi,Σj)|.\kappa_{ij}:=\bigl|S_{\mathrm{cross}}(\Sigma_{ij};\Sigma_{i},\Sigma_{j})-S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Sigma_{i},\Sigma_{j})\bigr|.

We estimate κi​j\kappa_{ij} using the Procrustes proxy κ^\hat{\kappa} in Appendix I.

Head Fisher terms.

For each task k∈{i,j}k\in\{i,j\}, let e(k)​(x,y)∈ℝKe^{(k)}(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{K} denote the backpropagated head error (i.e., the loss gradient with respect to logits). Define g(k)​(x,y):=vec⁡(∇Wℓ(k)​(x,y))=a(k)​(x)⊗e(k)​(x,y)g^{(k)}(x,y):=\mathrm{vec}(\nabla_{W}\ell^{(k)}(x,y))=a^{(k)}(x)\otimes e^{(k)}(x,y) (Lemma 4.1).44 4 The Kronecker order a⊗ea\otimes e matches our column-stacking vec\mathrm{vec} convention (so vec⁡(u​v⊤)=v⊗u\mathrm{vec}(uv^{\top})=v\otimes u). Using row-major vectorization swaps the Kronecker factors; all alignment scores are unchanged by this fixed permutation, but residuals such as δk\delta_{k} must be computed with the matching order. Define the head Fisher blocks

Σψ,k:=𝔼(x,y)∼𝒟k​[g(k)​(x,y)​g(k)​(x,y)⊤],AFhead​(i,j):=Scov​(Σψ,i,Σψ,j).\Sigma_{\psi,k}:=\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}_{k}}\!\big[g^{(k)}(x,y)\,g^{(k)}(x,y)^{\top}\big],\qquad A_{F}^{\mathrm{head}}(i,j):=S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Sigma_{\psi,i},\Sigma_{\psi,j}).

Also define activation and error second moments

Ma,k:=𝔼⁡[a(k)​a(k)⊤],Γe,k:=𝔼⁡[e(k)​e(k)⊤],μa,k:=𝔼⁡[a(k)],Σa,k:=Cov⁡(a(k)),M_{a,k}:=\mathbb{E}[a^{(k)}a^{(k)\top}],\quad\Gamma_{e,k}:=\mathbb{E}[e^{(k)}e^{(k)\top}],\quad\mu_{a,k}:=\mathbb{E}[a^{(k)}],\quad\Sigma_{a,k}:=\mathrm{Cov}(a^{(k)}),

(all expectations under 𝒟k\mathcal{D}_{k}). Define the diagnostics

δk:=‖Σψ,k−Ma,k⊗Γe,k‖F‖Σψ,k‖F,εe:=1−Scov​(Γe,i,Γe,j),εμ,k:=‖μa,k‖22‖Σa,k‖F.\delta_{k}:=\frac{\|\Sigma_{\psi,k}-M_{a,k}\otimes\Gamma_{e,k}\|_{F}}{\|\Sigma_{\psi,k}\|_{F}},\qquad\varepsilon_{e}:=1-S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Gamma_{e,i},\Gamma_{e,j}),\qquad\varepsilon_{\mu,k}:=\frac{\|\mu_{a,k}\|_{2}^{2}}{\|\Sigma_{a,k}\|_{F}}.

If a denominator is zero, we follow the paper-wide ε\varepsilon-regularized convention; in practice we set the corresponding ratio/alignment to 00.

Deviation bound under matched probe/task input marginals.

Assume the probe input marginal matches each task’s input marginal, 𝒟0=𝒟ix=𝒟jx\mathcal{D}_{0}=\mathcal{D}_{i}^{x}=\mathcal{D}_{j}^{x}, so that Σk=Σa,k\Sigma_{k}=\Sigma_{a,k} for k∈{i,j}k\in\{i,j\}. Then

|CKA⁡(Zi,Zj)−AFhead​(i,j)|≤γn+κi​j+2​(εμ,i+εμ,j)+εe+2​(δi+δj).\bigl|\mathrm{CKA}(Z_{i},Z_{j})-A_{F}^{\mathrm{head}}(i,j)\bigr|\leq\gamma_{n}+\kappa_{ij}+2(\varepsilon_{\mu,i}+\varepsilon_{\mu,j})+\varepsilon_{e}+2(\delta_{i}+\delta_{j}). (26)
Proof.

Define the (separable) proxy

Aproxy​(i,j):=Scov​(Ma,i,Ma,j)⋅Scov​(Γe,i,Γe,j)=Scov​(Ma,i⊗Γe,i,Ma,j⊗Γe,j),A_{\mathrm{proxy}}(i,j):=S_{\mathrm{cov}}(M_{a,i},M_{a,j})\cdot S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Gamma_{e,i},\Gamma_{e,j})=S_{\mathrm{cov}}(M_{a,i}\otimes\Gamma_{e,i},\,M_{a,j}\otimes\Gamma_{e,j}),

The last equality follows from ⟨A⊗B,C⊗D⟩F=⟨A,C⟩F​⟨B,D⟩F\langle A\otimes B,\,C\otimes D\rangle_{F}=\langle A,C\rangle_{F}\langle B,D\rangle_{F} and ‖A⊗B‖F=‖A‖F​‖B‖F\|A\otimes B\|_{F}=\|A\|_{F}\|B\|_{F}.

By adding and subtracting intermediate terms and applying the triangle inequality,

|CKA−AFhead|\displaystyle|\mathrm{CKA}-A_{F}^{\mathrm{head}}| ≤|CKA−Scross|+|Scross−Scov​(Σi,Σj)|\displaystyle\leq|\mathrm{CKA}-S_{\mathrm{cross}}|+|S_{\mathrm{cross}}-S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Sigma_{i},\Sigma_{j})|
+|Scov​(Σi,Σj)−Scov​(Ma,i,Ma,j)|+|Scov​(Ma,i,Ma,j)−Aproxy|\displaystyle\quad+|S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Sigma_{i},\Sigma_{j})-S_{\mathrm{cov}}(M_{a,i},M_{a,j})|+|S_{\mathrm{cov}}(M_{a,i},M_{a,j})-A_{\mathrm{proxy}}|
+|Aproxy−AFhead|.\displaystyle\quad+|A_{\mathrm{proxy}}-A_{F}^{\mathrm{head}}|.

The first two terms are γn\gamma_{n} and κi​j\kappa_{ij}, respectively.

For the third term, since Σi=Σa,i\Sigma_{i}=\Sigma_{a,i} and Σj=Σa,j\Sigma_{j}=\Sigma_{a,j} under the matched-marginal assumption, Lemma M.1 yields

|Scov​(Σi,Σj)−Scov​(Ma,i,Ma,j)|≤2​(εμ,i+εμ,j).|S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Sigma_{i},\Sigma_{j})-S_{\mathrm{cov}}(M_{a,i},M_{a,j})|\leq 2(\varepsilon_{\mu,i}+\varepsilon_{\mu,j}).

For the fourth term, write Aproxy=Scov​(Ma,i,Ma,j)⋅Scov​(Γe,i,Γe,j)A_{\mathrm{proxy}}=S_{\mathrm{cov}}(M_{a,i},M_{a,j})\cdot S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Gamma_{e,i},\Gamma_{e,j}). Since 0≤Scov​(Ma,i,Ma,j)≤10\leq S_{\mathrm{cov}}(M_{a,i},M_{a,j})\leq 1 for PSD matrices,

|Scov​(Ma,i,Ma,j)−Aproxy|=Scov​(Ma,i,Ma,j)​(1−Scov​(Γe,i,Γe,j))≤εe.|S_{\mathrm{cov}}(M_{a,i},M_{a,j})-A_{\mathrm{proxy}}|=S_{\mathrm{cov}}(M_{a,i},M_{a,j})\bigl(1-S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Gamma_{e,i},\Gamma_{e,j})\bigr)\leq\varepsilon_{e}.

Finally, write Σψ,k=Ma,k⊗Γe,k+Rk\Sigma_{\psi,k}=M_{a,k}\otimes\Gamma_{e,k}+R_{k} and note that δk=‖Rk‖F/‖Σψ,k‖F\delta_{k}=\|R_{k}\|_{F}/\|\Sigma_{\psi,k}\|_{F}. Apply Corollary L.2 with (Σi,Σj)=(Σψ,i,Σψ,j)(\Sigma_{i},\Sigma_{j})=(\Sigma_{\psi,i},\Sigma_{\psi,j}) and (Σi(0),Σj(0))=(Ma,i⊗Γe,i,Ma,j⊗Γe,j)(\Sigma_{i}^{(0)},\Sigma_{j}^{(0)})=(M_{a,i}\otimes\Gamma_{e,i},\,M_{a,j}\otimes\Gamma_{e,j}) to obtain

|Aproxy−AFhead​(i,j)|=|Scov​(Ma,i⊗Γe,i,Ma,j⊗Γe,j)−Scov​(Σψ,i,Σψ,j)|≤2​(δi+δj).|A_{\mathrm{proxy}}-A_{F}^{\mathrm{head}}(i,j)|=\bigl|S_{\mathrm{cov}}(M_{a,i}\otimes\Gamma_{e,i},\,M_{a,j}\otimes\Gamma_{e,j})-S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Sigma_{\psi,i},\Sigma_{\psi,j})\bigr|\leq 2(\delta_{i}+\delta_{j}).

Combining the bounds yields (26). ∎

Probe mismatch.

If the probe input marginal 𝒟0\mathcal{D}_{0} differs from the task input marginals 𝒟ix,𝒟jx\mathcal{D}_{i}^{x},\mathcal{D}_{j}^{x}, the only change is in the mean-correction step. Insert the additional term |Scov​(Σi,Σj)−Scov​(Σa,i,Σa,j)|\bigl|S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Sigma_{i},\Sigma_{j})-S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Sigma_{a,i},\Sigma_{a,j})\bigr| to account for replacing probe covariances by task covariances. The error term εe\varepsilon_{e} and coupling residuals δk\delta_{k} are often the dominant obstructions in many-class settings, explaining why CKA can decouple from head Fisher when label/error structures differ.

Estimating κi​j\kappa_{ij}.

When dd is moderate and we form explicit sample covariances, κi​j\kappa_{ij} can be estimated directly as |Scross​(Σ^i​j,Σ^i,Σ^j)−Scov​(Σ^i,Σ^j)|\big|S_{\mathrm{cross}}(\hat{\Sigma}_{ij};\hat{\Sigma}_{i},\hat{\Sigma}_{j})-S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\hat{\Sigma}_{i},\hat{\Sigma}_{j})\big|. For high-dimensional representations where it is undesirable to interpret Scov​(Σ^i,Σ^j)S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\hat{\Sigma}_{i},\hat{\Sigma}_{j}) in a fixed coordinate basis, we additionally report the rotation-invariant Procrustes diagnostic κ^\hat{\kappa} from Appendix I as a proxy for cross-vs.-auto mismatch.

Appendix H Relationship to K-FAC and Prior Work

This appendix clarifies how our work relates to prior work on Kronecker-factored approximations to the Fisher information matrix, particularly K-FAC (Martens and Grosse, 2015; Grosse and Martens, 2016). Subsequent work has extended K-FAC to recurrent networks, eigenbasis approximations, and distributed training (Martens et al., 2018; George et al., 2018; Ba et al., 2017).

H.1 What K-FAC Established

K-FAC (Kronecker-Factored Approximate Curvature; Martens and Grosse 2015) introduced a Kronecker-factored approximation of layer-wise Fisher information matrices for efficient second-order optimization. Key components include:

Exact gradient structure.

K-FAC observes that for layer ll with weight matrix WlW_{l}, the per-example gradient has an exact Kronecker structure:

vec⁡(∇Wlℓ)=al−1⊗δl\mathrm{vec}(\nabla_{W_{l}}\ell)=a_{l-1}\otimes\delta_{l}

Here al−1a_{l-1} is the layer input and δl\delta_{l} is the backpropagated error. This identity follows directly from the chain rule.

Independence approximation.

K-FAC’s central approximation is that activations and errors are approximately independent, yielding the approximation:

𝔼⁡[(a⊗δ)​(a⊗δ)⊤]≈𝔼⁡[a​a⊤]⊗𝔼⁡[δ​δ⊤]\mathbb{E}[(a\otimes\delta)(a\otimes\delta)^{\top}]\approx\mathbb{E}[aa^{\top}]\otimes\mathbb{E}[\delta\delta^{\top}]

This factorization enables efficient Fisher inversion (two small matrix inversions instead of one giant one).

Block-diagonal approximation.

K-FAC further approximates the full Fisher as block-diagonal across layers, ignoring cross-layer correlations.

H.2 Our Novel Contributions Beyond K-FAC

Our work builds on K-FAC’s structural insights but addresses a different question. K-FAC asks: “How can we efficiently approximate the natural gradient for optimization?” We ask: “Why do representation similarity metrics fail to predict gradient alignment?”

1. Error covariance alignment as the critical factor.

While K-FAC uses the approximation Σψ,k≈Ma,k⊗Γe,k\Sigma_{\psi,k}\approx M_{a,k}\otimes\Gamma_{e,k} (Lemma B.2) for computational efficiency, we identify error-covariance alignment Scov​(Γe,i,Γe,j)S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Gamma_{e,i},\Gamma_{e,j}) as the missing factor that explains why CKA can decouple from Fisher alignment. K-FAC does not study cross-task alignment or representation metrics.

2. Formal characterization of CKA’s limitation.

We prove that CKA (and all representation-only metrics) structurally cannot, in general, access error covariance information (Theorem 3.2). This is a fundamental limitation independent of any approximation quality.

3. Quantitative diagnostics for the CKA–Fisher gap.

Our analysis exposes measurable drivers of the gap, including the coupling correction ρ\rho (Theorem 4.2), the Kronecker residual δ\delta (Remark 4.4), and the coupling-misalignment term κ\kappa (Appendix I). K-FAC focuses on optimization convergence, not metric reliability.

4. Label structure dependence.

We show that Scov​(Γe,i,Γe,j)S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Gamma_{e,i},\Gamma_{e,j}) drops to zero for disjoint KK-class tasks under the shared output-space embedding (Appendix F), illustrating a failure mode for CKA when label structures differ. This is orthogonal to K-FAC’s optimization focus.

5. Practical estimator (FA-CKA).

FA-CKA provides a forward-pass-only estimator of head Fisher alignment without computing gradients or Fisher matrices. K-FAC requires gradient computation for natural gradient steps.

H.3 Independence Assumption: Our Analysis vs. K-FAC

K-FAC relies on approximate independence between activations and backpropagated errors (denoted δ\delta in H.1 and ee elsewhere in this paper). Under this assumption, Σψ,k=𝔼⁡[(a⊗e)​(a⊗e)⊤]≈Ma,k⊗Γe,k\Sigma_{\psi,k}=\mathbb{E}[(a\otimes e)(a\otimes e)^{\top}]\approx M_{a,k}\otimes\Gamma_{e,k} (Lemma B.2). Our analysis is unconditional: Theorem 4.2 is an exact identity for head Fisher alignment with no independence assumption.

In K-FAC:

Violating independence reduces optimization efficiency but does not fundamentally break the method; even with imperfect factorization, K-FAC can remain a reasonable preconditioner.

In our work:

Head Fisher alignment decomposes exactly as AFhead​(i,j)=Aproxy​(i,j)⋅ρi​jA_{\mathrm{F}}^{\mathrm{head}}(i,j)=A_{\mathrm{proxy}}(i,j)\cdot\rho_{ij} (Theorem 4.2). Here Aproxy:=Scov​(Ma)⋅Scov​(Γe)A_{\mathrm{proxy}}:=S_{\mathrm{cov}}(M_{a})\cdot S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Gamma_{e}), and ρi​j\rho_{ij} is defined when the denominator is nonzero. Independence implies ρi​j=1\rho_{ij}=1 (Corollary 4.3), but ρ≠1\rho\neq 1 does not invalidate the theory—it is simply a measurable correction. The Kronecker residual δ\delta yields a worst-case alignment bound (Appendix L); whether ρ≈1\rho\approx 1 is architecture-dependent (on ViT, ρ\rho varies from 0.35 to 1.11; see Appendix J).

Crucially, even with perfect independence (ρ=1\rho=1), CKA can fail when error covariances are misaligned (small Scov​(Γe,i,Γe,j)S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Gamma_{e,i},\Gamma_{e,j})), e.g., for disjoint label subsets under the shared output-space embedding (Appendix F).

H.4 Summary of Attribution

  • •

    Gradient Kronecker structure (Eq. (3)): Exact identity, noted by K-FAC (Martens and Grosse, 2015)

  • •

    Fisher independence factorization (Lemma B.2): K-FAC’s foundational approximation

  • •

    Error covariance alignment factor: Our contribution

  • •

    CKA limitation theorem (Theorem 3.2): Our contribution

  • •

    Quantitative diagnostics for the CKA–Fisher gap (ρ\rho, δ\delta, κ\kappa): Our contribution

  • •

    FA-CKA estimator: Our contribution

Appendix I Estimation and Diagnostic Experiments

This appendix provides implementation details for estimating the structural quantities in our theory and presents diagnostic experiments that validate the theory across different architectures.

I.1 Estimating Structural Quantities

Each term in our decomposition can be estimated from finite samples.

Representation misalignment (κ\kappa).

Define the population mismatch κi​j:=|Scross​(Σi​j,Σi,Σj)−Scov​(Σi,Σj)|.\kappa_{ij}:=\big|S_{\mathrm{cross}}(\Sigma_{ij};\Sigma_{i},\Sigma_{j})-S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Sigma_{i},\Sigma_{j})\big|. Direct estimator (when covariances are materialized). When the representation dimension dd is shared across models and we form explicit sample covariances, we estimate κi​j\kappa_{ij} directly via

κ^i​jdir:=|S^cross​(Σ^i​j,Σ^i,Σ^j)−Scov​(Σ^i,Σ^j)|,S^cross​(Σ^i​j,Σ^i,Σ^j):=‖Σ^i​j‖F2‖Σ^i‖F​‖Σ^j‖F.\hat{\kappa}^{\mathrm{dir}}_{ij}:=\Big|\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{cross}}(\hat{\Sigma}_{ij};\hat{\Sigma}_{i},\hat{\Sigma}_{j})-S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\hat{\Sigma}_{i},\hat{\Sigma}_{j})\Big|,\qquad\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{cross}}(\hat{\Sigma}_{ij};\hat{\Sigma}_{i},\hat{\Sigma}_{j}):=\frac{\|\hat{\Sigma}_{ij}\|_{F}^{2}}{\|\hat{\Sigma}_{i}\|_{F}\|\hat{\Sigma}_{j}\|_{F}}.

This is the plug-in estimator that matches the definition of κi​j\kappa_{ij}.

Rotation-invariant diagnostic (Procrustes proxy). For high-dimensional representations, it can be undesirable to interpret Scov​(Σ^i,Σ^j)S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\hat{\Sigma}_{i},\hat{\Sigma}_{j}) in a fixed coordinate basis. We therefore also report a rotation-invariant Procrustes diagnostic κ^\hat{\kappa}, computed from the regularized whitened cross-covariance (below). This κ^\hat{\kappa} is a proxy for cross- and auto-covariance mismatch rather than an unbiased estimator of κi​j\kappa_{ij}. Let Zi∈ℝni×dZ_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{i}\times d} and Zj∈ℝnj×dZ_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{j}\times d} be centered representations on probe inputs, with a shared feature dimension dd. Unless stated otherwise, we use the same probe set as CKA; if sample counts differ, we form a paired subset of size ni​jn_{ij} with matched inputs. Let Zi(i​j),Zj(i​j)∈ℝni​j×dZ_{i}^{(ij)},Z_{j}^{(ij)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{ij}\times d} denote those paired rows (in our experiments ni=nj=ni​jn_{i}=n_{j}=n_{ij}). Choose rsubr_{\mathrm{sub}} as the smallest rr such that the top-rr eigenvalues of both Σ^i\hat{\Sigma}_{i} and Σ^j\hat{\Sigma}_{j} explain at least 90% of the trace (equivalently, take the larger of the two 90% ranks). Define O⁡(rsub):={Q∈ℝrsub×rsub:Q⊤​Q=I}O(r_{\mathrm{sub}}):=\{Q\in\mathbb{R}^{r_{\mathrm{sub}}\times r_{\mathrm{sub}}}:Q^{\top}Q=I\}.

  1. 1.

    Compute sample covariances with regularization: Σ^i(λ)=Zi⊤​Zi/ni+λ​I\hat{\Sigma}_{i}^{(\lambda)}=Z_{i}^{\top}Z_{i}/n_{i}+\lambda I, Σ^j(λ)=Zj⊤​Zj/nj+λ​I\hat{\Sigma}_{j}^{(\lambda)}=Z_{j}^{\top}Z_{j}/n_{j}+\lambda I, Σ^i​j=(Zi(i​j))⊤​Zj(i​j)/ni​j\hat{\Sigma}_{ij}=(Z_{i}^{(ij)})^{\top}Z_{j}^{(ij)}/n_{ij}. We use λ≈10−6\lambda\approx 10^{-6} for numerical stability.

  2. 2.

    Compute eigendecompositions and extract the leading rsubr_{\mathrm{sub}}-dimensional subspace bases: take U^i,U^j∈ℝd×rsub\hat{U}_{i},\hat{U}_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r_{\mathrm{sub}}} from the top-rsubr_{\mathrm{sub}} eigenvectors of Σ^i\hat{\Sigma}_{i} and Σ^j\hat{\Sigma}_{j}.

  3. 3.

    Compute regularized whitened cross-covariance: C~^=(Σ^i(λ))−1/2Σ^i​j(Σ^j(λ))−1/2\hat{\tilde{C}}=(\hat{\Sigma}_{i}^{(\lambda)})^{-1/2}\hat{\Sigma}_{ij}(\hat{\Sigma}_{j}^{(\lambda)})^{-1/2}.

  4. 4.

    Project onto the shared subspace: C^r=U^i⊤​C~^​U^j\hat{C}_{r}=\hat{U}_{i}^{\top}\hat{\tilde{C}}\hat{U}_{j}.

  5. 5.

    Solve the orthogonal Procrustes problem Q⋆=arg⁡minQ∈O⁡(rsub)⁡‖C^r−Q‖FQ^{\star}=\arg\min_{Q\in O(r_{\mathrm{sub}})}\|\hat{C}_{r}-Q\|_{F} (via SVD). Define

    κ^​(i,j)=‖C^r−Q⋆‖Frsub.\hat{\kappa}(i,j)=\frac{\|\hat{C}_{r}-Q^{\star}\|_{F}}{\sqrt{r_{\mathrm{sub}}}}.

If the spectrum is simple, sign-aligning the eigenvectors yields Q⋆=IQ^{\star}=I, so κ^\hat{\kappa} reduces to ‖C^r−I‖F/rsub\|\hat{C}_{r}-I\|_{F}/\sqrt{r_{\mathrm{sub}}}. Because Q⋆Q^{\star} solves the Procrustes problem, κ^\hat{\kappa} depends only on the singular values of C^r\hat{C}_{r} and is invariant to orthogonal basis rotations within the chosen subspaces. Small κ^\hat{\kappa} indicates aligned coupling in the whitened cross-covariance. With the normalization above, uncorrelated representations (whitened cross-covariance near zero in the shared subspace) yield κ^≈1\hat{\kappa}\approx 1.

Kronecker independence violation (δ\delta).

For head gradients, we use the column-stacking vec\mathrm{vec} convention so g=a⊗eg=a\otimes e. With row-major vectorization, g=e⊗ag=e\otimes a and the Kronecker factors swap. We estimate the Kronecker approximation error per task kk by comparing the empirical gradient second moment Σ^ψ,k=1nk​∑igi​gi⊤\hat{\Sigma}_{\psi,k}=\frac{1}{n_{k}}\sum_{i}g_{i}g_{i}^{\top} to the Kronecker product M^a,k⊗Γ^e,k\hat{M}_{a,k}\otimes\hat{\Gamma}_{e,k} (with M^a,k=1nk​∑iai​ai⊤\hat{M}_{a,k}=\frac{1}{n_{k}}\sum_{i}a_{i}a_{i}^{\top}):

δ^k=‖Σ^ψ,k−M^a,k⊗Γ^e,k‖F‖Σ^ψ,k‖F.\hat{\delta}_{k}=\frac{\|\hat{\Sigma}_{\psi,k}-\hat{M}_{a,k}\otimes\hat{\Gamma}_{e,k}\|_{F}}{\|\hat{\Sigma}_{\psi,k}\|_{F}}.

We set δ^k:=0\hat{\delta}_{k}:=0 when ‖Σ^ψ,k‖F=0\|\hat{\Sigma}_{\psi,k}\|_{F}=0.

Block dominance (rr).

We compute layer-wise Fisher blocks ℱ^l​l\hat{\mathcal{F}}_{ll} and cross-layer blocks ℱ^l​m\hat{\mathcal{F}}_{lm} from gradient samples, then estimate

r^=∑l≠m‖ℱ^l​m‖F2∑l‖ℱ^l​l‖F2.\hat{r}=\sqrt{\frac{\sum_{l\neq m}\|\hat{\mathcal{F}}_{lm}\|_{F}^{2}}{\sum_{l}\|\hat{\mathcal{F}}_{ll}\|_{F}^{2}}}.

Error covariance alignment (Scov​(Γe)S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Gamma_{e})).

For KK-class classification, define the error vector e(k)=p^−𝟏y∈ℝKe^{(k)}=\hat{p}-\mathbf{1}_{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{K} and the error second moment Γe,k=𝔼⁡[e(k)​e(k)⊤]\Gamma_{e,k}=\mathbb{E}[e^{(k)}e^{(k)\top}], a K×KK\times K matrix. To estimate Γe\Gamma_{e}: (i) run forward passes on nn samples to obtain softmax outputs p^\hat{p} and targets yy; (ii) compute e=p^−𝟏ye=\hat{p}-\mathbf{1}_{y} per sample; (iii) estimate Γ^e=1n​∑iei​ei⊤\hat{\Gamma}_{e}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}e_{i}e_{i}^{\top}; and (iv) compute

Scov​(Γ^e,i,Γ^e,j)=⟨Γ^e,i,Γ^e,j⟩F‖Γ^e,i‖F​‖Γ^e,j‖F.S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\hat{\Gamma}_{e,i},\hat{\Gamma}_{e,j})=\frac{\langle\hat{\Gamma}_{e,i},\hat{\Gamma}_{e,j}\rangle_{F}}{\|\hat{\Gamma}_{e,i}\|_{F}\|\hat{\Gamma}_{e,j}\|_{F}}.

Computational cost is O⁡(n​K2)O(nK^{2}), tractable for ImageNet (K=1000K{=}1000) with n≈1000n\approx 1000 samples. We set Scov​(Γ^e,i,Γ^e,j):=0S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\hat{\Gamma}_{e,i},\hat{\Gamma}_{e,j}):=0 when ‖Γ^e,i‖F=0\|\hat{\Gamma}_{e,i}\|_{F}=0 or ‖Γ^e,j‖F=0\|\hat{\Gamma}_{e,j}\|_{F}=0. For very large KK, a diagonal proxy Scov​(diag⁡(Γe,i),diag⁡(Γe,j))S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\mathrm{diag}(\Gamma_{e,i}),\mathrm{diag}(\Gamma_{e,j})) provides a cheaper O⁡(n​K)O(nK) approximation, though it is not a general lower bound.

I.2 Diagnostic Experiments

Setup.

We evaluate feedforward networks of varying depth and width on classification tasks. We measure: (i) penultimate-layer CKA, (ii) empirical head Fisher alignment AℱheadA_{\mathcal{F}}^{\text{head}}, (iii) full-network Fisher alignment AℱfullA_{\mathcal{F}}^{\text{full}}, and (iv) the structural quantities κ\kappa (reported as κ^\hat{\kappa}), δ\delta, rr, and wheadw_{\mathrm{head}} (head dominance; see (44)).

CKA–Fisher correlation.

Across 30 task pairs with varying similarity, we observe strong correlation between CKA and full-network Fisher alignment (Pearson corr. =0.90=0.90, Fisher-z 95% CI [0.80,0.95][0.80,0.95]) and moderate correlation with head Fisher alignment (Pearson corr. =0.77=0.77, Fisher-z 95% CI [0.57,0.88][0.57,0.88]). The correlation between task similarity and CKA (Pearson corr. =0.86=0.86, Fisher-z 95% CI [0.72,0.93][0.72,0.93]) confirms that CKA captures meaningful task relationships. When the structural conditions in our theory degrade (e.g., larger κ^\hat{\kappa} or δ\delta, or weaker head dominance), the CKA–Fisher gap increases from a minimum of 0.04 to a maximum of 0.51.

Coupling strength validation.

We verify that κ^\hat{\kappa} tracks representation coupling: for highly similar networks κ^≈0\hat{\kappa}\approx 0 (strong coupling), while for uncorrelated representations κ^≈1\hat{\kappa}\approx 1 after normalization (weak coupling). Intermediate task similarities yield intermediate κ^\hat{\kappa} values as expected.

Block dominance across architectures.

We observe that block dominance rr varies dramatically with architecture:

  • •

    Shallow-wide (depth 1–2, width ≥32\geq 32): r≈0.2r\approx 0.2–0.50.5, whead≈0.94w_{\mathrm{head}}\approx 0.94–0.990.99.

  • •

    Deep networks (depth ≥3\geq 3): r>1r>1, whead<0.5w_{\mathrm{head}}<0.5.

These ranges suggest that head dominance (large wheadw_{\mathrm{head}}) holds reliably only for shallow-wide architectures; deeper networks require the full-network diagnostics in Appendix O.

I.3 Independence Violation Across Architectures

The Kronecker independence assumption (δ=0\delta=0) is violated across all architectures tested (δ≈0.34\delta\approx 0.34, Table 12). By Theorem 4.2, head Fisher alignment satisfies AFhead​(i,j)=Aproxy​(i,j)⋅ρi​jA_{\mathrm{F}}^{\mathrm{head}}(i,j)=A_{\mathrm{proxy}}(i,j)\cdot\rho_{ij} exactly, where ρi​j\rho_{ij} is the coupling correction.

This has two consequences:

  1. 1.

    Empirical validation: Head-level validation uses exact Fisher alignment via the kernel identity (Appendix A), while full-network LLM validation uses parameter-subsampled gradients across all layers for computational tractability.

  2. 2.

    Negative proxy rank correlation on ViT: On ViT-B/16 (n=40n=40 same-dataset pairs), Pearson Corr⁡(ρ^,Aproxy)=−0.85\mathrm{Corr}(\hat{\rho},A_{\mathrm{proxy}})=-0.85, and the proxy is negatively correlated with exact Fisher (Pearson corr. =−0.34=-0.34, Spearman corr. =−0.30=-0.30; Table 5), indicating an inverted ranking signal. FA-CKA succeeds (Pearson corr. =0.79=0.79, Spearman corr. =0.90=0.90) because it is validated against exact Fisher.

Architecture-dependent coupling.

Independence implies ρi​j=1\rho_{ij}=1 (Corollary 4.3), but ρ≠1\rho\neq 1 for both CNNs and transformers. The key difference is Pearson Corr⁡(ρ^,Aproxy)\mathrm{Corr}(\hat{\rho},A_{\mathrm{proxy}}): positive on ResNet (+0.88+0.88, n=75n=75) and negative on ViT (−0.85-0.85, n=40n=40). Consistent with this, the proxy correlates positively with exact Fisher on ResNet (Pearson corr. =0.98=0.98, Spearman corr. =0.69=0.69; n=75n=75) and negatively on ViT (Pearson corr. =−0.34=-0.34, Spearman corr. =−0.30=-0.30; n=40n=40; Table 5). FA-CKA works regardless because it is validated against exact Fisher, not the proxy.

Appendix J Empirical Distribution of Coupling Correction ρ^\hat{\rho}

We compute the empirical coupling correction

ρ^i​j:=AFexact​(i,j)Aproxy​(i,j),Aproxy​(i,j)=Scov​(Ma,i,Ma,j)⋅Scov​(Γe,i,Γe,j),\hat{\rho}_{ij}:=\frac{A_{\mathrm{F}}^{\mathrm{exact}}(i,j)}{A_{\mathrm{proxy}}(i,j)},\qquad A_{\mathrm{proxy}}(i,j)=S_{\mathrm{cov}}(M_{a,i},M_{a,j})\cdot S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Gamma_{e,i},\Gamma_{e,j}),

using exact head Fisher alignment AFexactA_{\mathrm{F}}^{\mathrm{exact}} (Appendix A), as a plug-in estimator of ρi​j\rho_{ij}. We retain pairs satisfying AFexact​(i,j)>εA_{\mathrm{F}}^{\mathrm{exact}}(i,j)>\varepsilon and Aproxy​(i,j)>εA_{\mathrm{proxy}}(i,j)>\varepsilon, using ε=10−6\varepsilon=10^{-6}. In our ViT/ResNet experiments, this filter keeps same-dataset pairs and excludes cross-dataset pairs under Assumption F.1. By Theorem 4.2, ρi​j=1\rho_{ij}=1 under independence. When coupling does not cancel, ρi​j\rho_{ij} deviates from 1; ρ^\hat{\rho} captures that deviation empirically.

For ResNet-50, we use five datasets, three seeds, and two training modes (fine-tuned and linear probe), yielding six tasks per dataset and 15 within-dataset task pairs (total n=75n=75).

Interpretation.

On ViT (n=40n=40), ρ^\hat{\rho} ranges from 0.35 to 1.11, and Pearson Corr⁡(ρ^,Aproxy)=−0.85\mathrm{Corr}(\hat{\rho},A_{\mathrm{proxy}})=-0.85. ρ^\hat{\rho} is not constrained to be at most 1; in our runs it reaches 1.11. Empirically, high-proxy pairs tend to have lower ρ^\hat{\rho}. Consistent with this, the proxy is negatively correlated with exact Fisher (Pearson corr. =−0.34=-0.34; Spearman corr. =−0.30=-0.30; Table 5). On ResNet-50 (n=75n=75), ρ^\hat{\rho} ranges from 0.15 to 0.99 and Pearson Corr⁡(ρ^,Aproxy)=+0.88\mathrm{Corr}(\hat{\rho},A_{\mathrm{proxy}})=+0.88. The proxy correlates positively with exact Fisher (Pearson corr. =+0.98=+0.98; Spearman corr. =+0.69=+0.69), indicating moderate rank agreement.

Why FA-CKA works despite ρ^\hat{\rho} variation.

FA-CKA (defined as CKA×Scov​(Γe)\mathrm{CKA}\times S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Gamma_{e})) correlates well with exact Fisher (Pearson corr. =0.79=0.79; Spearman corr. =0.90=0.90; n=40n=40; Table 5). By contrast, Aproxy=Scov​(Ma)×Scov​(Γe)A_{\mathrm{proxy}}=S_{\mathrm{cov}}(M_{a})\times S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Gamma_{e}) is negatively correlated (Pearson corr. =−0.34=-0.34). Since AFexact=Scov​(Ma)⋅Scov​(Γe)⋅ρ^A_{\mathrm{F}}^{\mathrm{exact}}=S_{\mathrm{cov}}(M_{a})\cdot S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Gamma_{e})\cdot\hat{\rho}, we can write

FA​-​CKA​(i,j)AFexact​(i,j)=CKA⁡(i,j)Scov​(Ma,i,Ma,j)⋅1ρ^i​j.\frac{\mathrm{FA\text{-}CKA}(i,j)}{A_{\mathrm{F}}^{\mathrm{exact}}(i,j)}=\frac{\mathrm{CKA}(i,j)}{S_{\mathrm{cov}}(M_{a,i},M_{a,j})}\cdot\frac{1}{\hat{\rho}_{ij}}.

Two factors explain this. First, on ViT, CKA differs from Scov​(Ma)S_{\mathrm{cov}}(M_{a}): centering contributes (Appendix M), and representation mismatch κi​j\kappa_{ij} can also drive the gap (Theorem G.1). Across same-dataset pairs (n=40n=40), the ratio CKA⁡(i,j)/Scov​(Ma,i,Ma,j)\mathrm{CKA}(i,j)/S_{\mathrm{cov}}(M_{a,i},M_{a,j}) averages about 2.28 and is strongly negatively correlated with 1/ρ^i​j1/\hat{\rho}_{ij} (Pearson corr. =−0.91=-0.91), which partially offsets coupling effects. Second, Scov​(Γe)S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Gamma_{e}) alone already correlates strongly with AFexactA_{F}^{\mathrm{exact}} (Pearson corr. =0.78=0.78; n=40n=40), suggesting that the Γe\Gamma_{e} component drives much of the signal. FA-CKA is validated empirically against exact Fisher, rather than justified solely by the ρ=1\rho=1 proxy assumption.

J.1 Proof of Remark 4.5: Proxy Approximation Bound

We prove that when the coupling tensor CkC_{k} is small relative to the rank-1 part, the separable proxy is guaranteed to be accurate.

Let xk:=μa​e,kx_{k}:=\mu_{ae,k}, uk:=μa,k⊗μe,ku_{k}:=\mu_{a,k}\otimes\mu_{e,k}, and vk:=Ckv_{k}:=C_{k}. Then xk=uk+vkx_{k}=u_{k}+v_{k}, where uku_{k} is the rank-1 component and vkv_{k} is the coupling residual. Define εk:=‖vk‖/‖uk‖\varepsilon_{k}:=\|v_{k}\|/\|u_{k}\|.

Lemma J.1 (Normalization perturbation).

If εk<1\varepsilon_{k}<1, then ‖x^k−u^k‖≤2​εk/(1−εk)\|\hat{x}_{k}-\hat{u}_{k}\|\leq 2\varepsilon_{k}/(1-\varepsilon_{k}), where z^:=z/‖z‖\hat{z}:=z/\|z\| denotes unit normalization.

Proof.

We have ‖xk‖=‖uk+vk‖≥‖uk‖−‖vk‖=(1−εk)​‖uk‖\|x_{k}\|=\|u_{k}+v_{k}\|\geq\|u_{k}\|-\|v_{k}\|=(1-\varepsilon_{k})\|u_{k}\|. Thus,

‖x^k−u^k‖\displaystyle\|\hat{x}_{k}-\hat{u}_{k}\| ≤‖vk‖xk‖‖+‖uk‖⋅|1‖xk‖−1‖uk‖|\displaystyle\leq\left\|\frac{v_{k}}{\|x_{k}\|}\right\|+\|u_{k}\|\cdot\left|\frac{1}{\|x_{k}\|}-\frac{1}{\|u_{k}\|}\right|
≤‖vk‖‖xk‖+‖uk‖⋅|‖xk‖−‖uk‖|‖xk‖​‖uk‖≤‖vk‖‖xk‖+‖vk‖‖xk‖=2​‖vk‖‖xk‖≤2​εk1−εk.\displaystyle\leq\frac{\|v_{k}\|}{\|x_{k}\|}+\frac{\|u_{k}\|\cdot|\|x_{k}\|-\|u_{k}\||}{\|x_{k}\|\|u_{k}\|}\leq\frac{\|v_{k}\|}{\|x_{k}\|}+\frac{\|v_{k}\|}{\|x_{k}\|}=\frac{2\|v_{k}\|}{\|x_{k}\|}\leq\frac{2\varepsilon_{k}}{1-\varepsilon_{k}}.

∎

Lemma J.2 (Cosine perturbation).

If ‖x^i−u^i‖≤ηi\|\hat{x}_{i}-\hat{u}_{i}\|\leq\eta_{i} and ‖x^j−u^j‖≤ηj\|\hat{x}_{j}-\hat{u}_{j}\|\leq\eta_{j}, then for any (i,j)(i,j), |⟨x^i,x^j⟩−⟨u^i,u^j⟩|≤ηi+ηj+ηi​ηj|\langle\hat{x}_{i},\hat{x}_{j}\rangle-\langle\hat{u}_{i},\hat{u}_{j}\rangle|\leq\eta_{i}+\eta_{j}+\eta_{i}\eta_{j}.

Proof.

Write x^i=u^i+δi\hat{x}_{i}=\hat{u}_{i}+\delta_{i} with ‖δi‖≤ηi\|\delta_{i}\|\leq\eta_{i}. Expanding the inner product yields

⟨x^i,x^j⟩=⟨u^i+δi,u^j+δj⟩=⟨u^i,u^j⟩+⟨δi,u^j⟩+⟨u^i,δj⟩+⟨δi,δj⟩.\langle\hat{x}_{i},\hat{x}_{j}\rangle=\langle\hat{u}_{i}+\delta_{i},\hat{u}_{j}+\delta_{j}\rangle=\langle\hat{u}_{i},\hat{u}_{j}\rangle+\langle\delta_{i},\hat{u}_{j}\rangle+\langle\hat{u}_{i},\delta_{j}\rangle+\langle\delta_{i},\delta_{j}\rangle.

By Cauchy-Schwarz, |⟨δi,u^j⟩|≤ηi|\langle\delta_{i},\hat{u}_{j}\rangle|\leq\eta_{i}, |⟨u^i,δj⟩|≤ηj|\langle\hat{u}_{i},\delta_{j}\rangle|\leq\eta_{j}, |⟨δi,δj⟩|≤ηi​ηj|\langle\delta_{i},\delta_{j}\rangle|\leq\eta_{i}\eta_{j}. ∎

Proof of Remark 4.5. Combining Lemmas J.1 and J.2 with ηk=2​εk/(1−εk)\eta_{k}=2\varepsilon_{k}/(1-\varepsilon_{k}) yields the stated proxy approximation bound. Note that Aproxy​(i,j)=cos⁡(μa,i⊗μe,i,μa,j⊗μe,j)=⟨u^i,u^j⟩A_{\mathrm{proxy}}(i,j)=\cos(\mu_{a,i}\otimes\mu_{e,i},\mu_{a,j}\otimes\mu_{e,j})=\langle\hat{u}_{i},\hat{u}_{j}\rangle. Also, AFhead​(i,j)=⟨x^i,x^j⟩A_{F}^{\mathrm{head}}(i,j)=\langle\hat{x}_{i},\hat{x}_{j}\rangle. ∎

Appendix K RSA and SVCCA are Representation-Only Metrics

This appendix proves that RSA and SVCCA, like CKA, are representation-only metrics (Definition 3.1). Therefore, they inherit the same fundamental limitation (Theorem 3.2).

K.1 RSA (Representational Similarity Analysis)

Proposition K.1 (RSA is representation-only).

RSA (Kriegeskorte et al., 2008) depends only on the representation Gram matrices Ki=Zi​Zi⊤K_{i}=Z_{i}Z_{i}^{\top} and Kj=Zj​Zj⊤K_{j}=Z_{j}Z_{j}^{\top} (equivalently, on all pairwise distances in ZiZ_{i} and ZjZ_{j}).

Proof.

RSA is the Spearman rank correlation between representational dissimilarity matrices (RDMs):

RSA​(Zi,Zj):=CorrSpearman​(RDMi,RDMj)\text{RSA}(Z_{i},Z_{j}):=\mathrm{Corr}_{\text{Spearman}}(\text{RDM}_{i},\text{RDM}_{j})

where RDMi\text{RDM}_{i} is the vector of pairwise Euclidean distances {‖za(i)−zb(i)‖2:a<b}\{\|z^{(i)}_{a}-z^{(i)}_{b}\|_{2}:a<b\} computed from ZiZ_{i}. We use Euclidean RDMs; other common dissimilarities (e.g., correlation distance) are also representation-only by the same reasoning. We assume ZiZ_{i} and ZjZ_{j} are evaluated on the same probe set so the RDMs are comparable. We further assume RDMi\text{RDM}_{i} and RDMj\text{RDM}_{j} are nonconstant so Spearman correlation is well-defined. Because Spearman correlation is invariant to monotone transforms, we can work with squared distances.

For any two samples za(i),zb(i)∈Ziz_{a}^{(i)},z_{b}^{(i)}\in Z_{i}, the squared distance is:

‖za(i)−zb(i)‖2\displaystyle\|z_{a}^{(i)}-z_{b}^{(i)}\|^{2} =‖za(i)‖2+‖zb(i)‖2−2​(za(i))⊤​zb(i)\displaystyle=\|z_{a}^{(i)}\|^{2}+\|z_{b}^{(i)}\|^{2}-2(z_{a}^{(i)})^{\top}z_{b}^{(i)}
=(Ki)a​a+(Ki)b​b−2​(Ki)a​b\displaystyle=(K_{i})_{aa}+(K_{i})_{bb}-2(K_{i})_{ab}

where Ki:=Zi​Zi⊤K_{i}:=Z_{i}Z_{i}^{\top} is the Gram matrix.

Define the (squared) distance matrix DiD_{i} with entries Di,a​b=‖za(i)−zb(i)‖22D_{i,ab}=\|z_{a}^{(i)}-z_{b}^{(i)}\|_{2}^{2}. Then

Di=𝟏​diag​(Ki)⊤+diag⁡(Ki)​ 1⊤−2​KiD_{i}=\mathbf{1}\,\mathrm{diag}(K_{i})^{\top}+\mathrm{diag}(K_{i})\,\mathbf{1}^{\top}-2K_{i}

where 𝟏\mathbf{1} is the all-ones vector. Thus all pairwise distances are determined by KiK_{i}. Since RDMi\text{RDM}_{i} is the vector of entries Di,a​bD_{i,ab} for a<ba<b, it is a deterministic function of KiK_{i} (and similarly for jj). Therefore

RSA​(Zi,Zj)=CorrSpearman​(f⁡(Ki),f⁡(Kj)),\text{RSA}(Z_{i},Z_{j})=\mathrm{Corr}_{\text{Spearman}}(f(K_{i}),f(K_{j})),

which depends only on (Zi,Zj)(Z_{i},Z_{j}) through (Ki,Kj)(K_{i},K_{j}) and not on errors or gradients. Hence RSA is representation-only. ∎

Corollary K.2 (RSA-Fisher gap).

For tasks with shared backbone (Zi=ZjZ_{i}=Z_{j}), nonconstant RDMs, and disjoint label subsets under the shared output-space embedding (Assumption F.1):

RSA​(Zi,Zj)=1,whileAFhead​(i,j)=0.\text{RSA}(Z_{i},Z_{j})=1,\quad\text{while}\quad A_{\mathrm{F}}^{\mathrm{head}}(i,j)=0.

This follows directly from Theorem 3.2 since RSA is a representation-only metric (Proposition K.1).

K.2 SVCCA (Singular Vector CCA)

Proposition K.3 (SVCCA is representation-only).

SVCCA (Raghu et al., 2017b) depends only on covariances of the SVD-reduced representations (i.e., on (Σ~i,Σ~j,Σ~i​j)(\tilde{\Sigma}_{i},\tilde{\Sigma}_{j},\tilde{\Sigma}_{ij}) computed from Zi,ZjZ_{i},Z_{j}).

Proof.

SVCCA is defined as:

SVCCA​(Zi,Zj):=1k​∑r=1kρr\text{SVCCA}(Z_{i},Z_{j}):=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{r=1}^{k}\rho_{r}

where ρ1,…,ρk\rho_{1},\ldots,\rho_{k} are the canonical correlation coefficients between the SVD-reduced representations (with k=min⁡(ri,rj)k=\min(r_{i},r_{j})).

Let Zi,ZjZ_{i},Z_{j} be centered over the probe samples (nn rows). Compute SVDs Zi=Ui​Si​Vi⊤Z_{i}=U_{i}S_{i}V_{i}^{\top} and Zj=Uj​Sj​Vj⊤Z_{j}=U_{j}S_{j}V_{j}^{\top}. Retain the top components (e.g., enough to explain a fixed variance fraction), yielding reduced representations Z~i:=Ui(:,1:ri)Si(1:ri,1:ri)\tilde{Z}_{i}:=U_{i}(:,1:r_{i})S_{i}(1:r_{i},1:r_{i}) and Z~j:=Uj(:,1:rj)Sj(1:rj,1:rj)\tilde{Z}_{j}:=U_{j}(:,1:r_{j})S_{j}(1:r_{j},1:r_{j}). CCA is then computed on the reduced representations using only their covariance blocks.

Define the (regularized) covariances
