Σ~i:=1n​Z~i⊤​Z~i+λ​I,Σ~j:=1n​Z~j⊤​Z~j+λ​I,Σ~i​j:=1n​Z~i⊤​Z~j,\tilde{\Sigma}_{i}:=\tfrac{1}{n}\tilde{Z}_{i}^{\top}\tilde{Z}_{i}+\lambda I,\quad\tilde{\Sigma}_{j}:=\tfrac{1}{n}\tilde{Z}_{j}^{\top}\tilde{Z}_{j}+\lambda I,\quad\tilde{\Sigma}_{ij}:=\tfrac{1}{n}\tilde{Z}_{i}^{\top}\tilde{Z}_{j},

with a small λ≥0\lambda\geq 0 for numerical stability, following the official implementation (Raghu et al., 2017a). The squared canonical correlations are the eigenvalues of Σ~i−1​Σ~i​j​Σ~j−1​Σ~j​i\tilde{\Sigma}_{i}^{-1}\tilde{\Sigma}_{ij}\tilde{\Sigma}_{j}^{-1}\tilde{\Sigma}_{ji}, where Σ~j​i=Σ~i​j⊤\tilde{\Sigma}_{ji}=\tilde{\Sigma}_{ij}^{\top} (or an equivalent generalized eigenproblem). Hence {ρr}\{\rho_{r}\} depend only on (Σ~i,Σ~j,Σ~i​j)(\tilde{\Sigma}_{i},\tilde{\Sigma}_{j},\tilde{\Sigma}_{ij}).

All subsequent CCA computations operate exclusively on these covariance blocks; the raw activations are never accessed after forming them. Therefore, SVCCA depends only on covariances of the reduced representations and is a representation-only metric. ∎

Implementation details (Appendix K.3). Our experiments use the official SVCCA implementation (Raghu et al., 2017b). It mean-centers activations (via np.cov), prunes low-variance directions below ϵ=10−10\epsilon=10^{-10} (equivalently λ=10−10\lambda=10^{-10} in Appendix K.2), and reports the mean canonical correlation up to the default truncation threshold 0.980.98. A standard 99% variance SVD truncation (Raghu et al., 2017b) yields the same representation-only conclusion.

Corollary K.4 (SVCCA-Fisher gap).

For tasks with shared backbone (Zi=ZjZ_{i}=Z_{j}) and disjoint label subsets under the shared output-space embedding (Assumption F.1):

SVCCA​(Zi,Zj)=1,whileAFhead​(i,j)=0.\text{SVCCA}(Z_{i},Z_{j})=1,\quad\text{while}\quad A_{\mathrm{F}}^{\mathrm{head}}(i,j)=0.

K.3 Empirical Verification

We verify these theoretical results numerically:

Implementation details.

Test 1 uses n=200n=200, d=64d=64, K=10K=10, seed =100=100. Test 2 (table) uses n=500n=500, d=128d=128, seed =42=42 (reset for each KK) with K∈{5,10,20,50,100}K\in\{5,10,20,50,100\}. Following the official implementation, SVCCA uses ϵ=10−10\epsilon=10^{-10} (equivalently λ=10−10\lambda=10^{-10}) and the default truncation threshold 0.980.98.

Test 1: Invariance to error structure.

For two task pairs with identical representations but different error covariances:

  • •

    Pair 1: Scov​(Γe,1)=0.999S_{\text{cov}}(\Gamma_{e,1})=0.999

  • •

    Pair 2: Scov​(Γe,2)=0.000S_{\text{cov}}(\Gamma_{e,2})=0.000 (disjoint classes)

Result: |RSA(pair 1)−RSA(pair 2)|<10−8|\text{RSA(pair 1)}-\text{RSA(pair 2)}|<10^{-8} and |SVCCA(pair 1)−SVCCA(pair 2)|<10−8|\text{SVCCA(pair 1)}-\text{SVCCA(pair 2)}|<10^{-8}.

Appendix L Explicit Perturbation Bound for Alignment

This appendix states a unit-normalization perturbation bound (with constant 22) used in later alignment bounds.

Lemma L.1 (Normalization perturbation).

Let x=x0+rx=x_{0}+r, where x≠0x\neq 0 and x0≠0x_{0}\neq 0. Let ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| be any norm (e.g., the Frobenius norm for matrices), and define δ:=‖r‖/‖x‖\delta:=\|r\|/\|x\|. Then

‖x‖x‖−x0‖x0‖‖≤2​δ.\left\|\frac{x}{\|x\|}-\frac{x_{0}}{\|x_{0}\|}\right\|\leq 2\delta.
Proof.

Observe that x‖x‖−x0‖x0‖=r‖x‖+x0​(1‖x‖−1‖x0‖)\frac{x}{\|x\|}-\frac{x_{0}}{\|x_{0}\|}=\frac{r}{\|x\|}+x_{0}\left(\frac{1}{\|x\|}-\frac{1}{\|x_{0}\|}\right). Taking norms and applying the reverse triangle inequality |‖x‖−‖x0‖|≤‖r‖|\|x\|-\|x_{0}\||\leq\|r\|, we obtain

‖x‖x‖−x0‖x0‖‖\displaystyle\left\|\frac{x}{\|x\|}-\frac{x_{0}}{\|x_{0}\|}\right\| ≤‖r‖‖x‖+|‖x‖−‖x0‖|‖x‖\displaystyle\leq\frac{\|r\|}{\|x\|}+\frac{|\|x\|-\|x_{0}\||}{\|x\|}
≤2​‖r‖‖x‖=2​δ.\displaystyle\leq 2\frac{\|r\|}{\|x\|}=2\delta.

∎

If we instead define ε:=‖r‖/‖x0‖<1\varepsilon:=\|r\|/\|x_{0}\|<1, then ‖x‖=‖x0+r‖≥‖x0‖−‖r‖=(1−ε)​‖x0‖\|x\|=\|x_{0}+r\|\geq\|x_{0}\|-\|r\|=(1-\varepsilon)\|x_{0}\|. Consequently,

‖x‖x‖−x0‖x0‖‖≤2​ε1−ε.\left\|\frac{x}{\|x\|}-\frac{x_{0}}{\|x_{0}\|}\right\|\leq\frac{2\varepsilon}{1-\varepsilon}.
Corollary L.2 (Alignment error bound).

Let Σi=Σi(0)+Ri\Sigma_{i}=\Sigma_{i}^{(0)}+R_{i} and Σj=Σj(0)+Rj\Sigma_{j}=\Sigma_{j}^{(0)}+R_{j}. Assume ‖Σi‖F,‖Σj‖F>0\|\Sigma_{i}\|_{F},\|\Sigma_{j}\|_{F}>0 and ‖Σi(0)‖F,‖Σj(0)‖F>0\|\Sigma_{i}^{(0)}\|_{F},\|\Sigma_{j}^{(0)}\|_{F}>0. For k∈{i,j}k\in\{i,j\}, define εR,k:=‖Rk‖F/‖Σk‖F\varepsilon_{R,k}:=\|R_{k}\|_{F}/\|\Sigma_{k}\|_{F}. Then

|Scov​(Σi,Σj)−Scov​(Σi(0),Σj(0))|≤2​(εR,i+εR,j).\big|S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Sigma_{i},\Sigma_{j})-S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Sigma_{i}^{(0)},\Sigma_{j}^{(0)})\big|\leq 2(\varepsilon_{R,i}+\varepsilon_{R,j}).

If all four matrices are positive semidefinite (PSD), then Scov​(⋅,⋅)∈[0,1]S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\cdot,\cdot)\in[0,1] and the bound can be clipped as

|Scov​(Σi,Σj)−Scov​(Σi(0),Σj(0))|≤min⁡{1,2​(εR,i+εR,j)}.\big|S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Sigma_{i},\Sigma_{j})-S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Sigma_{i}^{(0)},\Sigma_{j}^{(0)})\big|\leq\min\{1,2(\varepsilon_{R,i}+\varepsilon_{R,j})\}.
Proof.

Let u=Σi/‖Σi‖Fu=\Sigma_{i}/\|\Sigma_{i}\|_{F}, u0=Σi(0)/‖Σi(0)‖Fu_{0}=\Sigma_{i}^{(0)}/\|\Sigma_{i}^{(0)}\|_{F}, and define v=Σj/‖Σj‖Fv=\Sigma_{j}/\|\Sigma_{j}\|_{F}, v0=Σj(0)/‖Σj(0)‖Fv_{0}=\Sigma_{j}^{(0)}/\|\Sigma_{j}^{(0)}\|_{F}. Then

|Scov​(Σi,Σj)−Scov​(Σi(0),Σj(0))|=|⟨u,v⟩F−⟨u0,v0⟩F|≤‖u−u0‖F+‖v−v0‖F.\big|S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Sigma_{i},\Sigma_{j})-S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Sigma_{i}^{(0)},\Sigma_{j}^{(0)})\big|=|\langle u,v\rangle_{F}-\langle u_{0},v_{0}\rangle_{F}|\leq\|u-u_{0}\|_{F}+\|v-v_{0}\|_{F}.

By Lemma L.1 with x=Σix=\Sigma_{i}, x0=Σi(0)x_{0}=\Sigma_{i}^{(0)}, and r=Rir=R_{i}, we have ‖u−u0‖F≤2​‖Ri‖F/‖Σi‖F=2​εR,i\|u-u_{0}\|_{F}\leq 2\|R_{i}\|_{F}/\|\Sigma_{i}\|_{F}=2\varepsilon_{R,i}, and likewise ‖v−v0‖F≤2​εR,j\|v-v_{0}\|_{F}\leq 2\varepsilon_{R,j}. The claim follows. ∎

Interpretation.

In the head-Fisher setting, set Σk(0):=Ma,k⊗Γe,k\Sigma_{k}^{(0)}:=M_{a,k}\otimes\Gamma_{e,k}. Then RkR_{k} is the coupling residual from Remark 4.4. Under this identification, εR,k\varepsilon_{R,k} matches the reported δ≈0.34\delta\approx 0.34. The corollary then yields a worst-case bound of 2​(0.34+0.34)=1.362(0.34+0.34)=1.36. Because Scov​(⋅,⋅)∈[0,1]S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\cdot,\cdot)\in[0,1] for PSD matrices, we may clip the bound at 11. The worst-case term 2​(εR,i+εR,j)2(\varepsilon_{R,i}+\varepsilon_{R,j}) can be vacuous. Empirically, observed deviations are typically much smaller (see Appendix J).

Appendix M Proof of the Mean-Term Correction Lemma

This appendix proves Lemma M.1, which quantifies the gap between covariance alignment computed from centered and uncentered second moments.

Lemma M.1 (Mean-term correction).

Consider two tasks with activation second moments Ma,i,Ma,jM_{a,i},M_{a,j} and centered covariances Σa,i,Σa,j\Sigma_{a,i},\Sigma_{a,j}, with means μa,i,μa,j\mu_{a,i},\mu_{a,j}. Assume Σa,i,Σa,j⪰0\Sigma_{a,i},\Sigma_{a,j}\succeq 0 and ‖Σa,i‖F,‖Σa,j‖F>0\|\Sigma_{a,i}\|_{F},\|\Sigma_{a,j}\|_{F}>0 (hence ‖Ma,i‖F,‖Ma,j‖F>0\|M_{a,i}\|_{F},\|M_{a,j}\|_{F}>0). Then the covariance alignment gap is bounded as:

|Scov​(Ma,i,Ma,j)−Scov​(Σa,i,Σa,j)|≤2​(εμ,i+εμ,j)\big|S_{\mathrm{cov}}(M_{a,i},M_{a,j})-S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Sigma_{a,i},\Sigma_{a,j})\big|\leq 2(\varepsilon_{\mu,i}+\varepsilon_{\mu,j})

where εμ,k:=‖μa,k‖22/‖Σa,k‖F\varepsilon_{\mu,k}:=\|\mu_{a,k}\|_{2}^{2}/\|\Sigma_{a,k}\|_{F} is the ratio of squared-mean magnitude to covariance Frobenius norm.

Proof.

By definition, Ma,k=Σa,k+μa,k​μa,k⊤M_{a,k}=\Sigma_{a,k}+\mu_{a,k}\mu_{a,k}^{\top}. Let A=Σa,iA=\Sigma_{a,i}, B=Σa,jB=\Sigma_{a,j}, ΔA=μa,i​μa,i⊤\Delta_{A}=\mu_{a,i}\mu_{a,i}^{\top}, and ΔB=μa,j​μa,j⊤\Delta_{B}=\mu_{a,j}\mu_{a,j}^{\top}. Define the normalized matrices u=A+ΔA‖A+ΔA‖Fu=\frac{A+\Delta_{A}}{\|A+\Delta_{A}\|_{F}} and u0=A‖A‖Fu_{0}=\frac{A}{\|A\|_{F}}. Similarly, define v=B+ΔB‖B+ΔB‖Fv=\frac{B+\Delta_{B}}{\|B+\Delta_{B}\|_{F}} and v0=B‖B‖Fv_{0}=\frac{B}{\|B\|_{F}}. Viewing matrices as vectors under the Frobenius inner product, we have

Scov​(Ma,i,Ma,j)=⟨u,v⟩F,Scov​(Σa,i,Σa,j)=⟨u0,v0⟩F.S_{\mathrm{cov}}(M_{a,i},M_{a,j})=\langle u,v\rangle_{F},\quad S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Sigma_{a,i},\Sigma_{a,j})=\langle u_{0},v_{0}\rangle_{F}.

Therefore,

|⟨u,v⟩F−⟨u0,v0⟩F|=|⟨u−u0,v⟩F+⟨u0,v−v0⟩F|≤‖u−u0‖F+‖v−v0‖F.\big|\langle u,v\rangle_{F}-\langle u_{0},v_{0}\rangle_{F}\big|=\big|\langle u-u_{0},v\rangle_{F}+\langle u_{0},v-v_{0}\rangle_{F}\big|\leq\|u-u_{0}\|_{F}+\|v-v_{0}\|_{F}.

The last inequality uses Cauchy-Schwarz with ‖u‖F=‖u0‖F=‖v‖F=‖v0‖F=1\|u\|_{F}=\|u_{0}\|_{F}=\|v\|_{F}=\|v_{0}\|_{F}=1. Applying Lemma L.1 with x=A+ΔAx=A+\Delta_{A}, x0=Ax_{0}=A, and r=ΔAr=\Delta_{A}, we obtain

‖u−u0‖F≤2​‖ΔA‖F‖A+ΔA‖F.\|u-u_{0}\|_{F}\leq 2\frac{\|\Delta_{A}\|_{F}}{\|A+\Delta_{A}\|_{F}}.

Because A,ΔA⪰0A,\Delta_{A}\succeq 0, we have ⟨A,ΔA⟩F≥0\langle A,\Delta_{A}\rangle_{F}\geq 0, and thus ‖A+ΔA‖F2=‖A‖F2+‖ΔA‖F2+2​⟨A,ΔA⟩F≥‖A‖F2\|A+\Delta_{A}\|_{F}^{2}=\|A\|_{F}^{2}+\|\Delta_{A}\|_{F}^{2}+2\langle A,\Delta_{A}\rangle_{F}\geq\|A\|_{F}^{2}. Substituting into the previous bound yields ‖u−u0‖F≤2​‖ΔA‖F/‖A‖F\|u-u_{0}\|_{F}\leq 2\|\Delta_{A}\|_{F}/\|A\|_{F}. Noting that ‖ΔA‖F=‖μa,i‖22\|\Delta_{A}\|_{F}=\|\mu_{a,i}\|_{2}^{2}, this gives ‖u−u0‖F≤2​εμ,i\|u-u_{0}\|_{F}\leq 2\varepsilon_{\mu,i}. The same argument yields ‖v−v0‖F≤2​εμ,j\|v-v_{0}\|_{F}\leq 2\varepsilon_{\mu,j}. Therefore,

|Scov​(Ma,i,Ma,j)−Scov​(Σa,i,Σa,j)|≤2​(εμ,i+εμ,j),\big|S_{\mathrm{cov}}(M_{a,i},M_{a,j})-S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Sigma_{a,i},\Sigma_{a,j})\big|\leq 2(\varepsilon_{\mu,i}+\varepsilon_{\mu,j}),

as claimed. ∎

Remark (tighter denominator).

Lemma L.1 directly gives ‖u−u0‖F≤2​‖ΔA‖F/‖A+ΔA‖F\|u-u_{0}\|_{F}\leq 2\|\Delta_{A}\|_{F}/\|A+\Delta_{A}\|_{F} and similarly for vv. Define ε~μ,k:=‖μa,k‖22/‖Ma,k‖F\tilde{\varepsilon}_{\mu,k}:=\|\mu_{a,k}\|_{2}^{2}/\|M_{a,k}\|_{F}. Then the always-valid bound |Scov​(Ma,i,Ma,j)−Scov​(Σa,i,Σa,j)|≤2​(ε~μ,i+ε~μ,j)\big|S_{\mathrm{cov}}(M_{a,i},M_{a,j})-S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Sigma_{a,i},\Sigma_{a,j})\big|\leq 2(\tilde{\varepsilon}_{\mu,i}+\tilde{\varepsilon}_{\mu,j}). Since ‖Ma,k‖F≥‖Σa,k‖F\|M_{a,k}\|_{F}\geq\|\Sigma_{a,k}\|_{F} under Σa,k⪰0\Sigma_{a,k}\succeq 0, this bound is never looser than the stated bound.

Interpretation.

If εμ,k\varepsilon_{\mu,k} is large, the bound can be vacuous (i.e., greater than 11), but it still quantifies a worst-case impact of mean terms; reporting εμ,k\varepsilon_{\mu,k} keeps the approximation auditable.

Empirical mean-term sizes (ViT-B/16).

Using the ViT-B/16 validation data from Appendix J (20 tasks; 40 same-dataset pairs), we find εμ,k∈[0.78,1.35]\varepsilon_{\mu,k}\in[0.78,1.35] with a median of 0.960.96. Accordingly, the worst-case bound 2​(εμ,i+εμ,j)2(\varepsilon_{\mu,i}+\varepsilon_{\mu,j}) ranges from 3.163.16 to 5.295.29 across same-dataset pairs (vacuous). The observed gap |Scov​(Ma,i,Ma,j)−Scov​(Σa,i,Σa,j)||S_{\mathrm{cov}}(M_{a,i},M_{a,j})-S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Sigma_{a,i},\Sigma_{a,j})| ranges from 0.0070.007 to 0.1470.147 (median 0.0850.085).

Appendix N Proof of Theorem 3.2

This appendix provides a full proof of Theorem 3.2, showing that representation-only metrics are fundamentally blind to error structure.

Proof of Theorem 3.2.

Consider two classification tasks 𝒯i,𝒯j\mathcal{T}_{i},\mathcal{T}_{j} sharing an encoder fθ:𝒳→ℝdf_{\theta}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} but using disjoint label sets 𝒴i∩𝒴j=∅\mathcal{Y}_{i}\cap\mathcal{Y}_{j}=\emptyset.

Setup. Both tasks share a head parameter matrix W∈ℝK×dW\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times d} where K=|𝒴i|+|𝒴j|K=|\mathcal{Y}_{i}|+|\mathcal{Y}_{j}|. Task ii uses rows 1,…,|𝒴i|1,\ldots,|\mathcal{Y}_{i}| (with masked softmax over this block), while task jj uses rows |𝒴i|+1,…,K|\mathcal{Y}_{i}|+1,\ldots,K. This shared-output embedding with masked softmax (equivalently logits set to −∞-\infty outside each task’s label block) ensures the label spaces are orthogonally embedded in the shared output space (Assumption F.1; see Appendix F). This construction is regime-specific: without masked softmax (i.e., with a full KK-way softmax even if weights are zero-padded), disjoint label sets do not necessarily imply orthogonal errors.

Gradient structure. By Lemma 4.1 (affine head) and cross-entropy loss, the gradient w.r.t. vec⁡(W)\mathrm{vec}(W) at sample (x,y)(x,y) is:

gk=a⊗ek,where ​a=fθ​(x)∈ℝd,ek=p^k−𝟏y∈ℝK.g_{k}=a\otimes e_{k},\quad\text{where }a=f_{\theta}(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{d},\;e_{k}=\hat{p}_{k}-\mathbf{1}_{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{K}.

Here p^k\hat{p}_{k} is the masked softmax over the task’s label block (equivalently logits set to −∞-\infty outside the block; Assumption F.1) and 𝟏y:=Pk​y~k\mathbf{1}_{y}:=P_{k}\tilde{y}_{k} (with Pk,y~kP_{k},\tilde{y}_{k} as in Assumption F.1) is the one-hot target embedded in ℝK\mathbb{R}^{K}.

Disjoint support. Since task ii only activates rows 1,…,|𝒴i|1,\ldots,|\mathcal{Y}_{i}| and task jj only activates rows |𝒴i|+1,…,K|\mathcal{Y}_{i}|+1,\ldots,K:

supp⁡(ei)⊆{1,…,|𝒴i|},supp⁡(ej)⊆{|𝒴i|+1,…,K}.\mathrm{supp}(e_{i})\subseteq\{1,\ldots,|\mathcal{Y}_{i}|\},\quad\mathrm{supp}(e_{j})\subseteq\{|\mathcal{Y}_{i}|+1,\ldots,K\}.

These supports are disjoint, so ei⊤​ej=0e_{i}^{\top}e_{j}=0 for any pair of samples.

Fisher inner product. Let ℱkhead:=𝔼⁡[gk​gk⊤]\mathcal{F}_{k}^{\mathrm{head}}:=\mathbb{E}[g_{k}g_{k}^{\top}] be the head Fisher. By Lemma D.2 with independent samples from 𝒟i\mathcal{D}_{i} and 𝒟j\mathcal{D}_{j}:

⟨ℱihead,ℱjhead⟩F=𝔼(xi,yi)∼𝒟i,(xj,yj)∼𝒟j​[(gi⊤​gj)2].\langle\mathcal{F}_{i}^{\mathrm{head}},\mathcal{F}_{j}^{\mathrm{head}}\rangle_{F}=\mathbb{E}_{(x_{i},y_{i})\sim\mathcal{D}_{i},(x_{j},y_{j})\sim\mathcal{D}_{j}}\bigl[(g_{i}^{\top}g_{j})^{2}\bigr].

Using the Kronecker structure:

gi⊤​gj=(ai⊗ei)⊤​(aj⊗ej)=(ai⊤​aj)​(ei⊤​ej)=0,g_{i}^{\top}g_{j}=(a_{i}\otimes e_{i})^{\top}(a_{j}\otimes e_{j})=(a_{i}^{\top}a_{j})(e_{i}^{\top}e_{j})=0,

since ei⊤​ej=0e_{i}^{\top}e_{j}=0 by disjoint support. Therefore ⟨ℱihead,ℱjhead⟩F=0\langle\mathcal{F}_{i}^{\mathrm{head}},\mathcal{F}_{j}^{\mathrm{head}}\rangle_{F}=0, which implies:

AFhead​(i,j)=⟨ℱihead,ℱjhead⟩F‖ℱihead‖F​‖ℱjhead‖F=0.A_{\mathrm{F}}^{\mathrm{head}}(i,j)=\frac{\langle\mathcal{F}_{i}^{\mathrm{head}},\mathcal{F}_{j}^{\mathrm{head}}\rangle_{F}}{\|\mathcal{F}_{i}^{\mathrm{head}}\|_{F}\|\mathcal{F}_{j}^{\mathrm{head}}\|_{F}}=0.

Since ℱkhead⪰0\mathcal{F}_{k}^{\mathrm{head}}\succeq 0, we have ℱkhead=0\mathcal{F}_{k}^{\mathrm{head}}=0 iff tr⁡(ℱkhead)=0\mathrm{tr}(\mathcal{F}_{k}^{\mathrm{head}})=0. Moreover tr⁡(ℱkhead)=𝔼​‖gk‖22\mathrm{tr}(\mathcal{F}_{k}^{\mathrm{head}})=\mathbb{E}\|g_{k}\|_{2}^{2}. Thus if ℙ⁡(‖a‖2>0∧‖ek‖2>0)>0\mathbb{P}(\|a\|_{2}>0\,\wedge\,\|e_{k}\|_{2}>0)>0 (equivalently 𝔼​‖gk‖22>0\mathbb{E}\|g_{k}\|_{2}^{2}>0), then ‖ℱkhead‖F>0\|\mathcal{F}_{k}^{\mathrm{head}}\|_{F}>0 for k∈{i,j}k\in\{i,j\}, hence AFhead​(i,i)=AFhead​(j,j)=1A_{\mathrm{F}}^{\mathrm{head}}(i,i)=A_{\mathrm{F}}^{\mathrm{head}}(j,j)=1.

Representation metric blindness. On the shared probe set, the encoder is shared, so Zi=ZjZ_{i}=Z_{j}. Any representation-only metric MM therefore satisfies M⁡(Zi,Zj)=M⁡(Zi,Zi)M(Z_{i},Z_{j})=M(Z_{i},Z_{i}) (and equals 11 if MM is normalized). Yet AFhead​(i,j)=0A_{\mathrm{F}}^{\mathrm{head}}(i,j)=0 while AFhead​(i,i)=1A_{\mathrm{F}}^{\mathrm{head}}(i,i)=1 for nondegenerate tasks.

The gap arises because representation metrics access only the marginal distribution of activations aa, while Fisher alignment depends on the joint distribution of (a,e)(a,e). The error vectors ei,eje_{i},e_{j}—which encode label structure—are invisible to any representation-only metric. ∎

N.1 Full Proofs for CKA Non-Identifiability

This section provides the complete proofs of the linear CKA identity (Eq. (2)) and Corollary 3.3, which appear in the main text.

Proof of Eq. (2).

Let Zi∈ℝn×diZ_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{i}} and Zj∈ℝn×djZ_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{j}} be representation matrices evaluated on a shared probe set of nn inputs, with columns centered: Zi⊤​𝟏=0Z_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{1}=0 and Zj⊤​𝟏=0Z_{j}^{\top}\mathbf{1}=0. Define the (centered) empirical covariances Σ^i:=1n​Zi⊤​Zi\hat{\Sigma}_{i}:=\tfrac{1}{n}Z_{i}^{\top}Z_{i}, Σ^j:=1n​Zj⊤​Zj\hat{\Sigma}_{j}:=\tfrac{1}{n}Z_{j}^{\top}Z_{j}, Σ^i​j:=1n​Zi⊤​Zj\hat{\Sigma}_{ij}:=\tfrac{1}{n}Z_{i}^{\top}Z_{j}. Since Zi⊤​Zj=n​Σ^i​jZ_{i}^{\top}Z_{j}=n\hat{\Sigma}_{ij} and Zi⊤​Zi=n​Σ^iZ_{i}^{\top}Z_{i}=n\hat{\Sigma}_{i} (and similarly for jj), we have

‖Zi⊤​Zj‖F2‖Zi⊤​Zi‖F​‖Zj⊤​Zj‖F=n2​‖Σ^i​j‖F2(n​‖Σ^i‖F)​(n​‖Σ^j‖F)=‖Σ^i​j‖F2‖Σ^i‖F​‖Σ^j‖F.∎\frac{\|Z_{i}^{\top}Z_{j}\|_{F}^{2}}{\|Z_{i}^{\top}Z_{i}\|_{F}\,\|Z_{j}^{\top}Z_{j}\|_{F}}=\frac{n^{2}\|\hat{\Sigma}_{ij}\|_{F}^{2}}{(n\|\hat{\Sigma}_{i}\|_{F})(n\|\hat{\Sigma}_{j}\|_{F})}=\frac{\|\hat{\Sigma}_{ij}\|_{F}^{2}}{\|\hat{\Sigma}_{i}\|_{F}\,\|\hat{\Sigma}_{j}\|_{F}}.\qed
Proof of Corollary 3.3.

By Theorem 3.2, there exist tasks i≠ji\neq j with Zi=ZjZ_{i}=Z_{j} and AFhead​(i,j)=0A_{\mathrm{F}}^{\mathrm{head}}(i,j)=0, while AFhead​(i,i)=1A_{\mathrm{F}}^{\mathrm{head}}(i,i)=1 for the self-pair. Since Zi=ZjZ_{i}=Z_{j}, we have CKA⁡(Zi,Zj)=CKA⁡(Zi,Zi)\mathrm{CKA}(Z_{i},Z_{j})=\mathrm{CKA}(Z_{i},Z_{i}) (and equals 11 when ‖Σ^i‖F>0\|\hat{\Sigma}_{i}\|_{F}>0). Thus no single-valued function gg can map that one CKA value to both 00 and 11. The same argument applies to Scov​(Γe,i,Γe,j)S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Gamma_{e,i},\Gamma_{e,j}) since in the construction Γe,i\Gamma_{e,i} and Γe,j\Gamma_{e,j} have disjoint support, yielding Scov=0S_{\mathrm{cov}}=0. ∎

Appendix O Extension to Full Networks

The main text establishes a rigorous bridge between CKA and head (final layer) Fisher alignment. This appendix provides exact structural decompositions that relate full-network Fisher alignment to head Fisher alignment, with measurable diagnostics that explain when and why the reduction works.

Scope.

The block-diagonal/off-diagonal decompositions below are purely algebraic and hold for any parameter partition. The exact three-factor identity in Section O.6 additionally assumes that per-layer gradients are rank-1 (affine layers without parameter sharing). For convolutional or attention layers, the identity changes because per-example gradients are sums of outer products across positions. Appendix C gives the exact shared-parameter kernel identity and an unbiased sketch. Our empirical validation in this appendix relies on the block-decomposition diagnostics.

O.1 Full-Network Fisher Block Structure

Consider an LL-layer network with parameters θ=(θ1,…,θL)\theta=(\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{L}) where θl=vec⁡(Wl)\theta_{l}=\mathrm{vec}(W_{l}). The full-network Fisher matrix has block structure:

ℱ=[ℱ11ℱ12⋯ℱ1​Lℱ21ℱ22⋯ℱ2​L⋱ℱL​1ℱL​2⋯ℱL​L],\mathcal{F}=\begin{bmatrix}\mathcal{F}_{11}&\mathcal{F}_{12}&\cdots&\mathcal{F}_{1L}\\ \mathcal{F}_{21}&\mathcal{F}_{22}&\cdots&\mathcal{F}_{2L}\\ \vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\ \mathcal{F}_{L1}&\mathcal{F}_{L2}&\cdots&\mathcal{F}_{LL}\end{bmatrix}, (27)

where ℱl​l=𝔼⁡[gl​gl⊤]\mathcal{F}_{ll}=\mathbb{E}[g_{l}g_{l}^{\top}] are the layer-wise Fisher blocks and ℱl​m=𝔼⁡[gl​gm⊤]\mathcal{F}_{lm}=\mathbb{E}[g_{l}g_{m}^{\top}] for l≠ml\neq m are cross-layer blocks.

Exact algebraic split.

Define, for each task kk:

  • •

    Block-diagonal part: Dk:=blkdiag⁡(ℱ11(k),…,ℱL​L(k))D_{k}:=\mathrm{blkdiag}(\mathcal{F}^{(k)}_{11},\ldots,\mathcal{F}^{(k)}_{LL})

  • •

    Off-diagonal part: Ok:=ℱ(k)−DkO_{k}:=\mathcal{F}^{(k)}-D_{k}

These have disjoint support in block coordinates: DkD_{k} is nonzero only on diagonal blocks (ℓ,ℓ)(\ell,\ell), while OkO_{k} is nonzero only on off-diagonal blocks (ℓ,m)(\ell,m) with ℓ≠m\ell\neq m. This implies ⟨Dk,Ok⟩F=0\langle D_{k},O_{k}\rangle_{F}=0 and ‖ℱ(k)‖F2=‖Dk‖F2+‖Ok‖F2\|\mathcal{F}^{(k)}\|_{F}^{2}=\|D_{k}\|_{F}^{2}+\|O_{k}\|_{F}^{2}.

Assumption O.1 (Nondegeneracy).

We assume ‖Dk‖F>0\|D_{k}\|_{F}>0 (nontrivial block-diagonal Fisher) and, when AoffA_{\mathrm{off}} is defined, ‖Ok‖F>0\|O_{k}\|_{F}>0. When head/rest quantities are defined below, we also assume ‖Hk‖F>0\|H_{k}\|_{F}>0 and ‖Rk‖F>0\|R_{k}\|_{F}>0.

Degenerate cases.

If any denominator is zero, we use ε\varepsilon-regularized norms ‖X‖F,ε:=max⁡(‖X‖F,ε)\|X\|_{F,\varepsilon}:=\max(\|X\|_{F},\varepsilon) and set the corresponding alignment to ⟨X,Y⟩F/(‖X‖F,ε​‖Y‖F,ε)\langle X,Y\rangle_{F}/(\|X\|_{F,\varepsilon}\|Y\|_{F,\varepsilon}) (which yields 00 when X=0X=0 or Y=0Y=0). Weights are computed directly from norms via the first equalities in (32) and (44); ratios rk,τkr_{k},\tau_{k} are used only when denominators are nonzero.

Definition O.2 (Alignment diagnostics).

Define the following measurable quantities for tasks i,ji,j:

AFfull​(i,j)\displaystyle A_{F}^{\mathrm{full}}(i,j) :=⟨ℱi,ℱj⟩F‖ℱi‖F​‖ℱj‖F\displaystyle:=\frac{\langle\mathcal{F}_{i},\mathcal{F}_{j}\rangle_{F}}{\|\mathcal{F}_{i}\|_{F}\|\mathcal{F}_{j}\|_{F}} (full-network alignment),\displaystyle\text{(full-network alignment)}, (28)
Ablk​(i,j)\displaystyle A_{\mathrm{blk}}(i,j) :=⟨Di,Dj⟩F‖Di‖F​‖Dj‖F\displaystyle:=\frac{\langle D_{i},D_{j}\rangle_{F}}{\|D_{i}\|_{F}\|D_{j}\|_{F}} (block-diagonal alignment),\displaystyle\text{(block-diagonal alignment)}, (29)
Aoff​(i,j)\displaystyle A_{\mathrm{off}}(i,j) :=⟨Oi,Oj⟩F‖Oi‖F​‖Oj‖F\displaystyle:=\frac{\langle O_{i},O_{j}\rangle_{F}}{\|O_{i}\|_{F}\|O_{j}\|_{F}} (off-diagonal alignment),\displaystyle\text{(off-diagonal alignment)}, (30)
rk\displaystyle r_{k} :=‖Ok‖F‖Dk‖F\displaystyle:=\frac{\|O_{k}\|_{F}}{\|D_{k}\|_{F}} (cross-layer energy ratio; defined when ‖Dk‖F>0).\displaystyle\text{(cross-layer energy ratio; defined when $\|D_{k}\|_{F}>0$)}. (31)

O.2 Step 1: Exact Decomposition for Full-to-Block-Diagonal

The key insight is that mixed terms vanish by disjoint support, yielding an exact weighted sum with nonnegative weights.

Definition O.3 (Decomposition weights).

Define the following weights:

wblk\displaystyle w_{\mathrm{blk}} :=‖Di‖F​‖Dj‖F‖ℱi‖F​‖ℱj‖F=11+ri2​1+rj2,\displaystyle:=\frac{\|D_{i}\|_{F}\|D_{j}\|_{F}}{\|\mathcal{F}_{i}\|_{F}\|\mathcal{F}_{j}\|_{F}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+r_{i}^{2}}\sqrt{1+r_{j}^{2}}}, (32)
woff\displaystyle w_{\mathrm{off}} :=‖Oi‖F​‖Oj‖F‖ℱi‖F​‖ℱj‖F=ri​rj1+ri2​1+rj2=ri​rj⋅wblk.\displaystyle:=\frac{\|O_{i}\|_{F}\|O_{j}\|_{F}}{\|\mathcal{F}_{i}\|_{F}\|\mathcal{F}_{j}\|_{F}}=\frac{r_{i}r_{j}}{\sqrt{1+r_{i}^{2}}\sqrt{1+r_{j}^{2}}}=r_{i}r_{j}\cdot w_{\mathrm{blk}}. (33)

The equalities involving ri,rjr_{i},r_{j} assume ‖Dk‖F>0\|D_{k}\|_{F}>0; otherwise use the norm-based first equality.

Remark O.4 (Weights do not sum to 1 in general).

By Cauchy–Schwarz on vectors (1,ri)(1,r_{i}) and (1,rj)(1,r_{j}) (for nondegenerate ri,rjr_{i},r_{j}):

wblk+woff=1+ri​rj1+ri2​1+rj2≤1,w_{\mathrm{blk}}+w_{\mathrm{off}}=\frac{1+r_{i}r_{j}}{\sqrt{1+r_{i}^{2}}\sqrt{1+r_{j}^{2}}}\leq 1, (34)

with equality if and only if ri=rjr_{i}=r_{j}. Thus we have a nonnegative weighted sum that is a true convex combination only when tasks have identical cross-layer energy profiles.

Definition O.5 (Profile cosine).

Define the profile cosine:

cr:=wblk+woff=1+ri​rj1+ri2​1+rj2∈(0,1].c_{r}:=w_{\mathrm{blk}}+w_{\mathrm{off}}=\frac{1+r_{i}r_{j}}{\sqrt{1+r_{i}^{2}}\sqrt{1+r_{j}^{2}}}\in(0,1]. (35)

This measures the alignment of the energy profiles (‖Dk‖F,‖Ok‖F)(\|D_{k}\|_{F},\|O_{k}\|_{F}) between tasks.

Lemma O.6 (Exact full-to-block-diagonal decomposition).

For any two tasks i,ji,j satisfying Assumption O.1:

AFfull​(i,j)=wblk⋅Ablk​(i,j)+woff⋅Aoff​(i,j)\boxed{A_{F}^{\mathrm{full}}(i,j)=w_{\mathrm{blk}}\cdot A_{\mathrm{blk}}(i,j)+w_{\mathrm{off}}\cdot A_{\mathrm{off}}(i,j)} (36)

This is an exact identity.

Proof.

By disjoint block support, the cross terms vanish identically:

⟨Di,Oj⟩F=0,⟨Oi,Dj⟩F=0.\langle D_{i},O_{j}\rangle_{F}=0,\quad\langle O_{i},D_{j}\rangle_{F}=0.

This follows from block structure: DiD_{i} has nonzero entries only on diagonal blocks (ℓ,ℓ)(\ell,\ell), while OjO_{j} has nonzero entries only on off-diagonal blocks (ℓ,m)(\ell,m) with ℓ≠m\ell\neq m.

Therefore:

⟨ℱi,ℱj⟩F=⟨Di,Dj⟩F+⟨Oi,Oj⟩F.\langle\mathcal{F}_{i},\mathcal{F}_{j}\rangle_{F}=\langle D_{i},D_{j}\rangle_{F}+\langle O_{i},O_{j}\rangle_{F}.

Expanding AFfullA_{F}^{\mathrm{full}}:

AFfull\displaystyle A_{F}^{\mathrm{full}} =⟨Di,Dj⟩F+⟨Oi,Oj⟩F‖ℱi‖F​‖ℱj‖F\displaystyle=\frac{\langle D_{i},D_{j}\rangle_{F}+\langle O_{i},O_{j}\rangle_{F}}{\|\mathcal{F}_{i}\|_{F}\|\mathcal{F}_{j}\|_{F}}
=‖Di‖F​‖Dj‖F‖ℱi‖F​‖ℱj‖F⋅Ablk+‖Oi‖F​‖Oj‖F‖ℱi‖F​‖ℱj‖F⋅Aoff\displaystyle=\frac{\|D_{i}\|_{F}\|D_{j}\|_{F}}{\|\mathcal{F}_{i}\|_{F}\|\mathcal{F}_{j}\|_{F}}\cdot A_{\mathrm{blk}}+\frac{\|O_{i}\|_{F}\|O_{j}\|_{F}}{\|\mathcal{F}_{i}\|_{F}\|\mathcal{F}_{j}\|_{F}}\cdot A_{\mathrm{off}}
=wblk⋅Ablk+woff⋅Aoff.∎\displaystyle=w_{\mathrm{blk}}\cdot A_{\mathrm{blk}}+w_{\mathrm{off}}\cdot A_{\mathrm{off}}.\qed

Exact gap identity.

Rewriting the weighted sum using the profile cosine:

AFfull=(wblk+woff)​Ablk+woff​(Aoff−Ablk)=cr⋅Ablk+woff​(Aoff−Ablk).A_{F}^{\mathrm{full}}=(w_{\mathrm{blk}}+w_{\mathrm{off}})A_{\mathrm{blk}}+w_{\mathrm{off}}(A_{\mathrm{off}}-A_{\mathrm{blk}})=c_{r}\cdot A_{\mathrm{blk}}+w_{\mathrm{off}}(A_{\mathrm{off}}-A_{\mathrm{blk}}). (37)

Thus the gap has the exact form:

AFfull−Ablk=(cr−1)​Ablk+woff​(Aoff−Ablk)\boxed{A_{F}^{\mathrm{full}}-A_{\mathrm{blk}}=(c_{r}-1)A_{\mathrm{blk}}+w_{\mathrm{off}}(A_{\mathrm{off}}-A_{\mathrm{blk}})} (38)
Definition O.7 (Off-diagonal non-adversariality).

Define the off-diagonal discrepancy:

Δoff:=|Aoff−Ablk|.\Delta_{\mathrm{off}}:=|A_{\mathrm{off}}-A_{\mathrm{blk}}|. (39)

This measures how “adversarial” the off-diagonal alignment is relative to the block-diagonal alignment. Note that AoffA_{\mathrm{off}} can be negative since off-diagonal blocks OkO_{k} are not PSD, but |Aoff|≤1|A_{\mathrm{off}}|\leq 1 still holds by Cauchy–Schwarz on the Frobenius inner product.

Corollary O.8 (Sharp bound via profile cosine and non-adversariality).

Since |Ablk|≤1|A_{\mathrm{blk}}|\leq 1:

|AFfull−Ablk|≤(1−cr)+woff⋅Δoff\boxed{|A_{F}^{\mathrm{full}}-A_{\mathrm{blk}}|\leq(1-c_{r})+w_{\mathrm{off}}\cdot\Delta_{\mathrm{off}}} (40)

This bound does not require the energy ratios rir_{i} or rjr_{j} to be less than 11.

Why this works for deep nets.

The bound has two measurable terms; each is small when:

  • •

    Profile mismatch: (1−cr)(1-c_{r}) is small when ri≈rjr_{i}\approx r_{j} (tasks have similar cross-layer energy profiles).

  • •

    Adversarial off-diagonal: woff⋅Δoffw_{\mathrm{off}}\cdot\Delta_{\mathrm{off}} is small when Δoff\Delta_{\mathrm{off}} is small (off-diagonal alignment tracks block-diagonal).

When tasks share similar architectures and training regimes, both conditions typically hold.

O.3 Step 2: Block-Diagonal to Head Fisher

Now split the block-diagonal part into head vs. rest:

  • •

    Head block: Hk:=ℱL​L(k)H_{k}:=\mathcal{F}^{(k)}_{LL}

  • •

    Non-head blocks: Rk:=blkdiag⁡(ℱ11(k),…,ℱL−1,L−1(k))R_{k}:=\mathrm{blkdiag}(\mathcal{F}^{(k)}_{11},\ldots,\mathcal{F}^{(k)}_{L-1,L-1})

Again, these have disjoint support: ⟨Hk,Rk⟩F=0\langle H_{k},R_{k}\rangle_{F}=0 and ‖Dk‖F2=‖Hk‖F2+‖Rk‖F2\|D_{k}\|_{F}^{2}=\|H_{k}\|_{F}^{2}+\|R_{k}\|_{F}^{2}.

Definition O.9 (Head dominance diagnostics).

Define:

Ahead​(i,j)\displaystyle A_{\mathrm{head}}(i,j) :=⟨Hi,Hj⟩F‖Hi‖F​‖Hj‖F\displaystyle:=\frac{\langle H_{i},H_{j}\rangle_{F}}{\|H_{i}\|_{F}\|H_{j}\|_{F}} (head alignment),\displaystyle\text{(head alignment)}, (41)
Arest​(i,j)\displaystyle A_{\mathrm{rest}}(i,j) :=⟨Ri,Rj⟩F‖Ri‖F​‖Rj‖F\displaystyle:=\frac{\langle R_{i},R_{j}\rangle_{F}}{\|R_{i}\|_{F}\|R_{j}\|_{F}} (non-head alignment),\displaystyle\text{(non-head alignment)}, (42)
τk\displaystyle\tau_{k} :=‖Rk‖F‖Hk‖F\displaystyle:=\frac{\|R_{k}\|_{F}}{\|H_{k}\|_{F}} (non-head energy ratio; defined when ‖Hk‖F>0).\displaystyle\text{(non-head energy ratio; defined when $\|H_{k}\|_{F}>0$)}. (43)

Since HkH_{k} is the head block, Ahead​(i,j)A_{\mathrm{head}}(i,j) coincides with the head Fisher alignment AFhead​(i,j)A_{F}^{\mathrm{head}}(i,j).

Definition O.10 (Head/rest weights and profile cosine).

Define the following weights:

whead\displaystyle w_{\mathrm{head}} :=‖Hi‖F​‖Hj‖F‖Di‖F​‖Dj‖F=11+τi2​1+τj2,\displaystyle:=\frac{\|H_{i}\|_{F}\|H_{j}\|_{F}}{\|D_{i}\|_{F}\|D_{j}\|_{F}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+\tau_{i}^{2}}\sqrt{1+\tau_{j}^{2}}}, (44)
wrest\displaystyle w_{\mathrm{rest}} :=‖Ri‖F​‖Rj‖F‖Di‖F​‖Dj‖F=τi​τj1+τi2​1+τj2=τi​τj⋅whead,\displaystyle:=\frac{\|R_{i}\|_{F}\|R_{j}\|_{F}}{\|D_{i}\|_{F}\|D_{j}\|_{F}}=\frac{\tau_{i}\tau_{j}}{\sqrt{1+\tau_{i}^{2}}\sqrt{1+\tau_{j}^{2}}}=\tau_{i}\tau_{j}\cdot w_{\mathrm{head}}, (45)
cτ\displaystyle c_{\tau} :=whead+wrest=1+τi​τj1+τi2​1+τj2∈(0,1].\displaystyle:=w_{\mathrm{head}}+w_{\mathrm{rest}}=\frac{1+\tau_{i}\tau_{j}}{\sqrt{1+\tau_{i}^{2}}\sqrt{1+\tau_{j}^{2}}}\in(0,1]. (46)

As with crc_{r}, we have cτ≤1c_{\tau}\leq 1 by Cauchy–Schwarz, with equality iff τi=τj\tau_{i}=\tau_{j}. The equalities involving τi,τj\tau_{i},\tau_{j} assume ‖Hk‖F>0\|H_{k}\|_{F}>0; otherwise use the norm-based first equality.

Lemma O.11 (Exact block-diagonal to head decomposition).

For any two tasks i,ji,j satisfying Assumption O.1:

Ablk​(i,j)=whead⋅Ahead​(i,j)+wrest⋅Arest​(i,j)\boxed{A_{\mathrm{blk}}(i,j)=w_{\mathrm{head}}\cdot A_{\mathrm{head}}(i,j)+w_{\mathrm{rest}}\cdot A_{\mathrm{rest}}(i,j)} (47)

This is an exact identity.

Proof.

Identical to Lemma O.6, with (D,O,r,wblk,woff)→(H,R,τ,whead,wrest)(D,O,r,w_{\mathrm{blk}},w_{\mathrm{off}})\to(H,R,\tau,w_{\mathrm{head}},w_{\mathrm{rest}}) and using that ⟨Hi,Rj⟩F=0\langle H_{i},R_{j}\rangle_{F}=0 by disjoint block support. ∎

Exact gap identity.

Ablk−Ahead=(cτ−1)​Ahead+wrest​(Arest−Ahead)\boxed{A_{\mathrm{blk}}-A_{\mathrm{head}}=(c_{\tau}-1)A_{\mathrm{head}}+w_{\mathrm{rest}}(A_{\mathrm{rest}}-A_{\mathrm{head}})} (48)
Definition O.12 (Non-head discrepancy).

Define the non-head discrepancy:

Δrest:=|Arest−Ahead|.\Delta_{\mathrm{rest}}:=|A_{\mathrm{rest}}-A_{\mathrm{head}}|. (49)
Corollary O.13 (Sharp bound via profile cosine and non-adversariality).

Since |Ahead|≤1|A_{\mathrm{head}}|\leq 1:

|Ablk−Ahead|≤(1−cτ)+wrest⋅Δrest\boxed{|A_{\mathrm{blk}}-A_{\mathrm{head}}|\leq(1-c_{\tau})+w_{\mathrm{rest}}\cdot\Delta_{\mathrm{rest}}} (50)

This bound does not require τi\tau_{i} or τj\tau_{j} to be less than 11.

O.4 Combined Full-Network Theorem

Theorem O.14 (CKA to full-network Fisher: sharp bound).

Under Assumption O.1 and finite fourth moments (so all alignments are well-defined, with ε\varepsilon-regularization in degenerate cases):

|CKA−AFfull|≤|CKA−Ahead|⏟head-layer term+[(1−cτ)+wrest​Δrest]⏟non-head contribution+[(1−cr)+woff​Δoff]⏟cross-layer contribution\boxed{|\mathrm{CKA}-A_{F}^{\mathrm{full}}|\leq\underbrace{|\mathrm{CKA}-A_{\mathrm{head}}|}_{\text{head-layer term}}+\underbrace{\big[(1-c_{\tau})+w_{\mathrm{rest}}\Delta_{\mathrm{rest}}\big]}_{\text{non-head contribution}}+\underbrace{\big[(1-c_{r})+w_{\mathrm{off}}\Delta_{\mathrm{off}}\big]}_{\text{cross-layer contribution}}} (51)

where all terms are measurable or can be bounded from activations and gradient samples.

Whenever a head-layer bound of the form |CKA−Ahead|≤εhead|\mathrm{CKA}-A_{\mathrm{head}}|\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{head}} is available, it plugs directly into (51) to yield a closed-form CKA-to-full-network bound (e.g., Theorem G.1 in Appendix G under matched probe/input distributions).

Proof.

By triangle inequality and the bounds from Corollaries O.8 and O.13:

|CKA−AFfull|\displaystyle|\mathrm{CKA}-A_{F}^{\mathrm{full}}| ≤|CKA−Ahead|+|Ahead−Ablk|+|Ablk−AFfull|\displaystyle\leq|\mathrm{CKA}-A_{\mathrm{head}}|+|A_{\mathrm{head}}-A_{\mathrm{blk}}|+|A_{\mathrm{blk}}-A_{F}^{\mathrm{full}}|
≤|CKA−Ahead|+[(1−cτ)+wrest​Δrest]+[(1−cr)+woff​Δoff].∎\displaystyle\leq|\mathrm{CKA}-A_{\mathrm{head}}|+\big[(1-c_{\tau})+w_{\mathrm{rest}}\Delta_{\mathrm{rest}}\big]+\big[(1-c_{r})+w_{\mathrm{off}}\Delta_{\mathrm{off}}\big].\qed

Why this theorem “works” for deep nets.

Unlike worst-case bounds that become vacuous when r,τ>1r,\tau>1, this bound remains informative because it has four measurable terms that are small when:

  • •

    Cross-layer profile mismatch: (1−cr)(1-c_{r}) is small when ri≈rjr_{i}\approx r_{j}.

  • •

    Head/rest profile mismatch: (1−cτ)(1-c_{\tau}) is small when τi≈τj\tau_{i}\approx\tau_{j}.

  • •

    Adversarial off-diagonal: woff⋅Δoffw_{\mathrm{off}}\cdot\Delta_{\mathrm{off}} is small when Δoff\Delta_{\mathrm{off}} is small.

  • •

    Adversarial non-head: wrest⋅Δrestw_{\mathrm{rest}}\cdot\Delta_{\mathrm{rest}} is small when Δrest\Delta_{\mathrm{rest}} is small.

When tasks share similar architectures/training (so ri≈rjr_{i}\approx r_{j}, τi≈τj\tau_{i}\approx\tau_{j}), the profile cosines cr,cτ≈1c_{r},c_{\tau}\approx 1. When the network exhibits consistent alignment patterns across blocks, Δoff,Δrest\Delta_{\mathrm{off}},\Delta_{\mathrm{rest}} are small. Both conditions typically hold in practice.

O.5 Estimating Diagnostics from Gradient Samples

All quantities can be estimated from mini-batch gradient samples:

Weights and profile cosines.

For each layer ll, collect per-example gradients gl(t)g_{l}^{(t)}. Estimate Fisher block norms:

‖ℱ^l​m‖F2≈‖1n​∑t=1ngl(t)​gm(t)⊤‖F2.\|\hat{\mathcal{F}}_{lm}\|_{F}^{2}\approx\left\|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{t=1}^{n}g_{l}^{(t)}g_{m}^{(t)\top}\right\|_{F}^{2}.

Then compute wblk,woff,crw_{\mathrm{blk}},w_{\mathrm{off}},c_{r} from (32)–(35) and whead,wrest,cτw_{\mathrm{head}},w_{\mathrm{rest}},c_{\tau} from (44)–(46). This plug-in estimator is biased for finite nn; an unbiased alternative is the U-statistic 1n⁡(n−1)​∑t≠t′⟨gl(t),gl(t′)⟩​⟨gm(t),gm(t′)⟩\frac{1}{n(n-1)}\sum_{t\neq t^{\prime}}\langle g_{l}^{(t)},g_{l}^{(t^{\prime})}\rangle\langle g_{m}^{(t)},g_{m}^{(t^{\prime})}\rangle.

Discrepancies Δoff,Δrest\Delta_{\mathrm{off}},\Delta_{\mathrm{rest}}.

Compute cross-task alignments Aoff,Arest,Ablk,AheadA_{\mathrm{off}},A_{\mathrm{rest}},A_{\mathrm{blk}},A_{\mathrm{head}} from gradient inner products, then take differences.

O.6 Exact Full-Network Decomposition with Depth Coupling

While the previous subsections provide bounds relating full-network Fisher to head Fisher, here we establish an exact identity analogous to Theorem 4.2 but for the full network.

Definition O.15 (Depth-profile vectors).

For independent samples x∼𝒟ix\sim\mathcal{D}_{i} and x′∼𝒟jx^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{D}_{j}, with layer-wise activations aℓ−1(i),aℓ−1(j)a_{\ell-1}^{(i)},a_{\ell-1}^{(j)} and backpropagated errors δℓ(i),δℓ(j)\delta_{\ell}^{(i)},\delta_{\ell}^{(j)}, define:

u∈ℝL,uℓ\displaystyle u\in\mathbb{R}^{L},\quad u_{\ell} :=⟨aℓ−1(i),aℓ−1(j)⟩(forward similarity profile),\displaystyle:=\langle a_{\ell-1}^{(i)},a_{\ell-1}^{(j)}\rangle\quad\text{(forward similarity profile)}, (52)
v∈ℝL,vℓ\displaystyle v\in\mathbb{R}^{L},\quad v_{\ell} :=⟨δℓ(i),δℓ(j)⟩(backward similarity profile).\displaystyle:=\langle\delta_{\ell}^{(i)},\delta_{\ell}^{(j)}\rangle\quad\text{(backward similarity profile)}. (53)

Rank-1 per-layer gradients.

For affine layers applied to a single activation vector (no parameter sharing), the per-example gradient satisfies gℓ=vec⁡(δℓ​aℓ−1⊤)g_{\ell}=\mathrm{vec}(\delta_{\ell}a_{\ell-1}^{\top}) (Lemma 4.1). In this rank-1 setting, the full gradient inner product factorizes across depth:

g(i)⊤​g(j)=∑ℓ=1L⟨aℓ−1(i),aℓ−1(j)⟩⋅⟨δℓ(i),δℓ(j)⟩=∑ℓ=1Luℓ​vℓ=u⊤​v.g^{(i)\top}g^{(j)}=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\langle a_{\ell-1}^{(i)},a_{\ell-1}^{(j)}\rangle\cdot\langle\delta_{\ell}^{(i)},\delta_{\ell}^{(j)}\rangle=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}u_{\ell}v_{\ell}=u^{\top}v. (54)

Biases can be incorporated by augmenting activations with a constant 11, as in the head-layer analysis.

Definition O.16 (Stacked second moments).

For task kk, define block-diagonal matrices of stacked second moments:

MA,k\displaystyle M_{A,k} :=blkdiag⁡(𝔼⁡[a0​a0⊤],…,𝔼⁡[aL−1​aL−1⊤]),\displaystyle:=\mathrm{blkdiag}\big(\mathbb{E}[a_{0}a_{0}^{\top}],\ldots,\mathbb{E}[a_{L-1}a_{L-1}^{\top}]\big), (55)
ΓΔ,k\displaystyle\Gamma_{\Delta,k} :=blkdiag⁡(𝔼⁡[δ1​δ1⊤],…,𝔼⁡[δL​δL⊤]).\displaystyle:=\mathrm{blkdiag}\big(\mathbb{E}[\delta_{1}\delta_{1}^{\top}],\ldots,\mathbb{E}[\delta_{L}\delta_{L}^{\top}]\big). (56)
Definition O.17 (Full-network coupling coefficient).

Let 𝔼i,j\mathbb{E}_{i,j} denote expectation over independent draws x∼𝒟ix\sim\mathcal{D}_{i} and x′∼𝒟jx^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{D}_{j} (and the resulting depth-profile vectors u,vu,v from Definition O.15). Define:

χi​jfull:=𝔼i,j​[(u⊤​v)2]𝔼i,j​[‖u‖2]⋅𝔼i,j​[‖v‖2],ρi​jfull:=χi​jfullχi​ifull​χj​jfull.\chi^{\mathrm{full}}_{ij}:=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{i,j}[(u^{\top}v)^{2}]}{\mathbb{E}_{i,j}[\|u\|^{2}]\cdot\mathbb{E}_{i,j}[\|v\|^{2}]},\quad\rho^{\mathrm{full}}_{ij}:=\frac{\chi^{\mathrm{full}}_{ij}}{\sqrt{\chi^{\mathrm{full}}_{ii}\chi^{\mathrm{full}}_{jj}}}. (57)
Theorem O.18 (Full-network three-factor decomposition).

For an LL-layer feedforward network with affine weight matrices and rank-1 per-layer gradients (no parameter sharing), full-network Fisher alignment satisfies the exact identity:

AFfull​(i,j)=Scov​(MA,i,MA,j)⋅Scov​(ΓΔ,i,ΓΔ,j)⋅ρi​jfull\boxed{A_{F}^{\mathrm{full}}(i,j)=S_{\mathrm{cov}}(M_{A,i},M_{A,j})\cdot S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Gamma_{\Delta,i},\Gamma_{\Delta,j})\cdot\rho^{\mathrm{full}}_{ij}} (58)

This is structurally identical to Theorem 4.2 (head layer), with the single-layer quantities replaced by depth-stacked versions.

Proof.

The proof follows the same structure as Theorem 4.2.

From (54), the Fisher inner product becomes:

⟨ℱi,ℱj⟩F=𝔼i,j​[(g(i)⊤​g(j))2]=𝔼i,j​[(u⊤​v)2].\langle\mathcal{F}_{i},\mathcal{F}_{j}\rangle_{F}=\mathbb{E}_{i,j}[(g^{(i)\top}g^{(j)})^{2}]=\mathbb{E}_{i,j}[(u^{\top}v)^{2}]. (59)

For the stacked second moments (with independent draws):

⟨MA,i,MA,j⟩F\displaystyle\langle M_{A,i},M_{A,j}\rangle_{F} =∑ℓ=1Ltr⁡(𝔼⁡[aℓ−1(i)​aℓ−1(i)⊤]⋅𝔼⁡[aℓ−1(j)​aℓ−1(j)⊤])\displaystyle=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\mathrm{tr}\big(\mathbb{E}[a_{\ell-1}^{(i)}a_{\ell-1}^{(i)\top}]\cdot\mathbb{E}[a_{\ell-1}^{(j)}a_{\ell-1}^{(j)\top}]\big) (60)
=∑ℓ=1L𝔼i,j​[uℓ2]=𝔼i,j​[‖u‖2],\displaystyle=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\mathbb{E}_{i,j}[u_{\ell}^{2}]=\mathbb{E}_{i,j}[\|u\|^{2}], (61)
⟨ΓΔ,i,ΓΔ,j⟩F\displaystyle\langle\Gamma_{\Delta,i},\Gamma_{\Delta,j}\rangle_{F} =∑ℓ=1L𝔼i,j​[vℓ2]=𝔼i,j​[‖v‖2].\displaystyle=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\mathbb{E}_{i,j}[v_{\ell}^{2}]=\mathbb{E}_{i,j}[\|v\|^{2}]. (62)

Define χi​jfull\chi^{\mathrm{full}}_{ij} such that 𝔼i,j​[(u⊤​v)2]=χi​jfull⋅𝔼i,j​[‖u‖2]⋅𝔼i,j​[‖v‖2]\mathbb{E}_{i,j}[(u^{\top}v)^{2}]=\chi^{\mathrm{full}}_{ij}\cdot\mathbb{E}_{i,j}[\|u\|^{2}]\cdot\mathbb{E}_{i,j}[\|v\|^{2}].

Similarly, ‖ℱi‖F2=χi​ifull⋅𝔼i,i​[‖u‖2]⋅𝔼i,i​[‖v‖2]\|\mathcal{F}_{i}\|_{F}^{2}=\chi^{\mathrm{full}}_{ii}\cdot\mathbb{E}_{i,i}[\|u\|^{2}]\cdot\mathbb{E}_{i,i}[\|v\|^{2}] and likewise ‖ℱj‖F2=χj​jfull⋅𝔼j,j​[‖u‖2]⋅𝔼j,j​[‖v‖2]\|\mathcal{F}_{j}\|_{F}^{2}=\chi^{\mathrm{full}}_{jj}\cdot\mathbb{E}_{j,j}[\|u\|^{2}]\cdot\mathbb{E}_{j,j}[\|v\|^{2}]. Normalizing to alignment form and defining ρi​jfull=χi​jfull/χi​ifull​χj​jfull\rho^{\mathrm{full}}_{ij}=\chi^{\mathrm{full}}_{ij}/\sqrt{\chi^{\mathrm{full}}_{ii}\chi^{\mathrm{full}}_{jj}} yields (58). ∎

Remark O.19 (Beyond rank-1 layers).

For convolutional or attention layers with parameter sharing, per-example gradients are sums of outer products across positions. In that regime (54) and Theorem O.18 require modification; Appendix C gives the shared-parameter kernel identity and an unbiased sketch, while the block-decomposition identities here remain exact.

Geometric interpretation.

The coupling coefficient ρfull\rho^{\mathrm{full}} measures depth interference: whether forward and backward similarity profiles align in depth space. Since (u⊤​v)2=‖u‖2​‖v‖2​cos2⁡θ(u^{\top}v)^{2}=\|u\|^{2}\|v\|^{2}\cos^{2}\theta where θ\theta is the angle between uu and vv:

χi​jfull=𝔼i,j​[‖u‖2​‖v‖2​cos2⁡θ]𝔼i,j​[‖u‖2]⋅𝔼i,j​[‖v‖2].\chi^{\mathrm{full}}_{ij}=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{i,j}[\|u\|^{2}\|v\|^{2}\cos^{2}\theta]}{\mathbb{E}_{i,j}[\|u\|^{2}]\cdot\mathbb{E}_{i,j}[\|v\|^{2}]}. (63)

When forward and backward similarities co-localize in depth (all layers contribute similarly), cos⁡θ≈1\cos\theta\approx 1 yields constructive interference. Misalignment across depth yields destructive interference.

Corollary O.20 (Constant depth profiles imply head = full).

Assume the rank-1 per-layer gradient setting of Theorem O.18. Suppose that for every pair of samples (x,x′)(x,x^{\prime}) used in the Fisher inner products, the forward and backward similarity profiles are constant across depth:

uℓ​(x,x′)≡u⋆​(x,x′)andvℓ​(x,x′)≡v⋆​(x,x′)∀ℓ∈{1,…,L}.u_{\ell}(x,x^{\prime})\equiv u_{\star}(x,x^{\prime})\quad\text{and}\quad v_{\ell}(x,x^{\prime})\equiv v_{\star}(x,x^{\prime})\qquad\forall\ell\in\{1,\dots,L\}.

Equivalently, for each sample pair the per-layer gradient inner products are identical:

⟨gℓ​(x),gℓ​(x′)⟩≡⟨gL​(x),gL​(x′)⟩∀ℓ.\langle g_{\ell}(x),g_{\ell}(x^{\prime})\rangle\equiv\langle g_{L}(x),g_{L}(x^{\prime})\rangle\qquad\forall\ell.

Then for all task pairs (i,j)(i,j),

AFfull​(i,j)=Ahead​(i,j).A_{F}^{\mathrm{full}}(i,j)=A_{\mathrm{head}}(i,j).

Moreover, in this regime the depth-coupling term in Theorem O.18 reduces to the head-layer coupling term (it need not equal 11).

Remark O.21 (A sufficient special case: deep linear orthogonal networks).

In a deep linear network aℓ=Wℓ​aℓ−1a_{\ell}=W_{\ell}a_{\ell-1} with no biases and orthogonal weights Wℓ⊤​Wℓ=IW_{\ell}^{\top}W_{\ell}=I, we have ⟨aℓ​(x),aℓ​(x′)⟩=⟨a0​(x),a0​(x′)⟩\langle a_{\ell}(x),a_{\ell}(x^{\prime})\rangle=\langle a_{0}(x),a_{0}(x^{\prime})\rangle for all ℓ\ell. Backpropagated errors satisfy an analogous invariance, yielding constant depth profiles and hence AFfull=AheadA_{F}^{\mathrm{full}}=A_{\mathrm{head}}. Such networks exhibit perfect dynamical isometry (input–output Jacobian singular values all 11).

Relation to profile diagnostics.

The profile cosine crc_{r} (Definition O.5) and discrepancy Δoff\Delta_{\mathrm{off}} (Definition O.7) from the bound analysis are indirect measures of depth coupling. Corollary O.8 bounds the gap between full and block-diagonal Fisher; the exact theorem above shows the gap is controlled by ρfull\rho^{\mathrm{full}} deviating from the head-layer coupling.

Computational note.

The head theorem (Theorem 4.2, L=1L=1) is a special case: the depth profiles reduce to scalars (u,v∈ℝ1)(u,v\in\mathbb{R}^{1}), so u⊤​v=u​vu^{\top}v=uv and ρfull=ρ\rho^{\mathrm{full}}=\rho.

O.7 Controlled Transfer Validation (CIFAR-100)

We validate that Scov​(Γe)S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Gamma_{e}) predicts transfer in a controlled setting where class overlap can be precisely manipulated.

Setup.

Using ResNet-18 on CIFAR-100, we train a source task on classes 0–49 (fixed), then measure linear probe transfer to target tasks with varying class overlap (0%, 24%, 50%, 74%, 100%; i.e., 0/50, 12/50, 25/50, 37/50, 50/50 shared). Linear probe transfer—training only the classification head while freezing the backbone—matches the head-layer theory assumptions. Because the backbone is shared, representation similarity is constant (CKA ≈1\approx 1), so any variation in transfer must come from error geometry. We compare Scov​(Γe)S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Gamma_{e}) against standard transferability metrics (LogME, LEEP, H-score, NCE) (You et al., 2021; Nguyen et al., 2020; Bao et al., 2019; Tran et al., 2019) that require explicit label information.

Results.

Table 15 shows that Scov​(Γe)S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Gamma_{e}) tracks class overlap (0.00 at 0% overlap, 1.00 at 100%) and predicts linear probe transfer gain as well as dedicated transferability metrics.

Why CKA fails.

With a frozen backbone, CKA is constant by construction (CKA ≈1.00\approx 1.00), so it cannot discriminate transfer quality: all source-target pairs appear identical to representation-only metrics regardless of label compatibility. Scov​(Γe)S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Gamma_{e}) captures the error structure that CKA misses, enabling meaningful source ranking.

Baseline comparison.

All metrics achieve high correlation with transfer gain (ρ>0.96\rho>0.96) because overlap is monotonically related to transfer. The key advantage of Scov​(Γe)S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Gamma_{e}) is scalability: standard LogME/LEEP-style finite-label implementations require explicit label maps or class statistics and are not designed to estimate full vocabulary-scale error covariance; FisherSketch estimates the corresponding joint update geometry in one pass without materializing Γe\Gamma_{e}, using O⁡(d+K+m)O(d+K+m) working memory plus projection state.

Limitation.

With only 5 overlap levels, correlation comparisons have limited statistical power. The vocab-scale experiment (100 domains, 24 candidates/target, 4,188 transfer pairs) provides stronger evidence.

O.8 Vision Transformer Validation

We validate the full-network decomposition (Corollary O.8) on Vision Transformers to address concerns about modern attention-based architectures.

Experimental setup.

We fine-tune ViT-B/16 (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021) (pretrained on ImageNet-21k) on four downstream classification tasks: CIFAR-100 (100 classes), Flowers102 (102 classes), Oxford Pets (37 classes), and DTD (47 classes). Each task is trained with 5 random seeds, yielding 20 models total. We analyze 50 pairwise task comparisons (40 same-dataset pairs with different seeds, 10 cross-dataset pairs, subsampled). Images are resized to 224×224224\times 224, representing a substantial scale increase from the CIFAR-32 experiments in the main text.

Full parameter partition.

Unlike prior work that tracks only the classification head, we collect per-example gradients across the complete parameter partition: patch embedding, all 12 transformer blocks, final layer norm, and classification head (14 parameter groups total). This ensures our validation matches the theorem’s assumptions—no layers are omitted. Gradients are computed in float64 precision with 1000 samples per task to ensure numerical stability.

Head gradient comparability across datasets.

To compare head gradients across datasets with different class counts (KCIFAR=100K_{\text{CIFAR}}=100, KFlowers=102K_{\text{Flowers}}=102, KPets=37K_{\text{Pets}}=37, KDTD=47K_{\text{DTD}}=47), we embed all error and prediction vectors into a shared Kshared=286K_{\mathrm{shared}}=286 dimensional space. Each dataset occupies a contiguous, disjoint block: CIFAR-100 uses coordinates [0,100)[0,100), Flowers102 uses [100,202)[100,202), Oxford Pets uses [202,239)[202,239), and DTD uses [239,286)[239,286). Predictions use masked softmax (logits set to −∞-\infty outside their respective blocks) and one-hot labels are embedded via the shared-output injection, yielding 286-dimensional error vectors with zeros outside their respective blocks. Head gradients thus have uniform dimension Kshared×d+Kshared=286×768+286=219 934K_{\mathrm{shared}}\times d+K_{\mathrm{shared}}=286\times 768+286=219\,934 parameters. For cross-dataset pairs, this construction yields exactly zero Fisher alignment: the error vectors have disjoint support, so ⟨ei,ej⟩=0\langle e_{i},e_{j}\rangle=0 for all sample pairs, making head gradient inner products zero.

Key finding: profile cosines remain near-unity.

Despite the attention-based architecture and larger scale, profile cosines crc_{r} remain extremely high (Table 16):

cr=0.9995±0.0011(mean ± std, n=50).c_{r}=0.9995\pm 0.0011\quad\text{(mean $\pm$ std, $n=50$)}. (64)

This confirms that ViT models trained on related fine-tuning tasks share similar cross-layer energy profiles, even though the absolute energy ratio r≈2.75r\approx 2.75 substantially exceeds unity (off-diagonal energy exceeds diagonal energy by ∼\sim2.7×\times). The deterministic bound is satisfied for all 50 pairs (numerical check), and the mean gap (0.077) closely matches the mean bound (0.078; Table 16).

Constructed orthogonality under shared-output embedding (sanity check).

Table 4 (main text) provides an illustrative regime on ViT: for cross-dataset pairs (e.g., CIFAR-100 vs. Flowers102), the error structures are orthogonal because disjoint label spaces are embedded via the masked-softmax shared-output embedding (logits set to −∞-\infty outside each block). CKA remains moderately high (≈0.57\approx 0.57) because representations share similar geometry, but Scov​(Γe)=0S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Gamma_{e})=0 and FA-CKA drops to zero, as required by the construction. (This orthogonality is with respect to the disjoint-block embedding of label spaces; alternative embeddings would define different cross-task error geometry.)

Kronecker proxy vs. exact head Fisher.

On the 40 same-dataset pairs (where exact Fisher is nonzero), we compare the Kronecker proxy with exact head Fisher computed via the kernel trick (Appendix A). The Kronecker proxy is anti-correlated with exact Fisher (r=−0.34r=-0.34, ρ=−0.30\rho=-0.30), while FA-CKA maintains strong correlation (r=0.79r=0.79, ρ=0.90\rho=0.90); see Table 5. This confirms that FA-CKA’s validity does not depend on the Kronecker approximation.

O.9 Large Language Model Validation

We extend the full-network decomposition validation to Large Language Models, demonstrating that Corollary O.8 generalizes beyond vision architectures to modern autoregressive transformers.

Experimental setup.

We evaluate on two architectures: Llama-3.1-8B (Grattafiori et al., 2024) (32 layers, 4096 hidden dim) and Qwen2.5-14B (Qwen Team, 2024) (48 layers, 5120 hidden dim). Using 30 MMLU subjects as tasks provides a natural multi-task setting with shared K=4K=4 output space (4-way multiple choice), eliminating masked-softmax block-embedding confounds. For each model, we sample 100 task pairs from the 435 possible combinations, collecting 100 gradient samples per subject across the full parameter partition: embeddings, all transformer layers, final layer norm, and a 4-way classification head.

Empirical tightness of the deterministic bound.

Despite architectural differences (32 vs. 48 layers, different training objectives), both models show cr≈0.99c_{r}\approx 0.99 and mean gaps 0.332/0.243 (Table 17). The inequality itself is deterministic, so satisfaction is a numerical check rather than a discovery:

|AFfull−Ablk|≤(1−cr)+woff​Δofffor all 100 pairs.|A_{F}^{\mathrm{full}}-A_{\mathrm{blk}}|\leq(1-c_{r})+w_{\mathrm{off}}\Delta_{\mathrm{off}}\quad\text{for all 100 pairs.} (65)

High profile cosines indicate consistent depth profiles in residual-stream architectures.

Scale validation: 70B parameters.

To validate that the decomposition extends to frontier-scale models, we evaluate on 8 models at 67–72B parameters across three architectures (Table 18). Profile cosines remain high (cr≈0.98c_{r}\approx 0.98) and gaps range 0.158–0.464 across models; bound satisfaction is a numerical check rather than a discovery. This suggests the residual stream geometry remains consistent even at 10×\times scale.

Comparison with ViT.

LLMs exhibit higher Δoff\Delta_{\mathrm{off}} than ViT (0.25–0.75 vs. 0.088), reflecting more cross-layer interaction variance in deeper models (32–80 layers vs. 12 layers). However, the bound remains tight: mean gap tracks mean bound closely across all 10 models tested. Bound satisfaction is expected from the inequality; the key insight is that profile cosines cr≈0.98c_{r}\approx 0.98–0.990.99 dominate the bound, making the block-diagonal reduction reliable even when Δoff\Delta_{\mathrm{off}} is elevated.

Vocabulary-scale transfer validation.

To validate FisherSketch at vocabulary scale, we measure correlation between FisherSketch-estimated Fisher alignment and actual LoRA transfer success. Protocol: (1) Compute base perplexity for each domain; (2) fine-tune LoRA adapter on source domain (rank=8, α\alpha=16, up to 50 steps with early stopping on source-dev loss, patience=3, lr=5×10−55\times 10^{-5}); (3) evaluate on target domain; (4) compute normalized transfer score in loss space: (log⁡baseppl−log⁡transferppl)/(log⁡baseppl−log⁡selfppl)(\log\text{base}_{\text{ppl}}-\log\text{transfer}_{\text{ppl}})/(\log\text{base}_{\text{ppl}}-\log\text{self}_{\text{ppl}}), with a small denominator floor (0.01) for stability. Negative transfer (transfer PPL >> base PPL) can occur; the normalized score handles this naturally. Setup: 100 domains constructed from eight HF datasets (Appendix B.11), 500 samples/domain for FisherSketch (mm=4096). LoRA transfer uses 200 train / 100 eval samples per domain; we evaluate 4,188 cross-domain pairs (union of uniform + stratified candidates) and report top-1 under the uniform 24-candidate protocol. Sketching and LoRA splits are disjoint by construction; candidate sets and sketch sample indices are saved for audit. Result: FisherSketch with SRHT error projections achieves 45.7% ±\pm 5.0 top-1 source selection (≈\approx10.9×\times random) with max regret 0.119 ±\pm 0.013 (mean ±\pm std over seeds 43–45), confirming that FisherSketch predicts cross-domain transfer at vocabulary scale (KK=128,256) where storing Γe\Gamma_{e} scales as O⁡(K2)O(K^{2}). Per-target Spearman corr. =0.47±0.02=0.47\pm 0.02; global off-diagonal Spearman corr. =0.47±0.01=0.47\pm 0.01 is lower because it mixes heterogeneous task families. A diagonal error-geometry proxy (cosine between diag⁡(Γe)\mathrm{diag}(\Gamma_{e}) vectors; LEEP-style) is weaker: 44.0% ±\pm 2.2 top-1 and max regret 0.210 ±\pm 0.011 under the same uniform-24 protocol, indicating off-diagonal error covariance carries signal at vocab scale. Sketch-only stability with fixed LoRA outcomes is moderate: across SRHT seeds 43–45, pairwise top-1 agreement is 0.51 ±\pm 0.02 and off-diagonal Spearman is 0.982 ±\pm 0.003.

O.10 Empirical Findings

What we measure.

  • •

    Shallow-wide networks (depth 1–2): cr≈0.95c_{r}\approx 0.95–0.990.99, cτ≈0.95c_{\tau}\approx 0.95–0.990.99. Profile cosines close to 1 mean tasks have similar energy profiles.

  • •

    Deep networks (depth ≥3\geq 3): cr,cτc_{r},c_{\tau} can be lower when tasks have different r,τr,\tau values, but this does not imply the bound is vacuous.

  • •

    Vision Transformers (ViT-B/16, Table 16): cr=0.9995c_{r}=0.9995, with mean gap 0.077 vs bound 0.078 across 50 task pairs. Full 14-layer partition (patch embedding through classification head) confirms profile alignment persists in modern attention-based architectures.

  • •

    Large Language Models (8B–70B, Tables 17–18): cr≈0.95c_{r}\approx 0.95–1.001.00, with mean gaps 0.158–0.464 across 8B–70B models. The residual stream architecture maintains geometric consistency from 32 to 80 transformer layers.

The key finding: discrepancies are small.

Even when cr,cτ<1c_{r},c_{\tau}<1 (deep nets with varying energy profiles), we observe:

  • •

    Δrest≈0.10\Delta_{\mathrm{rest}}\approx 0.10–0.200.20: non-head alignment tracks head alignment.

  • •

    ViT-B/16: Δoff≈0.05\Delta_{\mathrm{off}}\approx 0.05–0.150.15 (mean 0.088), with mean gap 0.077 vs bound 0.078 across the full 14-layer parameter partition (Figure 3).

  • •

    LLMs (8B–70B): Δoff=0.25\Delta_{\mathrm{off}}=0.25–0.750.75 (higher due to deeper architectures), with gaps 0.158–0.464; high profile cosines (cr≈0.95c_{r}\approx 0.95–1.001.00) keep the bound tight.

This explains why, in residual-stream architectures with aligned profile cosines, CKA can correlate strongly with full-network Fisher (r>0.89r>0.89) in our validation suite (Vision Transformers and Large Language Models). This does not contradict non-identifiability for transfer: when error geometry differs, CKA can remain high while head alignment (and transfer) collapse.

Key takeaway.

The exact decompositions (36) and (47) show that what matters is not “r<1r<1” but “cr≈1c_{r}\approx 1 and Δoff\Delta_{\mathrm{off}} small.” Our theory predicts exactly what to measure: the profile cosines cr,cτc_{r},c_{\tau} and discrepancies Δoff,Δrest\Delta_{\mathrm{off}},\Delta_{\mathrm{rest}}. When these are favorable, the head-layer analysis transfers to full-network Fisher—and empirically, they are.

Appendix P Why Error Geometry Ranks While Activation Geometry Screens

This appendix provides a stylized explanation for the empirical asymmetry observed in Section 6.1: the error-geometry score Scov​(Γe)S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Gamma_{e}) can yield higher top-1 source selection accuracy, while incorporating activation geometry reduces worst-case regret. We model source selection for a fixed target task as follows.

Let 𝒮\mathcal{S} be a finite set of candidate sources. For each s∈𝒮s\in\mathcal{S} define a nonnegative error score Es∈(0,1]E_{s}\in(0,1] (e.g., Es:=Scov​(Γe,s,Γe,t)E_{s}:=S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Gamma_{e,s},\Gamma_{e,t})). Define also a nonnegative compatibility factor As≥0A_{s}\geq 0 (e.g., an activation/coupling term such as Scov​(Ma,s,Ma,t)S_{\mathrm{cov}}(M_{a,s},M_{a,t}), optionally folding ρ\rho into AsA_{s}). The product score is Ps:=As​EsP_{s}:=A_{s}E_{s}. We compare the error-only selector s^E:=arg⁡maxs∈𝒮⁡Es\hat{s}_{E}:=\arg\max_{s\in\mathcal{S}}E_{s} and the product selector s^P:=arg⁡maxs∈𝒮⁡Ps\hat{s}_{P}:=\arg\max_{s\in\mathcal{S}}P_{s}.

Lemma P.1 (Tight-race flips under multiplicative universality noise).

Let 𝒞\mathcal{C} be a finite set and let {Es}s∈𝒞\{E_{s}\}_{s\in\mathcal{C}} be deterministic scores with a unique maximizer s⋆:=arg⁡maxs∈𝒞⁡Ess^{\star}:=\arg\max_{s\in\mathcal{C}}E_{s} and Es>0E_{s}>0 for all s∈𝒞s\in\mathcal{C}. Let {Zs}s∈𝒞\{Z_{s}\}_{s\in\mathcal{C}} be independent mean-zero σ\sigma-subGaussian random variables, i.e., 𝔼⁡[exp⁡(λ​Zs)]≤exp⁡(λ2​σ2/2)\mathbb{E}[\exp(\lambda Z_{s})]\leq\exp(\lambda^{2}\sigma^{2}/2) for all λ∈ℝ\lambda\in\mathbb{R}. Define As:=exp⁡(Zs)A_{s}:=\exp(Z_{s}) and Ps:=As​EsP_{s}:=A_{s}E_{s}.

Then the probability that the multiplicative factors change the maximizer satisfies

ℙ⁡(arg⁡maxs∈𝒞⁡Ps≠s⋆)≤∑s∈𝒞∖{s⋆}exp⁡(−log2⁡(Es⋆Es)4​σ2).\mathbb{P}\!\left(\arg\max_{s\in\mathcal{C}}P_{s}\neq s^{\star}\right)\;\leq\;\sum_{s\in\mathcal{C}\setminus\{s^{\star}\}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{\log^{2}\!\big(\frac{E_{s^{\star}}}{E_{s}}\big)}{4\sigma^{2}}\right).

In particular, letting E(2):=maxs∈𝒞∖{s⋆}⁡EsE_{(2)}:=\max_{s\in\mathcal{C}\setminus\{s^{\star}\}}E_{s} and Δ:=log⁡(Es⋆/E(2))\Delta:=\log(E_{s^{\star}}/E_{(2)}), we have

ℙ⁡(arg⁡maxs∈𝒞⁡Ps≠s⋆)≤(|𝒞|−1)​exp⁡(−Δ24​σ2).\mathbb{P}\!\left(\arg\max_{s\in\mathcal{C}}P_{s}\neq s^{\star}\right)\;\leq\;(|\mathcal{C}|-1)\exp\!\left(-\frac{\Delta^{2}}{4\sigma^{2}}\right).
Proof.

Fix s≠s⋆s\neq s^{\star}. If Ps≥Ps⋆P_{s}\geq P_{s^{\star}} then

Zs−Zs⋆≥log⁡(Es⋆Es).Z_{s}-Z_{s^{\star}}\geq\log\!\Big(\frac{E_{s^{\star}}}{E_{s}}\Big).

Since ZsZ_{s} and Zs⋆Z_{s^{\star}} are independent σ\sigma-subGaussian, Zs−Zs⋆Z_{s}-Z_{s^{\star}} is 2​σ\sqrt{2}\sigma-subGaussian, hence ℙ(Zs−Zs⋆≥t)≤exp(−t2/(4σ2))\mathbb{P}(Z_{s}-Z_{s^{\star}}\geq t)\leq\exp(-t^{2}/(4\sigma^{2})). Applying this with t=log⁡(Es⋆/Es)t=\log(E_{s^{\star}}/E_{s}) and union bounding over s∈𝒞∖{s⋆}s\in\mathcal{C}\setminus\{s^{\star}\} yields the first inequality. The second follows because log⁡(Es⋆/Es)≥Δ\log(E_{s^{\star}}/E_{s})\geq\Delta for all s≠s⋆s\neq s^{\star}. ∎

Theorem P.2 (When the product screens catastrophes and can lose top-1 in tight races).

Let 𝒮\mathcal{S} be a finite candidate set and fix a target. Let Us∈ℝU_{s}\in\mathbb{R} be the (unknown) transfer utility of selecting source ss, and let r⁡(s):=Us⋆−Usr(s):=U_{s^{\star}}-U_{s} denote regret, where s⋆:=arg⁡maxs∈𝒮⁡Uss^{\star}:=\arg\max_{s\in\mathcal{S}}U_{s} is the oracle source.

Assume there exists a subset 𝒞⊆𝒮\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathcal{S} of compatible sources such that:

  1. (A1)

    (Oracle is compatible) s⋆∈𝒞s^{\star}\in\mathcal{C}.

  2. (A2)

    (EE ranks within 𝒞\mathcal{C}) There exist deterministic scores Es∈(0,1]E_{s}\in(0,1] with a unique maximizer over 𝒞\mathcal{C} at s⋆s^{\star}, i.e., s⋆=arg⁡maxs∈𝒞⁡Ess^{\star}=\arg\max_{s\in\mathcal{C}}E_{s}.

  3. (A3)

    (Universality within 𝒞\mathcal{C}) For c∈𝒞c\in\mathcal{C}, the compatibility factors satisfy Ac=exp⁡(Zc)A_{c}=\exp(Z_{c}) where {Zc}c∈𝒞\{Z_{c}\}_{c\in\mathcal{C}} are independent, mean-zero, σ\sigma-subGaussian random variables.

  4. (A4)

    (Screening outside 𝒞\mathcal{C}) For all b∉𝒞b\notin\mathcal{C}, Ab≤βA_{b}\leq\beta for some β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1).

  5. (A5)

    (Catastrophic incompatibility) There exists R>0R>0 such that r⁡(c)<Rr(c)<R for all c∈𝒞c\in\mathcal{C} and r⁡(b)≥Rr(b)\geq R for all b∉𝒞b\notin\mathcal{C} (i.e., catastrophes occur iff an incompatible source is selected).

Define the selectors s^E:=arg⁡maxs∈𝒮⁡Es\hat{s}_{E}:=\arg\max_{s\in\mathcal{S}}E_{s} and s^P:=arg⁡maxs∈𝒮⁡(As​Es)\hat{s}_{P}:=\arg\max_{s\in\mathcal{S}}(A_{s}E_{s}).

(1) Product screening (tail safety).

If Es⋆>βE_{s^{\star}}>\beta, then

ℙ⁡(s^P∉𝒞)≤exp⁡(−log2⁡(Es⋆β)2​σ2).\mathbb{P}(\hat{s}_{P}\notin\mathcal{C})\;\leq\;\exp\!\left(-\frac{\log^{2}\!\big(\frac{E_{s^{\star}}}{\beta}\big)}{2\sigma^{2}}\right).

By (A5),

ℙ⁡(r⁡(s^P)≥R)=ℙ⁡(s^P∉𝒞)≤exp⁡(−log2⁡(Es⋆β)2​σ2).\mathbb{P}(r(\hat{s}_{P})\geq R)\;=\;\mathbb{P}(\hat{s}_{P}\notin\mathcal{C})\;\leq\;\exp\!\left(-\frac{\log^{2}\!\big(\frac{E_{s^{\star}}}{\beta}\big)}{2\sigma^{2}}\right).

(2) Tight-race degradation (top-1 loss).

Let Δ:=minc∈𝒞∖{s⋆}⁡log⁡(Es⋆/Ec)\Delta:=\min_{c\in\mathcal{C}\setminus\{s^{\star}\}}\log(E_{s^{\star}}/E_{c}). Then

ℙ⁡(s^P≠s⋆,s^P∈𝒞)≤(|𝒞|−1)​exp⁡(−Δ24​σ2).\mathbb{P}(\hat{s}_{P}\neq s^{\star},\ \hat{s}_{P}\in\mathcal{C})\;\leq\;(|\mathcal{C}|-1)\exp\!\left(-\frac{\Delta^{2}}{4\sigma^{2}}\right).

In particular, when Δ≲σ\Delta\lesssim\sigma (tight races), the product selector can mis-rank within 𝒞\mathcal{C} with non-negligible probability.

(3) Top-1 comparison from bounds.

Let pbad:=ℙ⁡(s^E∉𝒞)p_{\mathrm{bad}}:=\mathbb{P}(\hat{s}_{E}\notin\mathcal{C}), where the probability is over any randomness in candidate-set generation or score estimation (if EE is deterministic and 𝒮\mathcal{S} is fixed, then pbad∈{0,1}p_{\mathrm{bad}}\in\{0,1\}). Under (A1)–(A2), ℙ⁡(s^E=s⋆)=1−pbad\mathbb{P}(\hat{s}_{E}=s^{\star})=1-p_{\mathrm{bad}}. Moreover,

ℙ⁡(s^P=s⋆)≥ 1−exp⁡(−log2⁡(Es⋆β)2​σ2)−(|𝒞|−1)​exp⁡(−Δ24​σ2).\mathbb{P}(\hat{s}_{P}=s^{\star})\;\geq\;1-\exp\!\left(-\frac{\log^{2}\!\big(\frac{E_{s^{\star}}}{\beta}\big)}{2\sigma^{2}}\right)-(|\mathcal{C}|-1)\exp\!\left(-\frac{\Delta^{2}}{4\sigma^{2}}\right).

Define

B:=exp⁡(−log2⁡(Es⋆β)2​σ2)+(|𝒞|−1)​exp⁡(−Δ24​σ2).B\;:=\;\exp\!\left(-\frac{\log^{2}\!\big(\frac{E_{s^{\star}}}{\beta}\big)}{2\sigma^{2}}\right)+(|\mathcal{C}|-1)\exp\!\left(-\frac{\Delta^{2}}{4\sigma^{2}}\right).

If pbad>Bp_{\mathrm{bad}}>B, then the product rule is guaranteed to have higher top-1 selection probability than the error-only rule. If pbad<Bp_{\mathrm{bad}}<B, these bounds do not determine which rule has higher top-1; either ordering is possible depending on the distribution of the multiplicative factors.

Proof.

(1) For any b∉𝒞b\notin\mathcal{C}, Ab​Eb≤β⋅1=βA_{b}E_{b}\leq\beta\cdot 1=\beta since Eb∈(0,1]E_{b}\in(0,1]. Thus s^P∉𝒞\hat{s}_{P}\notin\mathcal{C} implies maxc∈𝒞⁡Ac​Ec≤β\max_{c\in\mathcal{C}}A_{c}E_{c}\leq\beta, which in particular implies As⋆​Es⋆≤βA_{s^{\star}}E_{s^{\star}}\leq\beta. Equivalently Zs⋆≤−log⁡(Es⋆/β)Z_{s^{\star}}\leq-\log(E_{s^{\star}}/\beta). A subGaussian lower-tail bound gives ℙ(Zs⋆≤−t)≤exp(−t2/(2σ2))\mathbb{P}(Z_{s^{\star}}\leq-t)\leq\exp(-t^{2}/(2\sigma^{2})), yielding the first inequality. By (A5), r⁡(s^P)≥Rr(\hat{s}_{P})\geq R iff s^P∉𝒞\hat{s}_{P}\notin\mathcal{C}, so ℙ⁡(r⁡(s^P)≥R)=ℙ⁡(s^P∉𝒞)\mathbb{P}(r(\hat{s}_{P})\geq R)=\mathbb{P}(\hat{s}_{P}\notin\mathcal{C}).

(2) Conditional on s^P∈𝒞\hat{s}_{P}\in\mathcal{C}, the event s^P≠s⋆\hat{s}_{P}\neq s^{\star} implies that for some c∈𝒞∖{s⋆}c\in\mathcal{C}\setminus\{s^{\star}\} we have Ac​Ec≥As⋆​Es⋆A_{c}E_{c}\geq A_{s^{\star}}E_{s^{\star}}, i.e., Zc−Zs⋆≥log⁡(Es⋆/Ec)≥ΔZ_{c}-Z_{s^{\star}}\geq\log(E_{s^{\star}}/E_{c})\geq\Delta. Applying Lemma P.1 (or directly union bounding the same tail event) yields the stated bound.

(3) If s^E∈𝒞\hat{s}_{E}\in\mathcal{C}, then by (A2) the unique maximizer of EE on 𝒞\mathcal{C} is s⋆s^{\star}, so s^E=s⋆\hat{s}_{E}=s^{\star}. Hence ℙ⁡(s^E=s⋆)=1−ℙ⁡(s^E∉𝒞)=1−pbad\mathbb{P}(\hat{s}_{E}=s^{\star})=1-\mathbb{P}(\hat{s}_{E}\notin\mathcal{C})=1-p_{\mathrm{bad}}. For the product, ℙ⁡(s^P≠s⋆)\mathbb{P}(\hat{s}_{P}\neq s^{\star}) is at most the probability of selecting outside 𝒞\mathcal{C} plus the probability of selecting a suboptimal element within 𝒞\mathcal{C}; combine (1) and (2). Comparing ℙ⁡(s^E=s⋆)=1−pbad\mathbb{P}(\hat{s}_{E}=s^{\star})=1-p_{\mathrm{bad}} with ℙ⁡(s^P=s⋆)≥1−B\mathbb{P}(\hat{s}_{P}=s^{\star})\geq 1-B yields the stated sufficient condition pbad>Bp_{\mathrm{bad}}>B for the product rule to be more accurate in top-1. For pbad<Bp_{\mathrm{bad}}<B, no ordering follows from these bounds alone. ∎

Appendix Q LEEP as a Diagonal Error-Geometry Proxy

We formalize the claim that LEEP (Nguyen et al., 2020) leverages error geometry. The statement below is deliberately about LEEP, not LogME: LogME is used elsewhere as a finite-label evidence baseline, while this appendix proves only a stylized LEEP–error-geometry connection. Empirically, the diagonal proxy underperforms at vocabulary scale (top-1 accuracy 44.0% ±\pm 2.2; max regret 0.210 ±\pm 0.011; Appendix B.11), consistent with the theory below. Let (X,Y)∼𝒟(X,Y)\sim\mathcal{D} be the target distribution with Y∈[K]Y\in[K], and let p(⋅∣x)∈ΔK−1p(\cdot\mid x)\in\Delta^{K-1} be a source classifier’s predictive distribution. Let Z∣X∼Cat(p(⋅∣X))Z\mid X\sim\mathrm{Cat}(p(\cdot\mid X)). Define the soft confusion matrix Cy,z:=𝔼[𝟏{Y=y}⋅p(z∣X)]C_{y,z}:=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}\{Y=y\}\cdot p(z\mid X)]. Define the marginal qz:=∑yCy,zq_{z}:=\sum_{y}C_{y,z}. Then Cy,z=ℙ⁡(Y=y,Z=z)C_{y,z}=\mathbb{P}(Y=y,Z=z) and qz=ℙ⁡(Z=z)q_{z}=\mathbb{P}(Z=z). Assume qz>0q_{z}>0, and define p⁡(y∣z):=Cy,z/qz=ℙ⁡(Y=y∣Z=z)p(y\mid z):=C_{y,z}/q_{z}=\mathbb{P}(Y=y\mid Z=z). Assume p⁡(y∣z)>0p(y\mid z)>0 whenever ℙ⁡(Y=y,Z=z)>0\mathbb{P}(Y=y,Z=z)>0 (or define LEEP=−∞\mathrm{LEEP}=-\infty otherwise). The population LEEP score is

LEEP⁡(p,𝒟):=𝔼X,Y​log​∑z=1Kp⁡(Y∣z)​p​(z∣X)=𝔼X,Y​log​𝔼Z|X​[p⁡(Y∣Z)].\mathrm{LEEP}(p;\mathcal{D}):=\mathbb{E}_{X,Y}\log\sum_{z=1}^{K}p(Y\mid z)\,p(z\mid X)=\mathbb{E}_{X,Y}\log\mathbb{E}_{Z\mid X}[p(Y\mid Z)]. (66)
Lemma Q.1 (Negative conditional entropy lower bounds LEEP).

Let Z∣X∼Cat(p(⋅∣X))Z\mid X\sim\mathrm{Cat}(p(\cdot\mid X)) be the sampled prediction. Then

LEEP⁡(p,𝒟)≥−H⁡(Y∣Z),\mathrm{LEEP}(p;\mathcal{D})\;\geq\;-H(Y\mid Z),

with equality when predictions are hard (deterministic).

Proof.

By Jensen’s inequality on the concave log\log: log⁡𝔼Z|X​[p⁡(Y∣Z)]≥𝔼Z|X​[log⁡p⁡(Y∣Z)]\log\mathbb{E}_{Z\mid X}[p(Y\mid Z)]\geq\mathbb{E}_{Z\mid X}[\log p(Y\mid Z)]. Taking 𝔼X,Y\mathbb{E}_{X,Y} yields the bound; equality holds when ZZ is deterministic given XX. ∎

Proposition Q.2 (Hard-prediction LEEP is monotone in diagonal Γedisc\Gamma_{e}^{\mathrm{disc}} under uniform confusion).

Assume hard predictions (ZZ deterministic given XX), uniform prior ℙ⁡(Y=y)=1/K\mathbb{P}(Y=y)=1/K, K≥2K\geq 2, and diagonal confusion: ℙ⁡(Y=y∣Z=z)=α\mathbb{P}(Y=y\mid Z=z)=\alpha if y=zy=z, else (1−α)/(K−1)(1-\alpha)/(K-1). This specifies the confusion in the reverse direction—ℙ⁡(Y∣Z)\mathbb{P}(Y\mid Z) (conditioned on predictions)—rather than the more common ℙ⁡(Z∣Y)\mathbb{P}(Z\mid Y). Let 𝟏Z,𝟏Y∈ℝK\mathbf{1}_{Z},\mathbf{1}_{Y}\in\mathbb{R}^{K} denote the one-hot vectors for ZZ and YY, and let edisc:=𝟏Z−𝟏Ye^{\mathrm{disc}}:=\mathbf{1}_{Z}-\mathbf{1}_{Y} and define Γedisc:=𝔼⁡[edisc​edisc⊤]\Gamma_{e}^{\mathrm{disc}}:=\mathbb{E}[e^{\mathrm{disc}}e^{\mathrm{disc}\top}]. This is the hard-prediction error; it differs from the soft error e=softmax⁡(W​a)−ye=\mathrm{softmax}(Wa)-y used elsewhere. Let d:=(Γedisc)c​c=2​(1−α)/Kd:=(\Gamma_{e}^{\mathrm{disc}})_{cc}=2(1-\alpha)/K be the diagonal error moment. Then

−H⁡(Y∣Z)=(1−K2​d)​log⁡(1−K2​d)+K2​d​log⁡K​d/2K−1,-H(Y\mid Z)=(1-\tfrac{K}{2}d)\log(1-\tfrac{K}{2}d)+\tfrac{K}{2}d\log\tfrac{Kd/2}{K-1}, (67)

and LEEP⁡(p,𝒟)=−H⁡(Y∣Z)\mathrm{LEEP}(p;\mathcal{D})=-H(Y\mid Z) is strictly decreasing in dd for accuracies above chance (α>1/K\alpha>1/K).

Proof.

Let My,z:=ℙ⁡(Y=y∣Z=z)M_{y,z}:=\mathbb{P}(Y=y\mid Z=z). With the stated symmetry, MM is doubly stochastic and has eigenvalues 11 and α−1−αK−1\alpha-\frac{1-\alpha}{K-1}. Viewing ℙ⁡(Y)\mathbb{P}(Y) and ℙ⁡(Z)\mathbb{P}(Z) as KK-vectors, the system ℙ⁡(Y)=M​ℙ​(Z)\mathbb{P}(Y)=M\mathbb{P}(Z) implies ℙ⁡(Z)=𝟏/K\mathbb{P}(Z)=\mathbf{1}/K for α≠1/K\alpha\neq 1/K. At α=1/K\alpha=1/K, MM is rank-1 and ℙ⁡(Z)\mathbb{P}(Z) is not identifiable from ℙ⁡(Y)\mathbb{P}(Y) alone; we set ℙ⁡(Z)=𝟏/K\mathbb{P}(Z)=\mathbf{1}/K by convention. Thus (Γedisc)c​c=𝔼⁡[ec2]=ℙ⁡(Z=c)+ℙ⁡(Y=c)−2​ℙ​(Y=c,Z=c)=2​(1−α)/K(\Gamma_{e}^{\mathrm{disc}})_{cc}=\mathbb{E}[e_{c}^{2}]=\mathbb{P}(Z=c)+\mathbb{P}(Y=c)-2\mathbb{P}(Y=c,Z=c)=2(1-\alpha)/K. The conditional entropy is

H⁡(Y∣Z)=−α​log⁡α−(1−α)​log⁡(1−αK−1),H(Y\mid Z)=-\alpha\log\alpha-(1-\alpha)\log\!\left(\frac{1-\alpha}{K-1}\right), (68)

so substituting α=1−K2​d\alpha=1-\tfrac{K}{2}d yields the displayed expression. Differentiating gives

dd​d​(−H⁡(Y∣Z))=−K2​log⁡(α⁡(K−1)1−α)=K2​log⁡(K​d2​(K−1)​(1−K2​d)),\frac{d}{dd}\big(-H(Y\mid Z)\big)=-\frac{K}{2}\log\!\left(\frac{\alpha(K-1)}{1-\alpha}\right)=\frac{K}{2}\log\!\left(\frac{Kd}{2(K-1)(1-\tfrac{K}{2}d)}\right),

which is negative for α>1/K\alpha>1/K. Hard predictions imply LEEP⁡(p,𝒟)=−H⁡(Y∣Z)\mathrm{LEEP}(p;\mathcal{D})=-H(Y\mid Z) by Lemma Q.1. ∎

This shows the conditional-entropy lower bound (and LEEP in the hard-prediction limit) is a monotone function of a diagonal error second moment under the uniform-confusion model. In this stylized regime, LEEP is a “diagonal proxy for error geometry” in a formal sense. This formal connection should not be read as a derivation of LogME; LogME remains a finite-label evidence baseline in our comparisons.

Appendix R Task Signatures and Retrieval

Algorithm 1 produces per-task mean embeddings μ^a​e,k∈ℝm\hat{\mu}_{ae,k}\in\mathbb{R}^{m} as a direct byproduct of computing pairwise Fisher alignments. These embeddings, which we call task signatures, enable efficient indexing, retrieval, and dynamic updates without recomputing all pairwise alignments.

R.1 Signature Storage

Storage footprint.

Each task signature consists of the joint embedding μ^a​e∈ℝm\hat{\mu}_{ae}\in\mathbb{R}^{m} stored in float32:

Storage per task=m×4​bytes=16​KB at ​m=4096.\text{Storage per task}=m\times 4\,\text{bytes}=16\,\text{KB at }m{=}4096. (69)

Optionally, the factorized components (μ^a,μ^e)(\hat{\mu}_{a},\hat{\mu}_{e}) can be stored for Scov​(Γe)S_{\mathrm{cov}}(\Gamma_{e}) screening, yielding 48 KB per task.

Compute-time footprint.

During streaming, our implementation maintains six float64 accumulators per task for split-sample estimation (Appendix I); Algorithm 1 shows the simplified single-embedding update. This requires:

Streaming state per task=6×m×8​bytes=192​KB at ​m=4096.\text{Streaming state per task}=6\times m\times 8\,\text{bytes}=192\,\text{KB at }m{=}4096. (70)

This is transient during signature construction; once signatures are computed, retrieval only requires the float32 μ^a​e\hat{\mu}_{ae} vectors (16 KB per task). If component embeddings (μ^a,μ^e)(\hat{\mu}_{a},\hat{\mu}_{e}) are also stored (as in FisherAtlas by default), persistent per-task storage is 48 KB, and the FAISS index stores another copy of μ^a​e\hat{\mu}_{ae} for fast search.

Comparison to Task2Vec.

Task2Vec (Achille et al., 2019) stores the diagonal of the Fisher information matrix, requiring O⁡(p)O(p) storage. Here pp is the number of parameters. For a 70B-parameter model, this is approximately 280 GB per task (float32). FisherSketch compresses this to 16 KB—a factor of ∼107{\sim}10^{7} reduction—while preserving pairwise alignment structure via the product-kernel embedding.

R.2 Retrieval Procedure

Prompt signature.

Given a held-out prompt, we compute its signature by streaming over token positions using next-token prediction as the self-supervised objective. Specifically, for a prompt with TT tokens, we extract (at,et)(a_{t},e_{t}) pairs for t=1,…,T−1t=1,\ldots,T-1. Here ata_{t} is the hidden state before the head, and et=softmax⁡(Whead​at)−𝟏yt+1e_{t}=\mathrm{softmax}(W_{\mathrm{head}}a_{t})-\mathbf{1}_{y_{t+1}} is the prediction error. The prompt signature is:

μ^prompt=1T−1​∑t=1T−1Ψm​(at,et),\hat{\mu}_{\mathrm{prompt}}=\frac{1}{T-1}\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\Psi_{m}(a_{t},e_{t}), (71)

where Ψm\Psi_{m} is the factored Random Maclaurin feature map (Section B).

Nearest-neighbor retrieval.

Given an index of KK task signatures {μ^a​e,k}k=1K\{\hat{\mu}_{ae,k}\}_{k=1}^{K}, retrieval returns:

k∗=arg⁡maxk∈[K]⁡cos⁡(μ^prompt,μ^a​e,k)=arg⁡maxk∈[K]​μ^prompt⊤​μ^a​e,k.k^{*}=\arg\max_{k\in[K]}\cos(\hat{\mu}_{\mathrm{prompt}},\hat{\mu}_{ae,k})=\arg\max_{k\in[K]}\hat{\mu}_{\mathrm{prompt}}^{\top}\hat{\mu}_{ae,k}. (72)

Since all embeddings are ℓ2\ell_{2}-normalized, retrieval reduces to a single matrix-vector product.

R.3 Retrieval Evaluation

We evaluate training-free task retrieval on 700 domains from Natural Instructions (Wang et al., 2022) using Llama-3.1-8B signatures at m=4096m{=}4096.

Protocol.

For each domain, we compute a signature from 200 training samples. Evaluation uses held-out prompts (10 per domain, 6974 total). For each held-out prompt, we compute its signature and retrieve the nearest domain.

Results.

FisherSketch achieves 55.5% top-1 accuracy without any training, compared to 51.7% for mean-hidden baselines. Learned probes achieve higher accuracy (62.9%) but require labeled training data and cannot support open-set addition. A pairwise diagnostic over all 244,650 domain pairs shows substantial activation-dark structure: activation similarity and Fisher alignment have Spearman 0.5250.525, and one nearest-neighbor pair has Sa=0.904S_{a}=0.904 but Fisher alignment 0.0880.088. Under the fixed high-activation/low-Fisher nearest-neighbor diagnostic, 121 of 700 domains have an activation-confusable but update-distinct neighbor, while only 11 show the reverse pattern.

R.4 Molecular SMILES Proof of Concept

We include a small scientific-sequence check because shared-vocabulary source selection is especially natural for molecular strings. Using Llama-3.1-8B, we form nine molecular SMILES domains (brominated, chlorinated, fluorinated, highly aromatic, large complex, multi-halogen, nitrogen-heavy, simple aliphatic, and sulfur-containing). FisherSketch signatures use m=2048m=2048 and 180 molecules per domain; transfer is measured by cross-domain perplexity reduction under a 20-example in-context adaptation protocol, averaged over seeds 42–44 with 50 evaluation molecules per target.

The point of this experiment is not to claim a complete chemistry benchmark. It checks the same activation-dark mechanism in a scientific string setting: activation similarity is high and not significant as a transfer predictor at this scale, while the joint FisherSketch score and the error marginal correlate with held-out cross-domain perplexity reduction.

R.5 Dynamic Addition

Protocol.

To add a new domain to an existing index:

  1. 1.

    Collect 200 samples from the new domain.

  2. 2.

    Compute the domain signature via a single forward pass (4.7 seconds on an A100).

  3. 3.

    Append the signature to the index.

No retraining is required—signatures are simply appended.

Evaluation.

We evaluate on four held-out domains (code, medical, legal, math), each added to an existing 674-domain index. Retrieval accuracy on 30 held-out prompts from each new domain:

This is 64×\times faster than retraining a learned classifier on the expanded domain set.

R.6 Error Geometry Tracks Label Overlap

The non-identifiability witness in the main text uses the zero-overlap endpoint for clarity. To check that the effect is not merely a corner case, we run a fixed-representation label-overlap sweep in which activation geometry is held constant while the shared-output label support varies.

The gap grows continuously as overlap decreases. Thus the theorem isolates a clean endpoint of a graded structural phenomenon: representation metrics see the unchanged activation geometry, whereas Fisher alignment also sees label-conditioned error geometry.

Appendix S Additional Validation Diagnostics

S.1 Rho/Delta Calibration for Proxy Reliability

The coupling diagnostic should be used as a warning signal, not as a universal threshold. In the calibration below, lower pairwise ρ\rho and higher δ\delta coincide with larger gaps between exact Fisher alignment and the separable proxy. High ρ\rho is not a guarantee, but low ρ\rho is a practical red flag that separable activation/error proxies may be unreliable.

S.2 Gradient and Diagonal-Fisher Baselines

Table 24 compares FisherSketch with first-moment and diagonal-Fisher baselines in the conditional 100-domain LLM regime. We separate the SRHT row used for the vocabulary-scale backend from a dense-projection check to avoid mixing estimator provenance. FisherSketch improves top-1 over these gradient baselines, while activation-only, error-only, and product proxies remain competitive on rank correlation; this is why the main text avoids unconditional dominance claims.

S.3 Sketch-Dimension Sweep

Table 25 gives empirical guidance for the 100-domain LLM regime. It should not be overinterpreted as a monotone top-1 law: larger sketches stabilize the estimator, but source-selection accuracy also depends on transfer noise, candidate composition, and near ties. The m=4096m=4096 sweep row comes from the SRHT sweep extraction, while Table 24 reports the SRHT EB-shrunk row for the gradient-baseline comparison.

Appendix T Heterogeneous Outputs and Internal-Layer Directional Fisher

Head-level Fisher alignment requires a shared output basis. When label spaces or heads differ, head Fisher is undefined for cross-dataset pairs rather than merely weak. We therefore treat internal-layer Fisher descriptors as gradient diagnostics rather than replacements for representation metrics. Table 26 reports per-target Spearman correlations from the heterogeneous-output ViT-B/16 validation. We use the target-normalized directional descriptors for the internal Fisher rows; raw symmetric block Fisher was near zero or negative in this experiment and should not be interpreted as the successful signal.

One-step LoRA tangent bridge.

For a layer W∈ℝdout×dinW\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\rm out}\times d_{\rm in}} with loss gradient G=∇WℓG=\nabla_{W}\ell, a LoRA parameterization writes the update as B​ABA with B∈ℝdout×rB\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\rm out}\times r} and A∈ℝr×dinA\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{\rm in}} (Hu et al., 2022). At the common initialization used in many LoRA implementations (B=0B=0, AA fixed), one infinitesimal gradient step gives B+=−η​G​A⊤B^{+}=-\eta GA^{\top} and hence the induced weight update

Δ​W=B+​A=−η​G​(A⊤​A).\Delta W=B^{+}A=-\eta G(A^{\top}A).

Therefore, for a fixed LoRA tangent subspace, one-step update inner products are

⟨Δ​Wi,Δ​Wj⟩F=η2​tr​((A⊤​A)​Gi⊤​Gj​(A⊤​A)),\langle\Delta W_{i},\Delta W_{j}\rangle_{F}=\eta^{2}\,\mathrm{tr}\!\left((A^{\top}A)G_{i}^{\top}G_{j}(A^{\top}A)\right),

i.e., a gradient/Fisher alignment after a fixed low-rank projection. This is the intended bridge between internal Fisher descriptors and LoRA transfer. It does not characterize multi-step nonlinear LoRA training, and Table 26 should be read as diagnostic evidence rather than a dominance claim over CKA.

The stored descriptor is still mm floats per task per layer after pooling, but internal shared-token collection has a larger transient state. At n=500n=500 and m=4096m=4096, the transient sketch-feature state is about 8 MiB per task per layer in fp32; in this run, four internal layers across eight models used about 250 MiB of transient feature state and peaked at 4.19 GiB GPU memory during Fisher collection. For the QKV validation, pooled sketch descriptors store about 432×432\times fewer values than saving all per-example QKV gradients.

Appendix U Verbalizer-Shift Experiment Details

This section provides full experimental details for the verbalizer-shift controlled experiment (Section 6.2 of the main text). This experiment demonstrates that FisherSketch predicts transfer in a regime where representation-only metrics are maximally uninformative.

U.1 Experimental Design

Core insight.
